Russia’s War Losses in Ukraine Exceed 2 Million, Independent Estimate Finds
Russia’s mounting battlefield losses are reaching a staggering scale, with new estimates revealing how heavily Moscow has paid for its prolonged war against Ukraine.
Russia may have suffered between 1.4 million and 2.1 million military casualties, including as many as 770,000 soldiers killed, since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Economist on October 30, an updated statistical assessment estimates Russian military deaths at between 374,000 and 770,000, with the remaining casualties consisting of wounded personnel.
The figures represent a substantial increase from the publication’s previous estimates. In July 2025, The Economist assessed Russia’s total casualties at 900,000 to 1.3 million, including 190,000 to 350,000 deaths. By May 2026, those estimates had risen to 1.1–1.5 million casualties and 280,000–518,000 deaths.
The Economist’s calculations combine Western intelligence assessments, defense ministry data, independent research, and battlefield tracking. Russia does not publish comprehensive official casualty figures, making independent verification difficult.
Despite these losses, Moscow continues its military operations. The Economist also reported that Ukrainian forces had recaptured approximately 73 square kilometers of territory over the previous three months.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 31 that Russian forces had suffered another 1,670 personnel losses over the previous 24 hours, bringing Ukraine’s cumulative estimate to approximately 1,588,170 since February 2022.
The Ukrainian military also reported the loss of two Russian air defense systems and 206 vehicles and fuel tankers during the same period.

Cambodia sees rise in drug arrests, drop in seizures in first 10 months of 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:22:35 CST
17:22:35 KST

PHNOM PENH, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia reported a rise in drug-related arrests but a drop in overall narcotics seizures during the first 10 months of 2026, according to an Anti-Drug Department (ADP) report released on Sunday.
The Southeast Asian nation detained 25,360 drug suspects during the January-October period, a 16.3 percent increase compared to 21,800 during the same period last year. Foreign nationals made up 1,248 of the detainees, representing 25 different nationalities.
Of the total suspects, 48.3 percent were classified as drug traffickers, manufacturers, possessors, or transporters, while 51.7 percent were recorded as drug users.
"Authorities confiscated 4.26 tons of illicit drugs and 537 kilograms of dry cannabis between Jan. 1 and Oct. 31, 2026," the report said, adding that this marked a decrease from the 5.48 tons of narcotics and 516 kilograms of dry marijuana seized during the same timeframe in 2025.
Other seized evidence included 73 pistols and 27 homemade rifles, the report said, adding that the confiscated narcotics largely consisted of ketamine, ecstasy, heroin, crystal methamphetamine, methamphetamine pills, cocaine, and cathinone.
Cambodia does not impose the death penalty for drug offenses. Under national law, individuals convicted of trafficking more than 80 grams of illicit drugs can face life imprisonment. ■

Protocol upgrading China-Peru FTA takes effect
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:22:31 CST
17:22:31 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- The protocol upgrading the China-Peru free trade agreement (FTA) took effect on Sunday, according to China's Ministry of Commerce (MOC).
China and Peru launched negotiations on the upgrade in November 2018 and signed the protocol on Nov. 14, 2024. The original FTA was signed in 2009 and took effect in 2010.
The protocol improves seven existing chapters of the original FTA, covering rules of origin, customs procedures and trade facilitation, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, intellectual property rights, trade in services, temporary entry of business personnel, and investment, the MOC said in an online statement.
The protocol also adds five new chapters on standards and conformity assessment cooperation, competition policy, e-commerce, global supply chains, and environment and trade.
The two sides also set out future provisions for negotiations on negative lists for trade in services and investment, aimed at further raising openness in these areas, according to the statement.
The China-Peru FTA was the first comprehensive free trade agreement China signed with a Latin American country.
China is Peru's largest trading partner, largest export market and largest source of imports, while Peru is China's fourth-largest trading partner in Latin America and an important investment destination, said an MOC official.
Under the protocol, the new chapter on global supply chains encourages multimodal transport and the development of foreign trade logistics corridors and infrastructure, an innovative arrangement that signals the two countries' commitment to keeping supply chains stable and unimpeded.
The chapter on standards and conformity assessment cooperation establishes a dedicated cooperation mechanism and sets out an intended cooperation list, creating a platform for mutual recognition of standards that is expected to reduce trade costs for enterprises.
The two sides agreed to launch negotiations on negative lists for trade in services and investment within two years after the protocol takes effect, in a bid to further raise the level of openness in these areas and continue to tap the potential of bilateral trade and investment, the official added.
Since the original FTA came into force in 2010, it has played an important role in promoting bilateral economic and trade cooperation. Two-way trade rose from 6.4 billion U.S. dollars in 2009 to 50.4 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, an increase of nearly seven times, official data show.
The protocol is expected to help tap further opportunities for bilateral trade and investment cooperation, provide a better business environment for enterprises of both countries and inject new vitality into bilateral economic and trade relations, the MOC said. ■

Chinese research ships map Taiwan’s undersea infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:22:25 UTC
17:22:25 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — China has ramped up undersea mapping operations in waters east and south of Taiwan to advance its ability to seize it, according to a Wall Street Journal report.
Chinese research vessels are surveying the subsurface landscape to help its submarines and underwater drones, which could be used to blockade or halt US intervention, Bryan Clark, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, said.
Surveying around Taiwan increased following an announcement by Japan and the Philippines in May of plans to hold discussions on overlapping maritime boundaries in waters east of Taiwan. The two countries have stepped up defense cooperation in response to what they see as threats from Beijing.
“China is capitalizing on the boundary talks as a pretext for what it likely wanted to do anyway: that is, to ratchet up the pressure on Taiwan,” said Allen Zhang, a Heritage Foundation research assistant. “Beijing has long sought legal cover for its gray-zone tactics—coercive activities short of lethal force—and research vessels fit that mold quite well,” Zhang added.
Su Chih-chieh (蘇志杰), an associate professor at National Taiwan University’s Institute of Oceanography, said, “They are launching research ships as fast as dropping dumplings into a pot. Taiwan is having a really hard time catching up right now.”
Taiwan has only five ships actively carrying out its own maritime research. It added two ships in August.
Chen Chung-ling (陳璋玲), president of the National Academy of Marine Research in Kaohsiung, said Taiwanese research efforts demonstrate Taiwan’s commitment to security, WSJ reported. “The more you understand the ocean, the more you can get from it,” she said.
However, Liao Te-yu (陳璋玲), director general of the Taiwan Ocean Research Institute, warned that Taiwan’s research ships are more academically focused and do not necessarily align with defense needs. “We actually understand very little about the waters surrounding us,” Liao said.
China also uses research vessels to locate telecommunications cables, which are another target in a conflict, WSJ cited analysts as saying.
“They’re trying to see what the undersea infrastructure looks like, because they probably want the ability to cut off Taiwan from outside communications if they can as part of a coercion campaign,” Clark said.
WSJ cited a Center for Strategic and International Studies report as saying China-linked research vessels “spent a disproportionately large share of their observed time near critical infrastructure compared with research vessels from 47 other countries.”

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Starlux Airlines and its codeshare partner Etihad Airways announced an expansion of their partnership to include their frequent flyer programs on Thursday.
Effective immediately, members of both airlines can now redeem their accumulated miles for award tickets on flights operated by the other airline. They can also earn miles on eligible flights and claim missing mileage credits retroactively, giving them greater flexibility in earning and using their rewards, according to Starlux.
Starlux CEO Glenn Chai (翟健華) said the airline remained committed to enhancing the flying experience for its members and creating more travel options through deeper cooperation with international airline partners.
The expanded partnership marks an important milestone in the relationship between the two airlines, Chai said, per Starlux. By combining their route networks and frequent flyer programs, Starlux COSMILE members can make more flexible use of their miles and travel to more than 120 destinations worldwide via Etihad's hub in Abu Dhabi, Chai said.
He said he hoped the partnership would enhance the benefits and value of the COSMILE program.
Etihad Guest Managing Director Mark Potter said each step in the partnership with Starlux is aimed at providing members with greater mileage rewards when traveling across the two airlines' networks, per Starlux. Members can now both earn miles and redeem them for award tickets, further strengthening the partnership and creating additional value for frequent flyers, Potter said.

Iran designates UK’s Royal Navy, Royal Air Force as terrorist organizations — MFA

TEHRAN, November 1. /TASS/. Iran has designated the UK’s Royal Navy and Royal Air Force as terrorist organizations and has classified the British foreign intelligence service MI6 as a hostile group, the Foreign Ministry said.
According to its statement, "the British foreign intelligence service (MI6) is subject to Note 2 of Article 1 of the law ‘On Tightening Penalties for Espionage and Collaboration with the Zionist Regime and Hostile Countries Against National Security and Interests’ as a hostile group, and the provisions of this law regarding it will apply" as of the publication of the statement.
The document noted that these measures were adopted by the Supreme National Security Council in response to London's hostile actions over the past year, which include participating in the US and Israeli war against Iran by providing bases and facilities on its territory. The document also referenced the July 13 decision to designate the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC, the elite units of Iran’s armed forces) as a terrorist organization on July 13 under the 2026 Law on State Threats. The ministry emphasized that the UK’s Royal Navy and Royal Air Force fall under the law on retaliatory measures in connection with the US designation of the IRGC as a terrorist organization and are, on this basis, considered terrorist entities. The statement stressed that responsibility for the consequences lies with the UK government.

The authorization does not grant permanent immigration status.

Trump's remarks come amid diplomatic tensions between Washington and Brasilia, with Brazilian officials seeking clarification about the circumstances of Bolsonaro's arrival in the US.

FBI blames North Korea for $6.3 billion Binance crypto hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:15:37 UTC
17:15:37 KST

According to the CISA, TraderTraitor is a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group that has been associated with cryptocurrency thefts and cyberattack tactics since at least 2020.
The US' Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has accused North Korea of being behind a major hack targeting the Binance cryptocurrency exchange earlier this week.
Binance suffered what its co-CEO Richard Teng described as a "complex attack" that saw hackers gain access to its hot wallets and steal $6.3 billion in digital assets.
"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the FBI said in a statement on Saturday.
"The FBI refers to this specific North Korean malicious cyber activity as 'TraderTraitor,'" it continued, adding that it had observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets into Ethereum and that it expected these to be "further laundered by converting them using DeFi and instant swap services."
According to the US' Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), TraderTraitor is a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group that has been associated with cryptocurrency thefts and cyberattack tactics since at least 2020.
It is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which the CISA says has carried out attacks against a variety of blockchain and cryptocurrency industry targets using spearphishing campaigns and malware.
Following the Binance attack, the exchange announced that it had suspended deposits and withdrawals as its team carried out security checks, froze funds and worked with law enforcement operatives to investigate the incident.
The company said that it has now covered around 90% of the impacted amount stolen in the hack and that withdrawals were resuming "in phases."
Binance said the remaining 10% of tokens were "less liquid," meaning they could take longer to buy.
In a video statement posted on social media, Teng said the company was "committed to covering all hacked losses through our company funds."
"Your assets are safe," he added.

Donald Trump loses allies after elections in Serbia and Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:11:00 UTC
17:11:00 KST

Donald Trump loses allies after elections in Serbia and Brazil
November 1, 2026
The midterm elections in the United States are just around the corner: On Tuesday, November 3, American voters will choose their representatives to the US Congress. The right-wing-conservative Republican party of President Donald Trump currently has a majority in both chambers.
But in other parts of the world election results are already in. The majority of voters in both Serbia and Brazil cast their ballots for left-wing parties. Those results will not influence the midterms in the US, but the victories of the Student List in Serbia and the incumbent president, Luiz Inacio "Lula" da Silva, in Brazil are bad news for Trump all the same.
In Serbia, he has lost an important European ally in outgoing president Aleksandar Vucic. And in Brazil, the Trump camp had been hoping Flavio Bolsonaro would triumph.
"Trump was a strong supporter of both Jair Bolsonaro, the Trump-like figure who served as president before Lula defeated him in 2022, and of his son Flavio," says Lawrence J. Haas, a senior fellow for US foreign policy at the American Foreign Policy Council, who was communications director for Al Gore, Bill Clinton's vice president, in the 1990s. "Trump wasn't happy about the defeat of either Bolsonaro," he continues, "and he doesn't feel warmly toward Lula. So relations will remain cool at best."
Trump declared Brazilian election looked "rigged"
Flavio Bolsonaro is under investigation in Brazil for alleged corruption and money laundering. After losing the election, he fled the country for Florida. The US State Department granted him and his family entry visas in spite of the pending legal action.
Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat. Instead, he claims there were irregularities in the vote. This is very reminiscent of Trump, who continues to claim – falsely – that Joe Biden and the Democratic Party "stole" the US election in 2020. Trump's comments on Bolsonaro's defeat sounded very familiar. "It looked like another rigged election, frankly," the US president said on Monday. "Elections have to be indisputable – and it looked very bad to me."
Good relations with Putin ally Vucic
Aleksandar Vucic had ruled Serbia as president with an iron fist since 2017. He resigned just before these elections in order to stand as prime minister, a role he previously held from 2014 to 2017. Vucic has commented in the past that he and President Trump are like-minded people. Trump's eldest son, Donald Jr., visited Vucic in Belgrade shortly before the US presidential elections in November 2024, and again a few months later.
The US Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC), which is closely connected with Trump's MAGA ("Make America Great Again") movement, recently announced that it was organizing a meeting in Belgrade in November, at which Vucic was to be a keynote speaker. It is unclear whether this is still the case.
Another thing Vucic and Trump have in common is that the soon-to-be-ex-president of Serbia has a much more positive attitude toward Russian president Vladimir Putin than do most other European heads of state. Vucic did not join EU countries in imposing sanctions on Russia after it launched its war of aggression against Ukraine. Belgrade still buys Russian raw materials, and Serbian state media under Vucic presented a more positive image of Russia than of the EU.
Trump also seems increasingly inclined toward Moscow. His special envoy Steve Witkoff recently described Putin as a "humanitarian," while, in an interview, Trump himself openly admitted that he got on better with Putin than with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The end of the Vucic government now means that Trump has lost one of his few allies in Europe who takes a similar view.
Israel: Outcome still unclear
There's still a chance of an outcome in the Israeli elections that might be to Trump's liking. With more than 96% of votes counted, the right-wing bloc led by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu is in the lead. However, Trump ally Netanyahu has lost his majority, and the coalition negotiations will be very difficult.
Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies since well before February this year, when they joined forces to launch a war against Iran. In 2018, during his first term in office, Trump moved the US embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. This was controversial, because both Israel and Palestinians claim Jerusalem as their capital. Netanyahu's camp welcomed the decision.
Today, the United States is still by far Israel's most important partner, while Israel is an important regional ally for the US. It is not clear what their relationship would be like with a different Israeli government. If Netanyahu remains in power, little, if anything, will change.
No rosy prospects for Trump in the midterms
With Vucic's defeat, Trump has lost a loyal ally. And Lula's victory means, for him, that a disagreeable president remains in power. None of this is good for Trump, but foreign policy analyst Haas said it won't influence the important midterm elections in his country. "Americans will be voting [...] on the basis of issues that affect them, and how they feel about the party in power."
But this doesn't bode well for Trump, either. "Trump has the lowest approval rating of any president on the eve of a mid-term election since Harry Truman in 1946," Haas explained. "Americans are very concerned about issues of affordability, [and] they strongly oppose the US-Iran war."
Benjamin Alvarez Gruber in Miami contributed to this report, which was originally written in German.

Judge rules on Trump’s defamation lawsuit against WSJ over Epstein letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

08:08:13 UTC
17:08:13 KST

Judge rules on Trump’s defamation lawsuit against WSJ over Epstein letter
A federal judge has permanently dismissed US President Donald Trump’s $10 billion amended defamation case against the Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a report about his letter to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
In July 2025, the WSJ published an article describing a sexually suggestive note, which Trump allegedly presented to the disgraced financier for his 50th birthday in 2003. It reportedly appeared in a book of congratulatory letters put together by Ghislaine Maxwell, who is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence for her participation in Epstein’s sex-trafficking scheme.
The note, which, among other things, said: “Happy Birthday – and may every day be another wonderful secret,” contained several lines of typed text framed by a hand-drawn outline of what looks to be a nude woman. A signature resembling the one used by Trump appeared in the area where the figure’s pelvic region might be.
Following the publication, the US president vigorously denied the authorship of the raunchy birthday card, claiming: “This is not me. This is a fake thing. I never wrote a picture in my life. I don’t draw pictures of women.”
Trump’s initial defamation case against the Wall Street Journal and Murdoch’s News Corp., which owns the outlet, was rejected by US District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami in April. However, he allowed the president’s team to fix the legal defects that he had identified and file another complaint.
On Saturday, the same judge threw out Trump’s second attempt to sue the WSJ and Murdoch, saying that “as with his first attempt, he has failed” to prove that the defendants acted with actual malice when they reported on the birthday card.
Gayles disagreed with Trump’s lawyers, who argued that the outlet should have dropped the story as soon as the president denied his involvement with Epstein. “That is not what the actual malice standard requires and runs afoul of the First Amendment,” he wrote in a 20-page ruling.
The judge dismissed the case “with prejudice,” meaning that it cannot be refiled again.
A spokesperson for the WSJ’s publisher, Dow Jones & Co., said in a statement that it’s “pleased with the court’s decision.”
The representative of Trump’s legal team insisted that “the president will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions.” A source told CBS News that the ruling by Gayles will likely be appealed.
Trump has repeatedly denied having been friendly with Epstein, who died in a New York jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex-trafficking charges. However, the US president’s name is mentioned on at least 3,000 occasions in a massive trove of files related to the investigation of Epstein’s case, which had been released by the US Department of Justice last year.

Germany's search for a nuclear waste site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:06:00 UTC
17:06:00 KST

Germany's search for a nuclear waste site
November 1, 2026
Hardly any environmental and political challenge is as complex as the disposal of radioactive waste from nuclear power plants. In almost all of the world's nuclear-powered nations — some 31 countries currently operate or once operated nuclear power plants — the issue remains largely unresolved, despite the fact that the first large-scale nuclear power plant went online in the Soviet Union in 1954.
Finland recently became the first country in the world to approve a repository for radioactive nuclear waste. Located 400 meters underground on an island in western Finland, it is situated at the site of one of the country's two nuclear power plants. The project took around 40 years to complete.
Germany's search underway for ten years
Yet in every other country, including Germany, the problem remains unresolved. To make an everyday analogy: The garbage has already been placed outside for collection, but the garbage truck has not yet arrived. There is simply no landfill to take it to. It is not a pleasant sight, yet hardly anyone wants to live near such a site.
Germany has made some progress: The specially established Federal Company for Radioactive Waste Disposal (BGE) has now been searching for a suitable site for almost ten years, one that, like the Finnish repository, would be located deep underground.
Most experts have long agreed on one point: Nuclear waste, especially the spent fuel elements from nuclear power plants, which will remain radioactive for many thousands of years, must be stored underground.
Only 5% of Germany's territory remains under consideration
Germany hopes to identify a site for a final repository by 2050. But that is still a long way off, which is why Environment Minister Carsten Schneider of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) wants to examine whether the search process can be accelerated.
And, the government says, at least there is a roadmap in place. "Russia, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Japan have not yet advanced their procedures as far as we have," ministry spokesperson, Stephan Gabriel Haufe, said at a regular government press conference this week. "Finland is certainly the country making the fastest progress worldwide. But Germany is among the leading countries."
This week, the BGE announced that only 5% of Germany's land area, spread across 11 of the country's 16 states, remains under consideration as a potential site for a final repository. The agency is consulting geologists, nuclear experts, and physicists, as well as citizens and politicians. What is already clear, is that the nuclear waste generated during decades of nuclear power production will remain in Germany.
Germany has phased out nuclear power
Most of the waste is currently stored at or near the sites where it was generated. These include the 19 former nuclear power plants currently being decommissioned, as well as several research facilities.
In 2011, following the reactor disaster in Fukushima, Japan, Germany decided to phase out the commercial use of nuclear energy, and the last nuclear power plant was shut down in 2023. The waste, however, remains in interim storage.
"It must be shown that a repository will remain safe over a very long period of time," said BGE spokesperson Dagmar Dehmer. "In Finland, that means 100,000 years; in Germany, Switzerland, and France, one million years. But no matter how far into the future scientists project, the effort involved is enormous. It requires a detailed analysis of developments over time, the interactions between geology and technology, and the decay of radionuclides, as well as an assessment of how these factors affect safety."
400 meters underground, protected by a rock barrier
The procedure is indeed complex: First, potential sites are evaluated for their geological suitability. Will the rock formation remain stable at a depth of 400 meters? Could groundwater become contaminated? The goal is to identify a location where the repository would be surrounded by a rock layer around 100 meters thick, providing a natural barrier. Suitable geological formations include layers of clay, granite, and rock salt.
As the requirements become progressively stricter, fewer and fewer potential sites remain under consideration. Other factors, such as proximity to major cities, come into play only much later in the process. Few communities are likely to welcome a repository for radioactive waste, whether in an urban area or in the countryside.
Dehmer: 'Finland has great trust in government action'
Building and maintaining trust is also part of Dehmer's job. She often has to explain why it is important to deal with the legacy of the nuclear age, regardless of where people stand on nuclear energy.
Finland has succeeded in doing so, Dehmer believes. "There is a high level of trust in government action in Finland," she said. "The country's supervisory and licensing authority, STUK, is one of its most respected institutions. Germany can learn from Finland by remaining consistent, avoiding frequent changes in direction, and demonstrating the patience needed to achieve a successful outcome."
The disposal of nuclear waste is extremely expensive. Even today, the search for a final repository and the storage of nuclear waste at former reactor sites cost around €1.4 billion ($1.6 billion) per year.
Experts estimate that the final repository itself will cost roughly €14 billion ($16.4 billion) once completed. If all goes according to plan, 28,000 cubic meters of radioactive waste will eventually be stored deep underground on a permanent basis.
This article was originally published in German.

Rail passenger travel in the European Union reached a record 457 billion passenger-kilometres (pkm) in 2025, according to the EU's statistics office, Eurostat, WAM reported.
The figure was up 2.6 percent from the previous year, reaching its highest level since data collection began in 2004. The figures exclude passenger transport by metro, tram and suburban rail services.

Russia has lost 1,590,270 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 31.
The number includes 2,100 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,451 tanks, 25,622 armored combat vehicles, 168,739 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,755 artillery systems, 2,249 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,730 air defense systems, 452 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,054 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
On Oct. 29, the General Staff reported that October 2026 was the deadliest month for Russian combat losses since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

‘Progress takes time’: Stonewall CEO on turning down the heat on the trans debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:00:06 UTC
17:00:06 KST

Transgender people fear social acceptance is going into reverse and some are retreating from public spaces, according to the first major analysis since last year’s supreme court ruling in the UK on the definition of a woman.
The Stonewall survey finds that while almost half of British LGBTQ+ people feel more accepted by society than a decade ago, 58% of trans+ people – and 75% of trans women – feel less so. Almost half of trans+ people now avoid certain bars and restaurants where they do not feel safe, 37% avoid single-sex spaces such as toilets and changing rooms, and 29% avoid exercise classes or sports teams. A striking 80% are pessimistic about the future of equality, in stark contrast to the net hope expressed when the same question was asked in 2017.
Last year’s ruling that sex in law means biological sex was a landmark moment for gender-critical campaigners, who had argued that trans access to single-sex spaces from changing rooms to prisons was endangering women, and who saw the verdict as a relief and vindication. But it has had significant consequences for trans lives, said Stonewall’s chief executive, Simon Blake, citing warnings that trans people may avoid going to hospital under new NHS guidance that they should use wards matching their birth sex.
“If you feel as though there’s guidance which is impacting on your ability to participate in public life, to get treatment when you’re unwell, to be able to use the toilets which you have been using successfully for 10 years at work, when it feels as though your rights are secondary rather than equal – that’s going to make you feel incredibly pessimistic,” Blake told the Guardian.
Recently, he said, he had been out with friends for a drink. “They were frightened about going to the toilet – each time that someone went to the toilet, it was a question mark. That’s not the way anybody should be expected to live.” He is calling on government to monitor the ruling’s impact and act on any harms revealed.
The survey, to be published on Monday, also found 22% of LGB and 32% of trans respondents reported having attempted suicide at some point in their lives.
“What so often people who have often experienced suicidal ideation say is ‘I don’t want to be dead, I just don’t want this any longer,’” said Blake. “I had three people over the weekend say we are very, very close to leaving this country – friends, colleagues (feeling) that this is a hostile country to be in.”
Gender-critical campaigners, however, consider the ruling not as a rollback but as a clarification of what the Equality Act always meant. They argue it has restored women’s ability to have single-sex toilets, changing rooms, wards and sports without having to justify each exclusion case by case, and that uncertainty for trans people about their current position partly reflects organisations, including Stonewall, having previously claimed the law said something it did not.
Stonewall was not, Blake stressed, aiming to overturn the supreme court ruling. “We understand that this is the law. But we also want to ensure that trans people are protected and, along with other organisations, we are looking at what that would look like.”
Discriminating against trans people on the grounds of gender reassignment remains illegal, he noted, and the supreme court judges argued their ruling should not be seen as one side in a bitter culture war triumphing over the other. “It’s on government and our watchdogs and everybody with responsibility to understand the impact, and where there is a negative impact to take action.”
If this approach seems unduly meek to some, Blake has reason to tread carefully. A former Stonewall trustee who cut his teeth on successful campaigns for equal marriage and the age of consent, he returned in 2024 to an organisation in crisis. Institutions from Whitehall departments to the BBC had quit its workplace diversity scheme – a key source of income – amid controversy over Stonewall’s tactics and the quality of its legal advice.
To rebuild public trust, Blake sought inspiration from Stonewall’s less combative early years, getting veterans such as the actor Ian McKellen – who co-founded Stonewall in 1989 – to talk to staff about winning hearts and minds in a hostile era. “Progress takes time. You’ve got to coalesce, to convene, sometimes you’ve got to be pragmatic,” he said of the new strategy.
“Our first value was about having the courage to do what we think is in the best interest of the LGBTQ+ community and sometimes that will mean absolutely pushing really, really quickly, and sometimes it might be understanding that there is a first step.” If the goal is now to air genuine disagreements without vitriol and agree on a way forward, that’s exactly what Stonewall managed to do in the past: “We were having the same conversations around equal marriage, the age of consent.”
For 52-year-old Blake, growing up gay in the 1990s was a “terrifying” experience. “When I came out to my parents their first thought was ‘Christ he won’t be alive for very much longer’, because of HIV.”
That was arguably the easy part. “In your formative years, when you’re learning to love yourself, every single day somebody or something is telling you either through explicit words or through silence that you’re not good enough; that you’re a danger to children; that you shouldn’t be allowed to teach … it’s just confusing. The (feeling of), ‘I’m a nice person, I don’t understand why you’d want to be frightened of me, what am I missing?’ – that sadly, despite the progress, is still happening.”
That the ban on conversion practices currently under parliamentary scrutiny is trans-inclusive matters to him personally because “it’s saying you don’t need to be changed, you’re good enough”, something he needed to hear as a teenager.
Blake credits Stonewall with transforming his life as a gay man. So why does he think its trans advocacy ended in so many feeling worse off?
“People knew less around trans issues and non-binary issues a decade ago, and it wasn’t part of a culture war which had been played out for a long period of time, people’s lives being talked about as if they’re abstract rather than they are lived,” Blake said, arguing that made trans people feel dehumanised.
Was the defensive “no debate” position some activists then took, refusing even to acknowledge any conflict between trans rights and women’s rights, counter-productive? “What I recall that period to be was saying that there is a reality which is that trans people exist and that actually trans people should be around the table having the conversation, and that when trans people went around the table in some of those conversations it felt really difficult and therefore (they) didn’t feel able to participate … everybody needs to be able to have questions, we need to be able to have discussion, but we do have to find ways to do that without heat.”
If that seems a forlorn hope in a climate where Reform-led councils are taking down rainbow flags and scrapping diversity training, Blake chooses to focus on the trade unions who rode to the financial rescue after Durham county council defunded their local Pride event.
“What you keep on seeing is most people – what I like to call the moral majority – saying ‘we just want to get on, we just want to live our lives, and for other people to be able to do so’.” But it’s precisely that ability to live ordinary lives that, according to his research, some trans people feel is slipping away.

English children’s homes are in crisis. Does Denmark hold the answers?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:00:05 UTC
17:00:05 KST

In a quiet suburb on the outskirts of Copenhagen sits a large white house, set back from the road behind a purple-leaved plum tree. It looks much like the rest of the buildings on the street and there is little outward sign this is Josephine Schneider’s House, considered one of the best children’s homes in the world.
Danish children’s homes are often cited as the gold standard of children’s residential care globally. They are now being studied by the British government as it tries to create a roadmap out of the crisis in which its own children’s home system has become mired.
Last year there were 669 children living in illegal, unregistered children’s homes across England, with councils paying more than £125m of taxpayers’ money to keep them there.
Overall spending on children’s homes soared 96% in five years to over £3.1bn in 2023-24, while standards have dropped, private equity firms are cashing in and a growing number of children are being sent to homes hundreds of miles away.
The situation is dire, the children’s minister, Josh MacAlister, admits. “We now have this shadow system of unregistered, illegal homes, which is certainly not providing therapeutic support and the costs are huge,” he said. “We need big changes, a major shake up, and I spend as many hours as I can a week on children’s social care reform.”
Earlier this week, MacAlister visited Denmark to see how its children’s homes operate and what can be exported back to England, as part of a Department for Education review into how the sector can be improved.
The 140-year-old Josephine Schneider’s House, which houses 12 children and young adults aged six to 23, is starkly different from many British equivalents.
In the centre of the house is a spacious kitchen staffed by the head chef, Rasmus, who cooks the children’s meals, lunch boxes and after-school snacks – pizza rolls are a particular favourite. He works with the children himself, encouraging them to help make the food and come grocery shopping.
The rest of the staff are all degree-level professionals in social pedagogy, a discipline focusing on psychology, child development and ethics, and they strive to recreate a traditional family home by cooking, eating and socialising with the children.
“We don’t have an in-house therapist but everything we do is therapeutic,” said Mads Sørensen, deputy director of the home.
One member of staff sleeps in the house at night and wakes the children up each day at 7am. “We ask them how they like to be woken up, to help them feel safe and create that predictability, make their nervous system calm a bit,” Sørensen said.
Many of the children here have suffered physical, emotional and social neglect, and issues such as self-harm, insomnia and eating disorders are common.
Unlike children’s homes in England, where many children report being isolated and cut off from family and friends, here children are encouraged to have friends stay at the weekends and holidays, there are regular parents evenings, including a Christmas banquet.
Each child also has a team of two to three staff members working with them on their education and wellbeing. In a semi-independent flat on the top floor live the older residents, aged 17 and above, who have their own living area and kitchen as they start to transition into adulthood.
The young people buy their own food and do their own chores, under the guidance of staff, preparing them for independent life beyond the home. They are allowed to stay in the home up until the age of 23, and encouraged to return for regular visits beyond that age.
This is a far cry from children’s homes in England, which teenagers must leave as soon as they turn 18, part of the cliff-edge loss of support that is causing the early deaths of care leavers.
MacAlister said he may change this. “Getting rid of the really binary date of birth point to decide where you live is something I’m really persuaded by,” he said. “I hear of children being forced to move when they turn 18, even if they’re in the middle of sitting their A-levels. We have to move away from that.”
He also wants to import some of the culture from Danish children’s homes, particularly their focus on personal growth and maintaining family relationships.
“A lot of residential care in England is actually about adults containing their own anxiety and concerns about teenagers, and that’s a really poor model,” MacAlister said. “The first question is always ‘how do we protect ourselves from risk?’ which is not what we should be asking first. It’s very different here in Denmark.”
The quality of staff is crucial, and something at the heart of the ongoing review, which is being led by Emmanuel Akpan-Inwang, the director of Lighthouse Pedagogy Trust, which runs a children’s home in Sutton based on pedagogy principles.
“What’s interesting about Denmark is working in a children’s home is a career that people really want to do,” he said. “It’s competitive. Homes are able to select really great people. They support and train them. They stay in the sector for long periods of time.
“But we can’t simply lift and shift the system to England. The Danes have spent more than 40 years developing it. But we can learn from it.”
At Josephine Schneider’s House, many staff members have been there 10 years or longer. In the UK, about 53% of children’s home staff have worked in the sector for three years or less. Poor pay, working conditions and a lack of training force many to leave the sector early.
But underpinning Danish children’s homes is extensive state funding – a third of homes are publicly owned, 42% are not-for-profit and 27% are private profit.
By contrast, in England, 83% of children’s homes places are now privately run, with some operators recording profit margins of more than 20%.
The government has passed laws giving itself the power to intervene and cap profits by private providers but has yet to use it, with MacAlister saying they need to wait for a new “market oversight body” to provide full transparency of exactly how much money is being made before they can push ahead.
The government of Wales is moving more quickly, and will ban all for-profit providers in children’s social care by 2030. But MacAlister said it would not be easy to replicate this in England, where numbers are much bigger.
“We need to massively boost local authorities so they can take back control of the whole purchasing process, curb demand by making sure more children can live in foster homes or kinship arrangements, and shape a system on our terms, not one that is driven by profit,” MacAlister said.

Cutting corners: Lithuanian artist builds unique home inspired by Gaudi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Rimas Navickas, 61, is nearing completion of a long-held dream in the Dubysa Valley – a distinctive oval-shaped house with no straight corners.
The house, built in the village of Padvarninkai in the northern Kelmė district, isn't finished yet, but Navickas and his wife, musician Rita, have already spent the entire summer there. They would stay through the winter, too, but some of the windows are still missing.
Inspired by a legendary architect
Those who know Navickas were not particularly surprised by the flowing curves of his home – for several decades, Navickas has been known for creating furniture from solid oak with irregular, flowing shapes.
Navickas, who holds a diploma in technology education, began making furniture out of necessity – he wanted to furnish a house he had renovated himself with pieces of his own design.
The artist was influenced by the work of the legendary Catalan architect Antoni Gaudí (1852–1926). Gaudí became world-famous for his buildings, furniture, lighting and parks inspired by natural forms.
His dream of living close to nature began to take shape nearly two decades ago, when Navickas discovered the spectacular Dubysa Valley.
It took several meetings with the landowner before she agreed to sell a 1.2-hectare plot. Navickas and his wife soon bought several more plots, eventually acquiring a total of 16 hectares.
The new owners landscaped the estate, digging ponds and setting aside half the land for a park. In just two and a half months, the couple planted more than 1,000 oak trees and over 4,000 pines, spruces and birches in the valley. The park was designed around the couple’s love of walking and running.
“The children joke that I will have repaid nature many times over for all the oak trees I have used to make furniture,” Navickas says.
Initially, the artist planned to build a round, straw house covered in clay, but eventually abandoned the idea.
Instead, he was fascinated by ferrocement, a technology invented in France in the mid-19th century that involves coating wire mesh with a cement-based mixture. Joseph Louis Lambot first used the technique on his estate in 1848, creating a boat from cement mortar and metal mesh.
The renowned Catalan architect Gaudí also made extensive use of the technology in his organic architecture.
Navickas first built a vegetable storage building and covered its roof with a thick layer of soil. The strength of the structure was put to an accidental test when a tractor driver forgot the owner's warning and drove a 24-tonne excavator onto the roof.
The unintended test showed just how strong the structure was: not a single crack appeared.
There was only one aspect of the technique that the artist disliked – the metal reinforcement placed inside the concrete shell.
“In my opinion, steel suppresses the natural flow of energy from both the Earth and the universe,” he says.
Navickas found a solution, replacing the metal reinforcement with fibreglass rods.
Built with his own hands
The original plan was for a 300-square-metre building, but the final version was almost half that size, at 185 square metres. For a family whose children have grown up and left home, it is more than enough.
“I brought together all the knowledge, experience and skills I have acquired throughout my life,” says the artist, who settled on the ninth version of the house before going on to refine it further.
Navickas did almost everything himself, which made the process lengthy. When it came to calculating the frame's connections, he turned to his son Paulius, a specialist in metalworking and fabrication.
Using computer software, Paulius calculated where and how the frame should be joined and secured to the slab foundation. He later helped shape it using fibreglass reinforcement rods.
Other family members also helped tie the reinforcement together, while Navickas did everything else himself.
The only work he had to hire professionals for was the plumbing and electrical installation. “If I don't know how to do something, I don't do it,” Navickas says.
The house's concrete-coated frame was sprayed with rigid, closed-cell polyurethane foam. The 15cm-thick layer provides protection against both freezing temperatures and heat, and the house meets the requirements for an A+ energy-efficiency rating.
The artist describes sanding the exterior layer as the most unpleasant part of the job.
“I would put on overalls and a mask and look like an astronaut, but my underpants would still end up full of dust,” he says.
The exterior was later painted white, but the owner hopes nature will add variety to its appearance, with moss and pollen eventually covering the façade.
Navickas shaped the interior spaces himself because he believes that a form cannot simply be described – it has to be felt.
The interior features separate domes, one for each room. The largest space is a 77-square-metre living room. The house also has two bedrooms, a kitchen area, bathrooms and a storage room. A huge terrace offers mesmerising views of the Dubysa Valley, with its mature trees.
The house is equipped with an air-to-water heat pump, while a solar power installation nearby generates electricity.
Navickas has covered the interior with plaster made from brown clay, but this is not the final finish. Eventually, the walls and ceilings will be smoothed with white clay brought from Ukraine. Friends gave the artist the powdered clay as a gift.
Although he has not yet moved into the house permanently, Navickas has already planned his next projects. He has designed another building that will house his workshop and storage room, as well as a carport.
More houses without corners are expected to rise on the family estate, as all four of the Navickas' children would also like to settle there.
The family has agreed that none of the houses in Padvarninkai will ever be sold. Otherwise, two decades of painstaking, almost titanic work would lose its meaning.

Former Mossad agent accompanied Flávio Bolsonaro in escape from Brazil, CNN reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:58:06 UTC
16:58:06 KST

A former Israeli Mossad agent accompanied Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro as he fled Brazil for Argentina before boarding a private jet to the United States, according to an investigation by Brazilian authorities obtained exclusively by CNN Brasil. The operation, reportedly involving assistance from individuals in Argentina and the United States, was planned before the final round of Brazil's presidential election and was internally dubbed "Operation Alba."
Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro and the defeated presidential candidate in last week's runoff election, crossed into Argentina by land on Tuesday, October 27, accompanied by his wife and two daughters. The family traveled in two separate vans across the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, which connects Foz do Iguaçu in southern Brazil with Puerto Iguazú in Argentina's Misiones province.
Brazilian agencies investigating the escape identified the vehicles through security camera footage recorded at the border crossing. According to CNN Brasil, the vans carried license plates TBB 4A65 and FDF 8E91, and their drivers were not required to present passports to enter Argentina.
One of the drivers, a former city councilman from Foz do Iguaçu, transported Bolsonaro, while his son drove a second van carrying the senator's wife and their two daughters.
The investigation found that preparations for Bolsonaro's departure had begun during the final stages of the presidential runoff campaign. A former Israeli intelligence operative who had worked for the Mossad and later became a naturalized US citizen arrived in Brazil on October 19, six days before the election.
According to records examined by investigators, the former Mossad agent accompanied Bolsonaro from Brasília to Argentina and was traveling in the same van as the senator when they crossed the border. CNN reported that members of Argentine President Javier Milei's government subsequently provided assistance.
From Puerto Iguazú, the Bolsonaro family boarded a Gulfstream G400 private jet, registered LV-JQW and operated by Argentine charter company Baires Fly. The aircraft stopped in Guayaquil, Ecuador, to refuel before continuing to Florida, landing at Miami's Opa-locka Executive Airport at approximately 10:30 a.m. on Wednesday, October 28. CNN broadcast the arrival live.
The private jet was reportedly arranged by Jason Miller, a political strategist close to US President Donald Trump who serves as a White House communications adviser, according to reporting by The New York Times. The newspaper reported that Miller had been in contact with Bolsonaro's brother Eduardo as the arrangements were made.
According to CNN Brasil, Bolsonaro used a Brazilian diplomatic passport upon arriving in the United States, despite the document having been canceled by Brazil's Federal Police following a court order.
Brazilian government officials familiar with the investigation believe the departure involved assistance from individuals and state authorities in Argentina and the United States. They described it as an "exfiltration," an operation designed to move a person out of a country covertly and without authorization.
Sources from three Brazilian agencies also told CNN that conflicting information circulated about Bolsonaro's whereabouts was part of a deliberate strategy to divert attention toward one possible departure point while the senator traveled along another route.
Investigators believe the escape was not an improvised, last-minute decision but a coordinated international operation involving extensive advance planning. The operation was reportedly assigned the internal codename "Alba."
The allegations of US government involvement have been disputed. On Saturday, October 31, Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that Washington had directly facilitated Bolsonaro's departure. Rubio said the Trump administration had not arranged his travel, although Trump had authorized the senator's admission to the United States.
Brazil's Federal Police are now considering asking the Supreme Federal Court to freeze Bolsonaro's assets, including his bank accounts.
The Justice Ministry is awaiting a Federal Police report on the circumstances of his departure, which came after he failed to comply with a judicial order requiring him to surrender his passports. Once the report is complete, the ministry will determine whether to pursue international cooperation through official diplomatic and law enforcement channels.

Enefit Power invokes exemption for shale oil use at Balti Power Plant
Unknown

Enefit Power invokes exemption for shale oil use at Balti Power Plant
Starting Sunday, Enefit Power will start using shale oil at its Balti Power Plant if its Unit 11 is out of service or uncompetitive on the electricity market.
Enefit Power CEO Raine Pajo informed Environmental Board Director Rainer Vakra and Climate Minister Erkki Keldo (Reform) that the company would use shale oil in the plant's reserve boilerhouse under an exemption granted by the board on October 21.
The order permits the preventive use of shale oil if natural gas supplies are at risk of disruption or restriction, or if district heating risks becoming unaffordable for Narva residents.
In his letter, Pajo said price volatility, rising winter demand and the risk of further supply disruptions threatened both natural gas security and the affordability of district heating. He warned that heating could become unaffordable even without an actual interruption in gas supplies.
"Given the current geopolitical and economic situation, Narva also considers it necessary to start using shale oil," the CEO wrote, pointing to Europe's lower-than-usual gas storage levels, high natural gas prices and winter supply risks.
He also cited the ongoing Middle East crisis, which drove European gas prices to a four-year high in October.
Shale oil use 'temporary and preventive'
Paju called the measure temporary and preventive, saying it would reduce Narva's dependence on volatile imported gas and help keep district heating affordable.
The amount of shale oil used, he added, would depend on gas supply conditions and the city's heating demand.
Enefit Power said the gas market situation and Narva residents' vulnerability justified using shale oil from November 1 if Balti Power Plant's Unit 11 was uncompetitive or out of service, formally notifying the Environmental Board of its plans.

Australia's latest World Cup smash-up helps nobody
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:53:51 UTC
16:53:51 KST

Fri, 18 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Tigers 0, Raiders 6
analysis
Australia's 124-6 win over Wales in the women's Rugby League World Cup helps nobody
Gallows humour was the order of the day for Australia's World Cup match against Wales, which was only fitting given it trudged towards its inevitable conclusion like the condemned to the executioner's block.
The Jillaroos ran out 124-6 winners in a game where the only element of contest was whether the reigning world champions could bring up the century.
They did it easily in the end, smashing their own record for biggest World Cup win, with Jamie Chapman's sixth try in the shadows of the full-time siren eclipsing France's 116-0 victory over Serbia in 2023 in the most lopsided result in women's international rugby league history.
In the first half, as they ran up a 60-0 lead, Australia scored 10 tries and Wales played the ball just 15 times. Five-eighth Jesse Southwell finished with 44 points on her own.
The Jillaroos did not make a tackle from the fifth minute until after the half-time siren and Australian halfback Tarryn Aiken did not make a tackle until 10 minutes before full-time.
After Australia scored its 15th try of the match it started getting booed by the sparse Parramatta Stadium crowd, who reserved their biggest cheer of the day for Welsh second rower Paige Travis's score that narrowed the gap to 100-6.
It was the sole bright spot of the match but the punters soon returned to an idle stupor as Australia added four more tries in the final seven minutes.
All World Cups are going to have their blowouts and rugby league's more than most. But they must serve a wider purpose and this one did not.
It benefited nobody and served to damage the tournament's credibility and its only legacy can be like Australia's 110-4 win over Russia in the men's 2000 World Cup, which is to say as a historical oddity for the trainspotters.
As the women's World Cup reckons with what has been an uneven tournament at best, marred by the same enormous scorelines of the men's edition but with few of the strong crowds, questions must be asked as to why a game like this could happen at all.
The uninterested and meagre turn-out for this match was proof it did not maximise the product, which very much felt like a curtain-raiser to the two men's matches that followed. Nor does it aid development.
It stuffed some stat sheets and gave ammunition to the bad-faith actors who are always on the hunt for an opportunity to take a shot at women's sport.
The Jillaroos are the best team in the world by an order of magnitude and have been for years. They gain nothing by putting the cleaners through Wales, who exist in a different universe.
That's why the Welsh should be spared any blame for how this went down. When the criticism comes it should not fall on them.
They qualified fair and square but they did not ask for this and there's no way to say it without sounding patronising but they did their best in the face of impossible odds.
While they have Canterbury halfback Tayla Preston and North Queensland winger Sian Williams as well as a smattering of Super League talent in Bethan Daiton, Carys Marsh and Agnes Wood, most of their players ply their trade in the women's second division in England.
It's a competition that can still have the draw disrupted by forfeits and a far cry from the semi-professional existence most of the Australians lead.
Cardiff plays the same sport as the Sydney Roosters, but the two teams live in different worlds.
Some of the Welsh players had only played a handful of rugby league games before this tour and their entire coaching staff is filled by volunteers.
As Australia moves on to the semi-finals, Wales heads home with a few bumps and bruises and perhaps a few stories to tell.
It is part of the developing arm of a developing sport and while it has its place on the international scene it is not across from an Australia side who are so dominant it's starting to become a problem.
They are overwhelming against everyone they play, let alone a team from the sport's frontiers packed with players who have never taken on athletes like Chapman, Tamika Upton or Jess Sergis in their lives.
Even so, lopsided results are not an issue on their own, so long as they serve a wider purpose.
The progress of Samoa, Fiji and Papua New Guinea through this World Cup would not have happened if they were not exposed to teams like Australia and New Zealand, even if there were growing pains.
Hours later, in the same stadium, Tonga and Samoa played out the most eagerly anticipated clash of the men's World Cup, one which could have sold out the ground twice over.
None of that happens without some blow-outs along the way.
But there are limits to what can be found amid the wreckage when a team who shouldn't be there are thrown into the fast lane.
Total obliteration leaves nothing behind. This was not a building block; this was a massacre that left no survivors.

Inflation is suppressing demand in Russia: incomes will grow by only 1% — intelligence

Inflation is suppressing demand in Russia: incomes will grow by only 1% — intelligence
Kyiv • UNN
Spending on goods and services is falling in Russia, while household incomes will grow by only 1% in 2026.
Due to inflation and slowing income growth, consumer demand in Russia is weakening. According to a forecast by Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development, the growth of real disposable household incomes will decline from 7.4% in 2025 to 1% in 2026, reports the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
As noted by the intelligence service, during the week of October 12–18, 2026, nominal consumer spending increased by 7.2% compared with the same period last year. In the third quarter, real spending, adjusted for seasonal fluctuations, decreased by 2.2% compared with the previous quarter.
Demand is falling for durable goods and services. During October 12–18, spending on electronics and telecommunications equipment fell by 13.5% year-on-year, furniture by 6.6%, taxis by 6.3%, clothing, footwear, and accessories by 4.1%, and sporting goods by 2.7%. Russians are postponing major purchases and saving on nonessential expenses. The cost of everyday services is also forcing them to save. In August–September 2026, residents of Russia’s central regions visited beauty salons, auto repair shops, and food-service establishments less frequently, opting for cheaper alternatives. In Moscow and the Moscow region, they switched to budget establishments and ready-made food from stores. In the northwest of the country, sales of new cars, household goods, and cosmetics declined
At the same time, most Russians do not feel any improvement in their financial situation. Only 6% of respondents said that their situation had improved over the past two or three months.
Another 25% reported a deterioration, while 68% noticed no changes. The share of the latter has remained at 66–68% for the past several years, indicating prolonged stagnation in the incomes of most of the population
We would like to remind you
The sharp rise in oil prices in September did not bring a corresponding increase in revenues to the Russian budget. The Kremlin is forced to return a significant portion of the taxes collected to oil companies, compensating them for the costs of supporting the domestic fuel market.

====================================================================================================

60 for Eisenkot, 46 for Netanyahu: Who gets first shot at forming Israel's government?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:52:25 UTC
16:52:25 KST

President Isaac Herzog plans to summon representatives of the parties elected to Israel's 26th Knesset to his official residence as early as Wednesday, November 4, even before the new parliament is sworn in, to begin the process of forming the country's next government. Herzog will hear which candidate each party recommends to lead the coalition-building effort. Unlike previous elections, however, there is no clear government in sight.
Herzog has called on party representatives to approach the consultations with an open mind, particularly because neither of the two main political blocs commands the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset. The presidential consultations could produce some surprises, including Arab parties recommending Gadi Eisenkot in an effort to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government, opposition to which was among the factors driving increased Arab voter turnout.
The election results leave Netanyahu's bloc with 53 seats, Eisenkot's bloc with 48 and the two Arab parties with a combined 19. So which candidate is each party expected to endorse, and which parties remain undecided?
Likud: 27 seats
Netanyahu's Likud will be the largest party in the next Knesset, with 27 seats. Unsurprisingly, it is expected to recommend its chairman, who led the outgoing government, for another term. Expected endorsement: Netanyahu.
Yashar!: 21 seats
There is little uncertainty here either. Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the largest party in the anti-Netanyahu bloc, has already declared his intention to form a government to replace Netanyahu's. In recent days, Eisenkot has met with the leaders of the other parties in his bloc, apart from Avigdor Lieberman, apparently in part to consolidate their support for his candidacy. Expected endorsement: Eisenkot.
B'Yachad (Together): 12 seats
Party chairman and former prime minister Naftali Bennett and his No. 2, Yair Lapid, met with Eisenkot in the days following the election. The third-largest party in the Knesset, with 12 seats, is expected to remain aligned with the bloc seeking a change of government. Expected endorsement: Eisenkot.
The Joint List: 11 seats
The Joint List, which won 11 seats, has issued an official statement expressing its willingness to cooperate politically in establishing an alternative government and has made clear that it intends to work toward ending Netanyahu's rule. Ahmad Tibi said again Saturday evening that the party was prepared to recommend Eisenkot and support a move to replace the Knesset speaker. Although the party has not formally announced its decision, it appears likely to endorse the Yashar! chairman during the presidential consultations. Likely endorsement: Eisenkot.
Ra'am: 8 seats
Mansour Abbas, whose Arab Islamist party won eight seats, is also expected to recommend Eisenkot. Abbas has not ruled out joining a new government or supporting one from outside the coalition. It remains unclear, however, whether other members of Eisenkot's bloc would agree to such an arrangement, particularly Yisrael Beiteinu chairman Avigdor Lieberman. Likely endorsement: Eisenkot.
The Democrats: 8 seats
Party chairman Yair Golan has been the most outspoken figure in Eisenkot's bloc in favor of forming a government with the Arab parties. Golan, whose party won eight seats, has argued in recent days that a broader alliance seeking to replace Netanyahu could command 67 seats and that the results present an opportunity to form a new government in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens. He has recently met with Eisenkot, Lapid and Abbas. Expected endorsement: Eisenkot.
Yisrael Beiteinu: 7 seats
One of the biggest unanswered questions concerns Avigdor Lieberman, whose party secured seven seats. Lieberman has yet to publicly declare whether he intends to recommend Eisenkot for prime minister. He has repeatedly ruled out joining Netanyahu, but has also said he will not serve in a government with the Arab parties or one dependent on their support. Before the election, figures within his party even raised the possibility that Yisrael Beiteinu would recommend Lieberman himself. Expected endorsement: Undecided, although support for Eisenkot remains possible.
Otzma Yehudit: 7 seats
Throughout the election campaign, Itamar Ben-Gvir, chairman of the far-right Otzma Yehudit party, repeatedly attacked Netanyahu, alleging that the prime minister was planning to establish a unity government with Eisenkot that would exclude him. That possibility continues to be discussed, but Ben-Gvir, who spoke with Netanyahu after the results became clear, has become a regular political ally of the Likud leader in recent years. His seven lawmakers are therefore expected to back Netanyahu in the presidential consultations. Expected endorsement: Netanyahu.
United Torah Judaism: 7 seats
Another major question mark hangs over the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party. Its chairman, Yaakov Asher, who replaced Moshe Gafni, visited the homes of senior rabbinical leaders on Saturday alongside other party lawmakers. They received the rabbis' blessings but avoided addressing the central political question: whether the party would join any future government, and under whose leadership. United Torah Judaism is demanding legislation regulating exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox yeshiva students before making any commitment. It has not pledged to recommend either candidate. Expected endorsement: Unclear, including whether the party will endorse anyone at all.
Shas: 6 seats
Aryeh Deri's ultra-Orthodox Shas party fell sharply from 11 seats to six. Although it withdrew from the government and coalition months ago following the failure to pass legislation providing military draft exemptions, it continues to support Netanyahu and considers itself part of his political bloc. Expected endorsement: Netanyahu.
Religious Zionism: 6 seats
Party chairman Bezalel Smotrich and his No. 2, Zehut leader Moshe Feiglin, regard themselves as integral members of Netanyahu's bloc. Smotrich has already met with the Likud chairman to coordinate political moves and is not expected to depart from his previous pattern of backing Netanyahu. Expected endorsement: Netanyahu.
The numbers: 60 for Eisenkot, 46 for Netanyahu
Herzog is expected to begin consultations with party representatives on Wednesday, with the meetings likely to continue Thursday and possibly into Friday. Under Israeli law, the president must complete the process and assign the task of forming a government within seven days of the official publication of the election results. With the results due to be formally presented on November 4, the deadline is November 11, although Herzog could make his decision earlier.
The president generally assigns the task to the Knesset member he believes has the best chance of forming a government. In practice, that is often the candidate who receives the largest number of recommendations from fellow lawmakers, although the number of endorsements is not the sole consideration.
Based on the current projections, that candidate would be Eisenkot. Even if Lieberman's Yisrael Beiteinu decides not to recommend him, Eisenkot could receive 60 endorsements, including those of the Joint List and Ra'am. If Lieberman also backs him, the total would rise to 67.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, is expected to receive 46 recommendations from Likud, Otzma Yehudit, Shas and Religious Zionism. United Torah Judaism's seven seats remain uncertain, potentially leaving the party outside either camp during the consultations.
Receiving the most recommendations, however, does not guarantee the formation of a government. The next challenge for either candidate will be turning political endorsements into a workable coalition capable of winning the Knesset's confidence.
What happens next?
The candidate who receives the first mandate from the president has 28 days to form a government. Herzog may grant an extension of up to 14 additional days, giving the candidate a maximum of 42 days to assemble a coalition.
If that candidate fails, the president has two options. He can assign the task to another Knesset member, most likely a candidate from the rival political bloc, who would then have 28 days to form a government, without the possibility of an extension.
Alternatively, Herzog can inform the Knesset speaker that he sees no prospect of forming a government. That triggers a final 21-day period during which at least 61 lawmakers can submit a written request asking the president to assign the task to a particular member of the Knesset.
A candidate nominated through this procedure would receive 14 days to form a government. The same 21-day procedure can also follow an unsuccessful second attempt to form a coalition.
If none of these attempts produces a government that wins the confidence of the Knesset, parliament is automatically dissolved and Israel heads for another election.
