Ancient Canaanite fortress from time of biblical Book of Judges reopens in southern Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:05:58 UTC
15:05:58 KST

The 12th century Canaanite Gal'on Fortress was re-inaugurated by Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund (KKL-JNF) on Thursday morning, following extensive conservation and renovation work completed alongside the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA).
The fortress is located in the heart of the Guvrin Forest in the Judean Lowlands, surrounded by conifers, broad-leaved trees, and Mediterranean shrub.
Discovered during 2018-2019 excavations by IAA archaeologists Dr. Saar Ganor and Dr. Itamar Weissbein near Kibbutz Gal On in southern Israel, it is believed to have likely been built to protect the local Canaanite inhabitants from foreign incursions, possibly from the Philistines.
“The Gal’on Fortress provides a glimpse into the geopolitical reality described in the Book of Judges, in which the Canaanites, Israelites, and Philistines fought each other,” said Ganor and Weissbein. “At the onset of the 12th century BCE, the Land of Canaan was still ruled by the Egyptians, and its inhabitants were their subjects.”
“At this juncture two additional major players appeared in the region: the Israelites and the Philistines, which led to a series of bloody territorial struggles. It seems that the Gal’on Fortress was built in a strategic location, overlooking the main road connecting the coastal plain to the Judean Lowlands; part of either a Canaanite or Egyptian attempt to deal with the new geopolitical situation.”
Resembling a square of roughly the size of 18 by 18 meters, the fortress stands with watch tower at each corner and a threshold carved of solid rock, weighing some 3 tons.
Its inner court was covered by stone plates with columns placed at the centers. Rooms, which served as living quarters and storehouses, were situated on both sides of the court.
In these inner chambers, thousands of pieces of earthenware were discovered. Some of them, however, were remarkably left intact. Archaeologists believe that they were used for worshiping local gods.
Thousands of shekels invested into renovations
KKL-JNF invested approximately 400,000 NIS into renovating the site, including preserving the citadel itself, coating the buildings with a preservative that blends in with the landscape and the site’s character, highlighting the citadel rooms and showcasing the entire structure.
Additionally, KKL-JNF installed new visitor infrastructure with parking, a new access road, a picnic area and a new signage system, with handicapped-accessible parking and an accessible path to the citadel.
The site was renovated as part of a collaboration between KKL-JNF and the IAA to excavate, preserve, and develop the site, while maintaining its historical values and making it accessible to the general public.
KKL-JNF Chairman Eyal Ostrinsky noted the importance of the organization’s work, especially at the site of the Gal’on Fortress.
“Preserving the heritage sites of the Land of Israel is part of our connection to our roots and our responsibility to pass on the story of this land to future generations,” said Ostrinsky. “Gal'on Fortress offers the public an opportunity to experience a fascinating chapter in the country's history firsthand, amid the landscapes of the Guvrin Forest.”
“At KKL-JNF, we work to preserve our historical heritage while developing our forests and making them accessible to the public, so that everyone can enjoy the unique combination of history, nature and outdoor recreation. Our collaboration with the Israel Antiquities Authority enables us to transform sites of historical significance into vibrant, accessible and meaningful places for the entire public.”
Archaeology is more than just excavations
According to Ami Shahar, conservation deputy director-general at the IAA, archaeology does not end with the excavation of ancient remains, but continues forth into the preservation and safeguarding of the discovered sites.
“For us, archaeology does not end with uncovering ancient remains; it is equally important to ensure that the sites excavated by the Israel Antiquities Authority are preserved for years to come, so that the public can continue to enjoy them in the future,” stated Shahar.
“Gal'on Fortress is a fine example of our collaboration with KKL-JNF, which begins at the archaeological excavation stage, continues through conservation work, and culminates in opening the site to visitors,” Shahar said. “We invite everyone to come, explore the remains of the ancient fortress, and enjoy a unique combination of history, nature and accessibility in the heart of the Guvrin Forest.”
“In these days when the State of Israel is required to be on vigilant guard for its security, the Gal’on Fortress reminds us that the struggle for the land is not a new story,” added Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu. “Already in the days of the Judges, the communities of ancient Israel faced the reality of conflicts with neighboring peoples, and just like today, out of a complex reality, Israel’s strong grasp on the land of our heritage was gradually established in this region.”
“Visiting the site connects us to our roots, and sharpens our responsibility to continue to watchfully protect our land, from every direction.”

EU Commission: Polish Parliament has right to appoint judges to the Constitutional Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:04:26 UTC
15:04:26 KST

The statement comes after a confrontation outside the Constitutional Tribunal building on Friday night, broadcast live on television, that has pushed a decade-old dispute into the wider European political debate.
The European Commission said on Saturday it was closely monitoring the crisis surrounding Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal, following a confrontation outside the court building on Friday night that was broadcast live on television. The incident has brought renewed attention to a dispute that has been ongoing for more than a decade.
“It is for the Polish authorities to ensure that the Constitutional Tribunal can function in accordance with the Polish constitution and in respect of the relevant case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union,” a Commission spokesperson told Euronews on Saturday.
“The appointment of eight new members of the Constitutional Tribunal lies within the constitutional power of the Sejm, Poland’s parliament,” the spokesperson added.
The Commission spokesperson also pointed to a ruling by the European Court of Human Rights, which on 5 May 2026 issued interim measures requiring the competent Polish authorities “to refrain from hindering the taking up and exercise of judicial duties by judges appointed by the Sejm in March 2026”.
Tusk: “Restoring calm does not mean accepting lawlessness”
Prime Minister Donald Tusk addressed Poles in a televised speech on Saturday evening, in his first major response to the crisis. He described Friday’s events as “scandalous incidents” and said he hoped such scenes would never be repeated in Poland.
Restoring calm could not mean accepting lawlessness or violence, Tusk said, as he vowed to restore conditions for independent justice and rule of law.
“A democratic state has to be strong and capable of enforcing justice,” he added, vowing that the rule of law would prevail over violence.
The crisis escalated on Friday night when President Karol Nawrocki attempted to enter the Tribunal building amid a deadlock over the appointment of new judges.
Police surrounded the building as the confrontation unfolded live on television, highlighting the growing stand-off between the president and the government over the composition of the country’s top court.
The Tusk government says it is pushing ahead with long-needed reforms to restore the rule of law after years of what it describes as interference in the judiciary by the Law and Justice (PiS) party. The opposition accuses Tusk’s government of attempting a coup.
European conservatives accuse EU of silence
The co-chairs of the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) group on Saturday condemned the Polish government’s actions, describing them as a violation of the rule of law, and backed President Nawrocki.
“The Tusk government’s actions constitute a clear and grave violation of the rule of law. We condemn this attack on judicial independence and Poland’s constitutional safeguards. No government stands above the law,” ECR co-chair Nicola Procaccini said.
He added that European institutions “must not avert their eyes” and said respect for national sovereignty and judicial independence must remain a matter of principle, “unaffected by political alliances”.
The Tribunal’s legitimacy has been contested for more than a decade. The dispute dates back to 2015, when the then-governing Civic Platform and the opposition Law and Justice party clashed over the appointment of five judges.
It has since developed into a wider conflict over judicial independence, the Tribunal’s composition and the authority of its rulings.

Europe’s crumbling coastlines face a €800 billion crisis. Is it time to move inland?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:02:54 UTC
15:02:54 KST

Economic losses from coastal erosion exceed €1 billion per year across 28 European countries
Nearly one in two Europeans live near a coastline, but their future remains uncertain.
Rising sea levels, largely caused by human-induced global warming, are gnawing away at vital infrastructure, family homes and heritage around the world.
Across 28 European countries, economic losses due to coastal erosion exceed €1 billion per year and could escalate to €800 billion annually by the end of the century if effective action is not taken.
It’s why a new report urges Europe to prepare to relocate homes, businesses and infrastructure from coastlines before it’s too late.
Should Europe’s crumbling coastlines be relocated?
The report by The Council of Europe argues that many of Europe’s coasts should urgently move towards “planned retreat”.
This means new development would be banned or restricted and homes, businesses and assets – including road and rail – would be moved to more climate resilient places inland.
For example, France estimates that around 900 kilometres of mainland coastline are receding, with more than 500 municipalities affected.
In Quiberville-sur-Mer in the Normandy region, a €9 million investment moved a public campsite inland. Municipal revenue subsequently increased by 25 per cent.
Of course, moving a campsite is a much easier feat than relocating entire residential villages or heritage structures. However, relocating coastal communities may be the only resort if alternative solutions fail.
In Venice, for example, experts predict that engineered banks called dikes may be necessary beyond 0.5 metres of sea level rise, which may occur by 2100 even if emissions are kept low. This would cost up to €4.5 billion, but would not be a permanent solution.
Closing the lagoon with a super levee (a wide reinforced embankment) could also be viable beyond 0.5 metres of sea-level rise, and could protect the city against sea level rise of up to 10 metres. However, the initial cost for this could exceed €30 billion.
Relocating the city, its residents and historic landmarks may be necessary beyond 4.5 metres of sea-level rise – which is projected to occur after 2300 – at a cost of up to €100 billion.
More than a quarter of Europe’s coastline is eroding
The report, titled ‘How can we cope with coastal erosion?’, also calls for authorities to update risk maps, introduce and periodically review no-build and buffer zones, and make adaptation plans that assess the legal, social and financial consequences of different choices.
This planning needs to be done in conjunction with those most directly affected: transparent consultation, public information and sustained political support are essential, alongside measures to protect livelihoods, coastal heritage and vulnerable communities, the report states.
40 per cent of Europe’s GDP comes from coastal regions and 80 per cent of low-elevation coast is at risk of future erosion. Better planning and relocation now, therefore, would save significant money later.
“Europe’s coastlines are among our most valuable assets,” says Greek politician and co-author of the report, Fanis Spanos. “They host major infrastructure, support vital economic activity and are centres of cultural and natural heritage.”
More than a quarter of Europe’s coastline is eroding, and the continued occupation of “high-risk zones” puts livelihoods at risk, Spanos adds.
Anthony Buchanan, co-author of the report, argues that defending Europe’s coasts with traditional methods such as building sea walls is becoming less sustainable due to the drastic rise in sea levels.
“Sea level rise has doubled in recent years and is on course to rise by another 44 cm by 2100, while storms are becoming more intense and frequent and extreme storm surges are likely to occur 20-to-30 times more often by 2050,” he explains.

Doha stopover travel guide: What to see and do on a city break in Qatar's capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:00:31 UTC
15:00:31 KST

Qatar’s capital Doha offers plenty for travellers on a stopover, whether it’s a 24-hour stay or a few days. Here’s what to see, where to dine and what to experience beyond the airport.
If you have an upcoming stopover in Doha, take it from me, you’re in for a treat.
Qatar etched its name in the history books as the first Arab nation to host a FIFA World Cup, which ushered in a wave of transformations. In the run-up to the 2022 tournament, the Gulf state introduced a raft of new hotels and infrastructure projects, such as Doha Metro.
The Qatari capital is the hub for Qatar Airways, which currently flies to more than 170 destinations around the world, including various direct links to Europe.
Arguably, Doha's Hamad International Airport is a destination in its own right. It features plenty of spots to eat and stunning public art, including Urs Fischer’s iconic Lamp Bear. There are even free 20-minute guided wellness sessions on offer at the massive 6,000 square metre ORCHARD space to keep travellers occupied.
A stopover leg of your journey, however, makes exploring the country beyond the airport doors and turning one holiday into two, very easy.
When you arrive, even if just for a few days, Doha is a destination of iconic landmarks, culture, desert adventures and great dining.
Landmarks and attractions
With its quaint cobble-stoned streets and pastel coloured buildings, Doha's Mina District and old port area is great for stretching your legs after a long-haul flight.
The popular Box Park features repurposed shipping containers that have been given a coating of technicolour paint and turned into shopping and food outlets that are perfect for taking that Instagrammable shot. During the winters, you can also see cruise ships docking at the Grand Terminal building.
For more waterfront views, you should head to the Doha Corniche. The seven kilometre stretch of promenade is one of the best places for views of the city’s skyline.
Here you can watch as traditional dhow vessels glide across the water, or even set sail on one, where each turn of the wooden boat reveals a new panoramic view.
Shopaholics have no shortage of high street stores and luxury labels to find souvenirs to take back home. At Place Vendôme Mall in Lusail, be sure to bring comfortable shoes to this huge retail centre which is inspired by classical French architecture. Across four floors, there are 580 high-end and mid-range stores to choose from.
Described as the “Arabian Riviera”, the Pearl Island’s Mediterranean-style and yacht-lined marina is also a scenic location for a late night stroll, where a restaurant or café is always a stone’s throw away.
While in neighbouring Gewan Island, the shopping and dining space is home to as many as 100 outlets. Its Crystal Walk also features around 180 illuminated panels embedded into the ground, studded with works of art created with crystals. Visitors can spot motifs such as caravans, desert and forest landscapes alongside a panel with a penguin colony.
In the summer, temperatures in this part of the world can also get… well, hot. But what if I told you there are outdoor spaces in Doha to explore that have air conditioning?
Gewan Island’s open-air promenade is a record holder, having earned the Guinness World Record titles for the longest outdoor air-conditioned mall and the largest outdoor interactive light canopy.
While parks such as Rawdat Al Hamama Park, Umm al Seneem Park, Al Gharrafa Park and Oxygen Park all have air conditioning placed in walkways for visitors to keep cool as they explore the greenery.
Souq Waqif and Katara: Doha’s cultural epicentres
Can you really say you’ve been to Doha if you’ve not paid Souq Waqif a visit? Nestled in the capital’s old town, the open-air market place of winding alleyways carries a centuries’ old history.
While it can be visited at any time of the day, the souq comes alive as evening falls. Here, the sounds of shoppers haggling with vendors, the smells of aromatics like saffron, zaatar and dried flowers as well as conversations held over coffee, known locally as “gahwa”, fill the air.
You can also meet some of the country’s most beloved animals. At the Falcon Souq, shopkeepers are more than happy to have tourists pose with the majestic bird perched on their arm.
Another stop to add to your Doha itinerary is the Katara Cultural Village. The waterfront destination is replete with galleries, performance spaces and architectural landmarks. Its amphitheatre blends classic Greek style with arched entrances as a nod to Islamic architectural influences. It can seat up to 5,000 spectators and has sweeping waterfront views.
Katara Cultural Village also has various public art installations, including the striking "Force of Nature II" by Italian contemporary artist, Lorenzo Quinn.
Doha is also home to an array of galleries, like Doha Fire Station, and museums, including the architectural marvel of the National Museum of Qatar. The exterior is inspired by the desert rose, while inside holds an immersive story back in time to Qatar's history that moulded the nation's identity and its modern achievements.
Other museums in Doha worth visiting include 3-2-1 Qatar Olympic and Sports Museum, Lawh wa Qalam: M. F. Husain Museum, and Msheireb Museums. Art Mill Museum, Lusail Museum and Qatar Auto Museum are set to be added to Doha's portfolio in the future.
Also part of the city’s cultural landscape is the Qatar National Library. This treasure trove is filled with books and periodicals in various European languages, alongside Arabic manuscripts, maps and globes. There are even printed materials that date back to the 15th century, when printing was first introduced in Europe.
Dining in Doha
Choosing where to eat is always a struggle – simply because I’m so spoiled for choice. Doha has more than 3,000 restaurants, serving up everything from traditional Qatari and Gulf cuisine, to Latin American, African, Asian and European flavours.
For traditional bites, visit Kamachi after a stroll at the Katara Cultural Village. Its must-try menu items include balaleet, a popular local dish made with saffron and cardamon spiced vermicelli noodles, slightly sweetened and topped with a fried egg.
Another no-brainer dining destination is Souq Waqif. If you have a craving for local street food, try the karak, a sweet and spicy tea, alongside any of the varieties of "khobz regag", a very thin and crispy flatbread, at the rustic Shay al Shamoos – established by the Souq’s first businesswoman, Shams Al-Qassabi.
When it comes to fine dining, Doha's food scene has attracted the attention of the Michelin Guide, which debuted in the country in 2024. As many as 41 restaurants are listed in the Michelin Guide Doha, including three that earned a Michelin star and eight with a Bib Gourmand.
IDAM by Alain Ducasse is located in the city’s Museum of Islamic Art, which overlooks the Doha Corniche. The Michelin-starred fine dining restaurant serves contemporary French cuisine paired with Qatari ingredients.
Alba, which serves Italian cuisine, and Jamavar, which serves Indian cuisine, are Doha's other one-Michelin starred establishments.
Where to stay
From luxury hotels to wallet-friendly accommodation, there are plenty of options for places to stay during a stopover.
Mandarin Oriental, Doha is a five-star property located in Msheireb, which is about a 20-minute drive from the airport. Offering 117 rooms, 41 suites and 91 apartments and villas, this luxury hotel also features two rooftop pools and a spa to unwind. This travel journalist cannot recommend the buffet breakfast at Mosaic enough, alongside the hotel’s other dining concepts, including IZU and Liang.
Doha’s luxury hotel portfolio also includes the Sheraton Grand Doha Resort & Convention Hotel, right on Corniche Street. Its distinctive pyramid shape has been a part of the Doha skyline since the early 1980s and today offers 371 rooms and suites where guests can choose between a sea or city view. Indoors, the hotel offers nine dining options, a 24-hour fitness centre and a spa. While outdoors, a pool and a 400-metre stretch of private beach awaits.
Day trips and desert adventures
About an hour and a half from Doha by road is the Inland Sea: Khor Al Adaid. Currently on the tentative list to be included as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, it’s one of Qatar’s most striking natural wonders as a landlocked lagoon surrounded by sand dunes of up to 40 metres high. It also features rocky ridges and cliffs.
Here, the water is calm and warm, making it perfect for swimming. The best time of year to visit is anywhere from November through to April, when the weather’s just right.
Stopover visitors can also venture to Al Khor, one of the oldest cities in Qatar. The sleepy city is about 45 minutes from Doha by car and is bursting with coastal charm. Visit Al Khor Towers, which date back to the early 20th-century. The cylindrical structures were first built to have watchmen defend the harbour after the discovery of a water source, once thought to possess medical properties.
My top tip for a day trip from Doha? Go kayaking through the mangroves. On my days off and on weekends, you can always find me kayaking through the mangroves and lush greenery at Al Khor’s Purple Island. The island is about an hour away from the capital and is my favourite escape away from the city (and dry land). If the season is right, you can spot flamingos and herons alongside fish and crabs.
On the west coast of Qatar, at the Brouq Nature Reserve near Zekreet, the late Richard Serra’s East-West/West-East permanent installation spans more than a kilometre and stands tall amid the desert landscape. Ras Brouq is also home to a unique area with white cliffs and geological forms like mushroom-shaped hills. Just remember to bring a cap, sunscreen and plenty of water.
Got a little longer for your Doha stopover? Swap the city skyline for the country’s desert with a stay at Regency Sealine Camp. Located an hour’s drive from the capital, on offer are tents, rooms and suites where the desert and sea are at your doorstep. Here, guests can go quad biking, dune bashing, camel riding and even enjoy a falconry show. After a day in the desert working up an appetite, guests can dine at the camp’s communal table over a selection of Arabic, Asian and international dishes.
Key info for travellers
All EU member-state passport holders, and non-EU European nationals, including travellers from the UK, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iceland, Azerbaijan and Switzerland, can benefit from visa-free travel if they have a confirmed hotel booking.
In terms of getting around Doha, visitors can rent a car, book a taxi – including Uber – or use public transport, such as the metro, Karwa bus or the country’s three tram lines from Lusail, Msheireb and Education City.

Moods, Leeds LS2: ‘Puzzling, if not quite a car crash’ – restaurant review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:00:05 UTC
15:00:05 KST

I’ve done some fairly rash things in my time, but I’ve never popped into anywhere for king scallops with ’nduja and come out with a swallow tattoo on my neck, though what is this life without adventure? Which is where Moods comes in: the space is an all-day restaurant, bar, tattoo parlour and hair salon in Leeds, offering violetta potato with ox cheek, a short back and sides, and the chance to tattoo “Mum” on your lower left arm, all in one Grade II-listed building.
It occupies the former First White Cloth Hall on Kirkgate, built in 1711 for the trade of white undyed cloth. This cavernous ark, with roof timbers dating back to the 1470s, lurked on Historic England’s Heritage at Risk register for more than 20 years, during which time it was under almost constant threat from the bulldozers. It took the National Lottery Heritage Fund, Leeds Civic Trust and Rushbond, a Leeds-based developer with a penchant for rescuing buildings, to drag it out of danger. Then Will and Hayley Moody arrived, slotting in their Buzz Club Tattoo Studio and a hair and beauty salon called Self, and now, on the ground floor, there’s Moods, a kitchen reportedly run by Craig Rogan. Laugh at the tattoo/hair/dinner triumvirate, if you want (I know I did), but it’s a grim joke that we treat our old buildings like this, and that hospitality is in a state so wild that this seems to be the solution. Bring on the bright new future of ye olde small plates, buzzcuts and half-sleeve emporiums, all under 400-year-old timbers.
Moods is incredibly cool, which I know immediately because of the gorgeous amounts of disdain with which I’m treated by the receptionist when I pop by at 2.30pm to try the all-day menu. She looks at me bamboozled, as many Gen Z-ers do, as if I have announced myself as an intergalactic equerry from Zarg requesting the keys to a plutonium source. Eventually, I’m tucked away by a wooden dresser that’s used as a base for cleaning supplies and cutlery. Only 42 other better tables are lying empty.
The all-day menu looks rather fabulous, though. There is a wild mushroom crumpet with Old Winchester and black truffle honey at £14. There is mead-glazed pancetta with potato rösti and mushroom ketchup, as well as fried chicken brioche with elderflower and pickled cucumber. And all of it cooked by Rogan, Simon Rogan’s son, trained by his father at L’Enclume and at Fera at Claridge’s. He’s channelling this greatness via osmosis; I can smell it in the air. Well, that and Jangro spray sanitiser.
Doubtless Moods is a fabulous place to drink cocktails at the long open bar in the centre of the room, where the signature peach melba comes with caramelised peach vodka and ice-cream foam. But the food proper turns out to be more of an uphill struggle. I order that crumpet, envisioning ceps, girolles, perhaps a random morel, on a home-baked sourdough crumpet with good butter. What arrives resembles nothing so much a Warburtons Giant Crumpet topped with chopped chestnut mushrooms fried in butter and a few herbs, and a big handful of cress. The buttery mushroom liquor has soaked into the crumpet while it waited, and it now has the texture of a damp Always Ultra. And where is the Old Winchester?
 
Next up, oak-smoked salmon with rye bread for £16: two tiny triangles of fish are draped over a shedload of creme fraiche– at least seven tablespoons of the stuff –a bit of roughly chopped kohlrabi, long pieces of chopped apple and yet more cress. If there are traces of the advertised yuzu and dill in here, they are destroyed by the sheer volume of cream. It is puzzling, if not quite a car crash. Then again, I was in an actual car crash once, and I definitely enjoyed the Sugar Puffs they gave me with my 10am discharge papers a lot more.
Writing all this off as a bad start, I return the next morning for breakfast, hoping to make more sense of the place. From the outset, things do not look good. Breakfast, a staff member mutters, doesn’t start until 10am, even though the doors open at eight, the music is on, the coffee machine is on and the cakes are being unloaded. There are also at least 11 staff bumbling about. How about just a coffee then, I ask. A white americano, please? God, I’m needy. By this point, I’m reducing myself to a small speck of a woman the size of a postage stamp, and I’m upsetting nobody. A black americano arrives, and then someone takes pity and allows me to order porridge, which turns up half cooked with a ramekin of what they call bramble preserve (AKA blackberry jam). I ask brightly if I might meet the famous chef, mainly out of mischief, but he’s not here. I might go back when the place is in a better mood.
- Moods 98 Kirkgate, Leeds LS2, 0113-390 4552. Open all week, brunch 8am-4pm, bar small plates noon-9pm. Brunch from about £15 a head; bar small plates from about £8 each, all plus drinks and service

High street ‘slot farms’ could evade budget tax rise through bingo hall loophole
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:00:03 UTC
15:00:03 KST

Hundreds of high street “slot farms” could continue claiming a discount on their business rates, unless the government closes a loophole that allows them to pose as bingo halls.
John Healey singled out adult gaming centres (AGCs) in his first budget this week, in which he increased duty on slot machine takings from 20% to 25%, claiming he was “raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street”.
As well as raising the duty, which will also affect bookmakers and casinos, he said AGCs and vape shops in England would no longer be eligible for a discount on business rates aimed at leisure and hospitality businesses.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been a vocal critic of AGCs and posted on Instagram after the budget to back the policy, a key plank of his pitch to improve British high streets.
However, many shops owned by the UK’s two largest slot farm companies, Merkur and Admiral, could escape the tax tweak, Guardian analysis suggests.
This is because they have obtained bingo licences for venues that appear to offer slot machines almost exclusively. Gambling Commission records suggest that hundreds of slot machine venues may have exploited this loophole.
When the Guardian visited four owned by Merkur and one owned by Admiral, all advertised bingo in their shop windows. However, the shops appeared to offer mainly slot machines inside. Bingo was available only on tablets stacked in one small corner of the room, allowing the venues to operate under a bingo licence.
In at least one case, captured in covert filming, a member of staff said nobody ever used the bingo tablets, and they appeared not to be in working order. The remainder of the venue was dedicated to slot machines offering a £2 spin every 2.5 seconds for a jackpot of £500. These category B3 machines are associated with higher levels of gambling-related harm than most other products, according to several studies.
One so-called bingo venue is the Merkur Slots shop in Stockport, where Wendy Hughes, who had terminal cancer, lost £2,000 over two spells lasting 16 hours. Merkur was fined £100,000 after the Guardian revealed the details of Merkur’s exploitation of Hughes, who has since died.
The Stockport branch of Merkur is among more than 200 arcades that are licensed as bingo venues, according to Gambling Commission records, despite appearing to be geared towards slot machine play. Some data is duplicated, making it hard to measure exact numbers.
Operators could also now convert their remaining AGC licences to bingo.
The Labour MP Alex Ballinger, a co-chair of the gambling reform all-party parliamentary group, welcomed the tax increase on slot machines but urged the government to be vigilant about the loophole. “We must ensure these licences cannot be used to sidestep the new business rates rules,” he said.
He urged the Department for Culture, Media and Sport to proceed with proposals to tighten the licensing rules, amid a consultation. “The government has already recognised this problem, and I am confident ministers will work with the regulator to close loopholes and ensure enforcement going forward,” he said.
The business rates expert Paul Turner-Mitchell of the real estate intelligence company Altus Group said the outcome of the tax change could hinge on how the Treasury defined an AGC and how local councils chose to enforce the rules. “A bingo licence alone does not settle its business rates treatment,” he said.
Merkur and Admiral did not respond to a request for comment.
Joseph Cullis, the president of the arcade operators’ trade body Bacta, said the industry would be hit hard by the tax changes.
“My great-grandfather started our family business back in 1962, and we’ve spent more than 60 years building it into what it is today,” he said. “Like many of the family-run businesses I represent across the sector, this decision will force us to reconsider investment and make difficult decisions about our future. Even larger operators will now be forced to scale back their plans.”

‘What’s our crime?’: A Palestinian family’s fight to get care for son injured by Hamas rocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:00:03 UTC
15:00:03 KST

It was 7.30am on 7 October 2023 when a Hamas rocket exploded next to 7-year-old Kinaan Dadou. The rocket was aimed at the Israeli settlement of Efrat in the occupied West Bank but missed its mark by a few hundred metres, landing in front of Kinaan’s family home instead.
A piece of shrapnel struck Kinaan in the head. He stood rigid, his hands frozen to his sides, and screamed “Baba!” before collapsing to the ground. An Israeli soldier who passed by promised to call an ambulance. No help ever came. Kinaan’s parents rushed him to the hospital themselves, but it was six hours before a doctor arrived due to the chaos of the day. All the while, Kinaan’s brain was haemorrhaging.
It was the last time that Kinaan’s parents heard his voice.
Now 10 years old, Kinaan lies in a small bed in a persistent vegetative state. His limbs, pale and thin from atrophy, are covered with Mickey Mouse blankets. On the wall above his bed, his parents have taped pictures of Kinaan before the injury. The lively boy climbing trees and beaming into the camera bears little resemblance to the one below, whose one open eye moves listlessly across the bedroom. He is fed through a tube and breathes through a tracheostomy.
“I look at him and I ask him what he wants, what does he need? But he can’t respond, so I begin to cry. I think he’s in pain,” says Alaa Hassan Yakoub Dadou, Kinaan’s 47-year-old father, looking down at his son.
Kinaan’s case is unusual: a Palestinian child wounded by a Hamas rocket on the same day that about 1,200 people were killed in a Hamas-led attack on Israel. Three years on, Kinaan’s parents are still seeking help to pay for his treatment, finding themselves stranded between the Palestinian Authority (PA), which is responsible for healthcare in their area, and the Israeli authorities, who control virtually all facets of their lives.
The Dadou family live in the small village of Um Rukbeh, west of Bethlehem, a part of the occupied West Bank classified as “Area C”, where the Palestinian population lives under Israeli military rule.
The Palestinian Authority, which administers healthcare for Palestinians in Area C, gave some medical support for Kinaan early on – he underwent multiple brain surgeries and had a part of his skull removed – but his parents say it has refused to cover further specialist care and has been inconsistent in providing medication. Under Palestinian law, people with disabilities have the right to have at least 75% of their rehabilitation costs covered, while children also have the right to “obtain the highest possible standard of free healthcare services”.
Officials in the Palestinian ministry of health did not respond to questions.
Meanwhile, Israel, as an occupying power, also has certain obligations under international law to provide medical services, though it’s unclear if that extends specifically to Kinaan’s case. It has told a lawyer representing the family that Kinaan was injured in an area outside its jurisdiction, something the family questioned due to Israel’s de facto control over their daily lives. Israeli authorities control construction permits in Area C, including for bomb shelters, and dictate much of the family’s movement, complicating their efforts to get access to healthcare. Three months ago, they received a warning Israeli authorities would soon demolish their home.
The family has appealed to the Israeli government on humanitarian grounds. If they were Israeli and living in one of the increasing number of illegal settlements surrounding their home, the family says they would have had access to a bomb shelter and medical treatment.
“We’ve knocked on every door. The Arabs and the Israelis, it’s the same response. The Palestinian side says: ‘This isn’t our area.’ What’s our crime? That we happen to live among settlements? Neither side takes responsibility for us,” Alaa says.
Cogat – the Israeli body that oversees the Palestinian territories – did not respond to questions about Kinaan’s case.
Without outside help, the family has been unable to pay for the medical treatment that may improve their son’s condition. A specialist in Turkey said that, with an intensive recovery programme and further surgery, Kinaan’s condition could improve. But the cost of the treatment – about $250,000 (£190,000) – is far beyond what the family can afford.
“I pay 4,000 shekels [£950] per month just for his medication. I borrow from here and there, but it’s too much,” says Alaa. He used to work as a labourer in Israel, but has been out of work since Israel stopped issuing work permits to most Palestinians in the West Bank after the 7 October attack, leaving the family without income.
To save money, Kinaan’s mother, Woroud Dadou, has begun to perform some of the routine medical procedures herself. She changes her son’s breathing tube, saving the family £225 each month.
“I try to keep the tube as clean as possible so it lasts longer, but sometimes if I use the same one too long he begins to cough,” says Woroud, who adds she learned by watching doctors perform the procedures in hospital.
Alaa was told about a former colleague of his in Israel whose child was injured on 7 October. The child was flown to Germany for treatment and has since improved. He is happy for his colleague, but cannot help but wish Kinaan had access to the same treatment.
“If this was an Israeli child, even a settler child, do you think they’d have left him like this? He’d have been taken to the best hospitals. They would have done everything for him,” Alaa says.
“That’s what Israel does for its injured. It takes care of them. But when it comes to us, as a humanitarian case, it’s as though they’re saying: ‘Just give him his medicine until he dies.’”
Memories of Kinaan are scattered around the house. A little blue notebook is filled with his childlike scrawl as he practised letters: “pepper, cabbage, knight”. His parents are proud of his handwriting and said he dreamed of becoming a pilot when he grew up.
Though Kinaan is the middle child, he was the loudest of the three brothers. “Always putting them in order, like a little sergeant,” his father says, smiling. He recalls how, whenever he would come home from work, Kinaan would be waiting at the door, bringing his two siblings along to greet him.
Now only his wife greets him, and the sounds of play have mostly disappeared.
Kinaan appears to wake up, his face seemingly forming a smile as his father speaks. He keeps opening his mouth and pausing, as if about to speak, but no words come out. The room is silent, save for the sucking sound every time Kinaan takes a breath.
“We are realistic – we know he probably will never be the same as he was. But at least we want to relieve his suffering and relieve our guilt,” his father says. “It’s another kind of pain for a mother and a father, not knowing what exactly is hurting your child. That’s an enormous burden for a parent.”

Companies promised AI gains— here's how the payoff showed up in earnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:00:01 UTC
15:00:01 KST

Some companies are beginning to report financial benefits from artificial intelligence investments, as interest in the technology shifts from hype to measurable returns in the latest quarter.
Corporate AI investment has surged as companies look to boost efficiency and become more profitable, reaching $581.7 billion in 2025, up 130% from the previous year, according to the Stanford HAI 2026 AI Index report.
As CEOs tout the tech's benefits and hyperscalers like Microsoft, Amazon, Google and Meta are expected to spend $700 billion combined this year on its infrastructure, investors are looking for measurable gains.
Now, with third-quarter earnings season underway, some companies are beginning to put numbers around those benefits.
Santander puts a number on AI gains
Spanish banking giant Santander said Wednesday that it saw AI initiatives generate 194 million euros ($216 million) in business value in the first nine months of 2026.
Santander Chief Financial Officer José García Cantera told CNBC that AI is helping the bank reduce low-value tasks so employees can focus on higher-value work.
"This affects both revenue and costs, so we are actually in the quarter where we can actually link directly to AI a positive contribution," Cantera said.
"AI is being embedded in all the processes that we are conducting at the bank, so it's really difficult to just say how much comes from AI, but clearly AI is improving the quality of our services to clients."
Novartis and Standard Chartered see AI in results
Swiss pharmaceutical giant Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan told CNBC that AI was beginning to contribute to the company's bottom line.
Novartis reported third-quarter core operating income of $6.04 billion, up 10% year-on-year at constant currencies. The company did not quantify how much of that was attributable to AI but Narasimhan told CNBC: "I think this is the first quarter I've really seen AI start to improve actually our P&L on a tangible basis."
"We're working on R&D [research & development] to see if it can really increase R&D productivity," Narasimhan said on "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday.
"We're already seeing some of the productivity you saw in the bottom-line performance of what we can do with AI from M&S [marketing & sales]."
Meanwhile, Standard Chartered Chief Financial Officer Manus Costello told "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday that the company is seeing AI "appear everywhere across the business."
The bank reported third-quarter operating income growth of 14% at constant currency, excluding notable items.
"I think you can see it in the top line growth that we're delivering, and you can see it in that operating leverage that I talked about," Costello said, adding that AI is helping managers drive better relationships with customers and generate more income.
"We're also seeing that strong operating leverage that I talked about, where income is growing much faster than costs, and some of that is because we've been able to deploy AI tools to improve core processes and enable us to scale those up very efficiently," he added.
Carlsberg says benefits are not yet at scale
Carlsberg CEO Jacob Aarup-Andersen said on "Squawk Box Europe" this week that it's not seeing AI benefits at scale, but the technology has impacted internal processes, cost efficiency, commercial and pricing processes, marketing and its supply chain.
The company's revenue grew 4.9% in the third quarter.
Big Tech points to AI-driven growth
Elsewhere, tech firms are also reporting gains. Meta said in its Oct. 21 earnings that its AI investments were delivering "substantial incremental advertising revenue," while total revenue jumped 26% in the quarter ended Sept. 30.
While Alphabet's Google Search revenue growth slowed amid concerns about AI competition, Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to nearly $31 billion in the third quarter, it reported on Wednesday.

‘Gravestones are sinking into the ground’: Preserving Lithuania’s Jewish cemeteries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Before the Second World War, there were between 200 and 240 Jewish cemeteries in Lithuania. Most of them today stand neglected. The non-profit organisation MACEVA, the Litvak Cemetery Catalogue, has been working in Lithuania since 2011 to preserve this heritage.
“Over the past 15 years, more than 70 cemeteries have been documented. It may be closer to 80 if we include this year’s work. Quite a few cemeteries have been destroyed, so there is nothing left to document. In reality, there are probably around 60 to 70 cemeteries still waiting to be documented,” says Milda Jakulytė, director of MACEVA.
Working alongside volunteers, MACEVA carefully catalogues the cemeteries. It translates Hebrew epitaphs into English and makes all the information it collects available in a public online database.
This year, the organisation has carried out work at cemeteries in Virbalis, Kelmė, Linkuva and Merkinė.
For the second consecutive year, soldiers from Germany’s 45th Armoured Brigade, stationed in Lithuania, have helped document Jewish heritage at the cemetery in Merkinė.
“Our task is to clean the gravestones, put them back upright and make the inscriptions legible. Then we document and photograph them so that these inscriptions can later help people find their relatives,” says a German captain named Lois.
“I think we are doing very important work. Germany feels a sense of responsibility because there is currently no Jewish community here that can look after these and other graves. It is very important that we, the Germans, are taking care of the community’s cemeteries now,” he added.
For the organisation, it is important not only to document the cemeteries and research the people buried in Jewish graveyards across Lithuania, but also to help relatives scattered around the world find the graves of their family members and ancestors.
The poetic epitaphs carved into gravestones not only highlight the deceased’s good qualities but also reveal the values cherished by individual Jewish communities.
“In some communities, for example, a woman’s modesty was particularly important, while in others, helping one’s neighbour was highly valued. Men’s epitaphs almost always emphasise their dedication to studying the Torah. Their professions are mentioned more often than women’s – in women’s epitaphs, a profession is mentioned only in one particular case, when the woman was a midwife,” Jakulytė says.
“We recently received an [...] inscription describing a woman in an unusual way, saying that she was beautiful. We will need to investigate a little further to find out who this beauty was, but it is certainly unusual and very interesting,” she adds.
Very little information, if any, has survived about the people buried in Jewish cemeteries. In its research, the organisation always seeks to involve local residents and help them better understand the history of their towns and villages.
“We want this heritage to be seen not as something foreign, but as part of the community. We want people to be able to come here, point things out, take pride in them and say: ‘Look, this is where Merkinė’s very own Čiurlionis is buried, or this is where the beauty of Merkinė lies.’
“We want it to become part of the town’s history, because these cemeteries also tell the story of the town itself. We would like local communities to embrace them as part of their own heritage, to get involved, engage with it and make use of the material we collect,” Jakulytė says.
The organisation plans to continue its work until all surviving Jewish cemeteries in Lithuania have been documented.

Scrapped marine rope recast as stools that rock like buoys
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Scrapped marine rope recast as stools that rock like buoys
Rotterdam studio The New Raw has used discarded rope salvaged from the city’s harbour to create a series of 3D-printed public seating for its waterfront.
Called Buoy, the urban furniture project is shortlisted for a 2026 Dezeen Award in the sustainable design category.
To create the stools, The New Raw founder Foteini Setaki collected a series of plastic ropes from Rotterdam harbour, which were formerly used for managing boats and would’ve otherwise gone to waste.
The ropes were then transported to Maastricht, in the south of the Netherlands, where they were cleaned, shredded and mechanically recycled into pellets.
After returning to The New Raw’s Rotterdam studio, the recycled plastic pellets were melted and 3D-printed to create the stools, layer by layer.
“The material fuses as it is deposited, so no separate binder is needed,” Setaki told Dezeen.
Setaki explained that marine ropes are challenging to recycle because they contain a cocktail of materials that accumulate various residues over time.
Careful selection is essential to determine the ropes with the highest polypropylene content to be transformed into recycled plastic pellets, she explained.
While no virgin plastic is used in the creation of the stools, a small percentage of additives support the furniture’s long-term outdoor use, including UV protection.
“These additives are compatible with recycling the material again,” said Setaki.
Each seat features a subtly different hue, which is determined by the colour of the original rope rather than additional pigments or coatings.
The stools were also designed with spinning top-style pointed bases, so that they rock when the user sits down.
This gentle rocking motion was chosen to mimic real buoys bobbing along on the water.
“We wanted the seats to carry a recognisable link to their maritime origin, through both their shape and the slow movement of floating buoys,” explained Setaki.
“Borrowing that movement brings a playful quality to sitting, and the connection to the harbour becomes something you can feel.”
Each unique stool was engraved with its batch and production number, and then placed by Rotterdam harbour.
The project was created as an example of how designers can seek out local, surplus resources in an effort to contextualise their practice with the place that they work.
“Working with a local waste stream is a way of strengthening the relationship between the city and its harbour,” said Setaki.
“The material’s journey and the experience of sitting make that relationship tangible. This approach could also be adapted to other harbour cities, starting with their own discarded materials and local networks.”
Founded in 2016, The New Raw is run by Setaki and Panos Sakkas. The studio 3D prints locally sourced plastic waste to create furniture.
Buoy is nominated alongside a vibrant shortlist of sustainable design projects, including a cement-free architectural material made of waste date pits and lighting for an Australia bookshop made of its own faulty publications rejected due to printing errors.

India news: Opposition holds major rally in Delhi over voter roll revisions

India opposition holds major rally against voter roll revisions
Published November 1, 2026last updated November 1, 2026
What you need to know
Here is our rolling coverage from India on Sunday, November 1:
- India's opposition parties are marching to Ramlila Maidan in New Delhi to seek the resignation of the election chief over alleged voter roll manipulation
- Pollution curbs have kicked-in in the Indian capital
Opposition leaders set off for Ramlila Maidan
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has shared visuals of the opposition INDIA alliance's rally headed toward Ramlila Maidan in New Delhi.
A split screen showed a large crowd of supporters gathered at the rally site as promient opposition lawmakers seated onboard an open-top vehicle made their way to the Ramlila Maidan through Delhi's roads.
"Come to Connaught Place, let's march together. Or meet directly at Ramlila Maidan - but you must come," Gandhi wrote on X earlier at noon local time as he called for the march to "Save the Vote, Save the Nation."
Delhi enforces winter pollution plan
With winter on the horizon in New Delhi, dread of the annual smog that season brings with it has also set in.
Starting today, the Indian capital is imposing strict and sweeping pollution curbs to tackle the toxic winter smog.
The restrictions include a ban on older vehicles registered outside the city, a suspension of dust-generating demolition activities and outdoor civil construction activities, doubling of parking fees to discourage the use of private vehicles and reduction of physical attendance in government and private-sector offices to 50%.
Agencies including the Delhi Pollution Control Committee, the Municipal Corporation, the city's transport department and traffic police have been tasked with ensuring a stringent enforcement of the winter pollution rules.
The measures will be implemeted for varying time frames, with some lasting until February 28.
"Delhi's Winter Action Plan 2026-27 comes into effect with stricter pollution controls, stronger enforcement and 24×7 monitoring. We humbly request all Delhiites to follow the guidelines and contribute towards making Delhi's air cleaner and healthier," Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta's office said.
How has Modi's BJP reacted to the opposition stir?
The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of Prime Minister Narendra Modi is staging a rally of its own in New Delhi, setting the stage for a battle of marches.
The BJP march will take place in West Delhi in remembrance of the 1984 anti-Sikh riots, with the ruling party accusing the Congress of staging a political rally on the anniversary of the violence.
The deadly riots took place following the assassination of the then prime minister, Congress'Indira Gandhi— opposition leader Rahul Gandhi's paternal grandmother — by two Sikh bodyguards on October 31, 1984.
"The sobs of the 1984 riot victims cannot be drowned out by the noise of rallies!" the BJP wrote on X.
"The wounds of 1984 are still raw today. Congress cannot bury them under the din of its theatrics!" the party added.
The BJP also shared videos from different states in the country of rallies held over the weekend under its campaign named "Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy" to counter the Congress and the opposition.
The BJP deems the opposition protests over alleged voter roll manipulations as attempts to "create anarchy."
INDIA bloc holds big rally against electoral irregularities, election chief
India's political opposition is carrying out a major march in New Delhi to protest the nationwide revision of electoral rolls that they say benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
They are also seeking the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The 'Chalo Dilli' march, heralded by the main opposition Congress party, will begin from Central Delhi's Connaught Place Minto Road Junction to reach Ramlila Maidan.
Top faces of the opposition alliance — called the INDIA bloc — are among those expected to participate. These include Congress' Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee, Samajwadi Party supremo Akhilesh Yadav and Rashtriya Janata Dal's Tejashwi Yadav.
India's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which carried out its own demonstrations against Kumar last month, has also backed the opposition rally.
What is India's electoral roll controversy?
Under a contentious nationwide voter-verification exercise, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), around 130 million names have been purged from electoral rolls.
The opposition and critics say that those struck off the voter lists include a large number of minority voters and accuse Modi's BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains. BJP denied the allegations.
The outcry against election chief Kumar began in September after an investigative report by an Indian daily said that there were divisions in the country's poll body — the Election Commission of India (ECI) — over the revision of voter lists, which it oversees.
Concerns emerged over the ECI's independence.
The ECI has maintained the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and helps prevent the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
Opposition stages symbolic impeachment of election chief
On Saturday evening, the INDIA bloc staged a mock impeachment of the chief election commissioner. The symbolic proceedings saw opposition members reenacting a parliamentary session in a garden at Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge's residence.
"I don't think anything like this has ever happened in history. The entire opposition sitting in a garden to discuss the impeachment of the CEC, it is absurd," leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi said.
He added that the opposition lawmakers had to hold the mock exercise — which even featured furniture, seating arrangements and carpeting resembling the Lok Sabha (lower house of the Indian parliament) — because they "have nowhere else to go."
"We have no other option. Every single institution ... is closed for us," Gandhi said.
Meanwhile on Sunday, the opposition expects thousands of supporters to descend upon Ramlila Maidan.
It is the first major demonstration to be held at the famous ground, located between Old and New Delhi, since it was labeled as one of the three designated protest sites in the capital last month.
Early visuals showed supporters beginning to gather at Ramlila Maidan and posters of the 'Chalo Dilli' march propped up in the capital.
The Delhi Police said that around 200 to 250 CCTV cameras have been set up at the site as part of the security arrangements.
News agency ANI reported that around 4,000 security personnel have been deployed at Ramlila Maidan.
"The organizers have set up various enclosures, and we have police personnel stationed within them. There are also pathways between these enclosures, where our police personnel are deployed to ensure the area remains secure,” deputy commissioner of police (Central District) Rohit Rajbir Singh told ANI.
The capital's traffic police announced curbs and diversions in Central Delhi ahead of the rally.
Welcome to our coverage
This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW’s studio in New Delhi, bringing you our daily capsule of all the biggest headlines making a splash in India.
New Delhi has been waking up to chillier mornings, but the political heat brought on by a weekend of protests by India's bloc of opposition parties is what's gripping the capital today.
The opposition is set to hold a massive rally today at Ramlila Maidan — New Delhi's newly designated protest site — against alleged voter roll irregularities and India's top poll official.
Last evening, the opposition parties staged a mock impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar as they stepped up their stir against a controversial nationwide revision of voter lists.
In other news, pollution curbs to tackle the annual winter smog in the Indian capital have come into force.

Rioters smash, loot storefronts amid cost of living protests in Germany
Masked rioters smashed storefronts and looted goods late Saturday in Frankfurt, Germany amid a protest against the rising cost of living.
The largely peaceful demonstrations were led by a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" - roughly translated to "Gen Z's got this" - rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.
Tensions peaked in the evening as some groups of protesters refused to disperse, sparking clashes and violence in major cities including Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg.
in Frankfurt's financial hub, masked protesters hurled stones, fireworks and pepper bombs, according to police.
Authorities also said looters stole weapons from a gun store, which were later retrieved. Some rioters also threw Molotov cocktails at police after pummeling them with stones and bottles earlier in the day, Frankfurt police said on X.
In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police responded by using water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds.
Earlier in the day, demonstrations had been largely peaceful. In Berlin, young protesters gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.
"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection - in short, in our future - because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.
Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.
"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.

Bulgaria returns to polls in presidential runoff

AA Photo
Bulgarians return to the polls on Nov. 1 to choose between acting President Iliana Yotova and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov after a first round marked by record-low turnout produced no outright winner.
Yotova and her running mate, Kiril Valchev, won 34.8 percent of the vote on Oct. 25, ahead of Gyurov and Georgi Kandev on 32 percent, according to the Central Election Commission. Only about 22.5 percent of eligible voters cast ballots, the lowest turnout in Bulgaria’s post-communist history.
Polling stations are scheduled to open at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT) and close at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT). The campaign has featured competing views on Bulgaria’s foreign policy and its relations with Russia, Ukraine and Western allies.
Yotova is seeking a full presidential mandate with the backing of Progressive Bulgaria, the party led by former President Rumen Radev. She served as his vice president and assumed the presidency after he resigned in January.
A victory would make her Bulgaria’s first elected female president. The office’s responsibilities include representing the country, serving as commander-in-chief of the armed forces and vetoing legislation.
Gyurov, an economist and former deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, is backed by opposition parties. He led a caretaker government before April’s parliamentary election.
A total of 27 candidates contested the first round. Electoral rules require a candidate to win more than half the valid votes, with participation exceeding 50 percent of registered voters, to secure a first-round victory. Otherwise, the two leading candidates advance to a runoff.
The presidential contest follows years of political instability. Bulgaria has held eight parliamentary elections since April 2021, including seven early votes, as parties repeatedly struggled to assemble stable governing coalitions. Failed coalition negotiations led to caretaker Cabinets and further elections.
In the latest parliamentary vote in April, Radev’s Progressive Bulgaria won 131 of the National Assembly’s 240 seats, securing an outright majority.

PHOTO BTA

Voting in Bulgaria's presidential and vice-presidential runoff begins at 7 a.m. on November 1, with Bulgarian citizens at home and abroad casting their ballots. The two tickets vying for voters' support are Iliana Iotova–Kiril Valchev and Andrey Gyurov–Georgi Kandev, who finished first and second, respectively, among the 27 candidate tickets in the first round held on October 25.
Campaigning and the publication of opinion poll results related to the election are prohibited until voting officially ends at 8 p.m.
According to the Central Election Commission, more than 6.58 million Bulgarians are eligible to vote. If voters are still queuing outside polling stations at 8 p.m., voting may be extended until 9 p.m. The same rule applies to Bulgarians voting abroad, according to local time.
Voting is taking place on 11,902 machines in more than three-quarters of all polling stations. Paper ballots are being used in polling stations with fewer than 300 registered voters.
A total of 613 polling stations have been set up for Bulgarians abroad in 60 countries. The largest numbers are in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, with 82, followed by Türkiye with 78 and Germany with 70.
Voting machines are available at 242 polling stations abroad.
A different set of voting machines, placed in storage before the first round, has been sent for use in the November 1 runoff, Central Election Commission (CEC) spokesperson Stoyanka Balova-Tsvetkova explained. The reason is that there is not enough time during the week between the two rounds to install the new software on the devices and send them abroad again.
To ensure transparency in the voting process, video surveillance has been provided during the counting of ballots and the completion of election protocols. The "Elections 360°" application offers an interactive map of polling stations, information about the candidates and the option to follow the election results.
The presidential ticket receiving the highest number of votes cast is declared the winner of the runoff, regardless of voter turnout.
The President is the head of state of the Republic of Bulgaria and Supreme Commander-in-Chief of the country's armed forces. The President is assisted by a Vice President in exercising these powers. The President and Vice President are directly elected by Bulgarian citizens for a five-year term.

Bulgaria's National Music Academy: 105 years of artistic excellence and spirit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:50:55 UTC
14:50:55 KST

Author
Tsvetana Toncheva
Article
Bulgaria's National Music Academy: 105 years of artistic excellence and spirit
Sunday 1 November 2026 07:05
Sunday, 1 November 2026, 07:05
PHOTO BTA
Font size
In 2026, the National Academy of Music “Prof. Pancho Vladigerov”, Bulgaria’s first institution of higher music education, marks its 105th anniversary with an extensive programme of concerts, academic forums and cultural initiatives. The institution was established under the name State Academy of Music by a decree of Tsar Boris III on 21 July 1921, in response to the pressing need for trained singing teachers in Bulgarian schools and highly qualified musicians for the country’s concert and operatic stages.
The Academy’s first rector was Dimitar Hadjigeorgiev, a composer and educator who had graduated from the Prague Conservatory. As early as 1904, he had been among the founders of Sofia’s first secondary music school, becoming its director in 1912. 
Bringing secondary and higher music education together under one roof in two separate divisions, the newly established Academy soon attracted an ever-growing number of pupils and students. Its teaching staff included some of Bulgaria’s most distinguished musicians: the eminent opera singer Ivan Vulpe; virtuoso flautist Nikola Stefanov; the celebrated brothers Todor and Ivan Torchanov, a violinist and pianist respectively; the great composer and pioneer of Bulgarian music Dobri Hristov; Nikola Atanasov, composer of Bulgaria’s first symphony; the legendary folklorist Vasil Stoin; and the distinguished Czech musicians Henrich Wisner, pianist and conductor, and Ivan Cibulka, cellist.
Composer Pancho Vladigerov
PHOTO Archives State Agency
“The Academy has become a platform for presenting outstanding, high-quality cultural content, of the kind that only the country’s most distinguished institutions can boast,” Rector Prof. Dr Sava Dimitrov recently told the media on the occasion of the anniversary. In a special interview with Radio Bulgaria, he described the significance of these 105 years:
Prof. Sava Dimitrov, rector of the National Music Academy
PHOTO Facebook /National Music Academy "Prof. Pancho Vladigerov"
“105 years of tradition, 105 years of statehood, I would say! The establishment of the Academy as an institution of higher music education in 1921 was a deliberate act of state policy. It gives us every reason to look back at the generations who came before us and to recognise the enthusiasm and energy with which they built what is now one of the most highly respected institutions, not only in Bulgaria and much of Europe, but, I can confidently say, throughout the world.
Our educational offering stands out in the academic landscape as a product of considerable substance and value. That is the fashionable way of putting it nowadays, although we know that education is, in fact, a mission of much broader significance. In many respects, it is education that safeguards our national tradition, strength and spirituality. It is through education that we are able to recognise progress and understand the skills required for life in the modern world.
In this sense, 105 years is both a long time and a short one. I would venture to say that these are the first five years of the Academy’s new century, marking the beginning of a new and different era. Just five years ago, the devastating COVID-19 pandemic brought the world to a standstill, and this is precisely how the first five years of the Academy’s new century began. I hope that all the years ahead will prove far more fruitful for its development than the period of stagnation we experienced. With considerable optimism, I would say that new generations and emerging trends in education are setting new standards, standards that the Academy both follows and helps to shape through its educational process.”
PHOTO Facebook /National Music Academy "Prof. Pancho Vladigerov"
Among the Academy’s earliest graduates were some of Bulgaria’s most renowned composers: Lyubomir Pipkov, Asen Karastoyanov, Veselin Stoyanov, Svetoslav Obretenov, Philip Koutev, Marin Goleminov and Georgi Zlatev-Cherkin. Its alumni also include legendary pianists and piano pedagogues such as Dimitar Nenov, Panka Pelishek, Lyuba Encheva and Tamara Yankova, as well as violinists Vasil Lolov and Vasil Chernaev.
From the outset, alongside the classical musical heritage, the Academy made Bulgarian musical creativity one of its priorities. At the end of its first academic year, its leadership issued an appeal to Bulgarian composers to submit their works for performance at public concerts. The first scholarly studies also began to emerge at this time, primarily in the field of musical folklore research.
In the 1930s, an exceptional generation of musicians joined the Academy’s teaching staff. They included composers Pancho Vladigerov, Veselin Stoyanov, Marin Goleminov and Asen Karastoyanov; violinists Nikola Abadzhiev, Vladimir Avramov and Hristo Obreshkov; pianists Dimitar Nenov, Panka Pelishek and Tamara Yankova; cellists Konstantin Popov and Konstantin Kugijski; oboist Vasil Spasov; bassoonist Atanas Gardev; singers Hristo Brambarov and Lyudmila Prokopova; and musicologists Stoyan Brashovanov and Stoyan Dzhudzhev. 
In 1936, the higher education programme was extended from three to four years and divided into two streams: one for the training of music teachers and the other for instrumentalists and singers.
Professors from the theoretical, composers' and conducting faculty
PHOTO Facebook /Museum for the History of Radio in Bulgaria "Prof. D-r Veselin Dimitrov"
In 1954, the State Academy of Music was renamed the Bulgarian State Conservatoire and restructured into three faculties: Theory, Composition and Conducting; Instrumental Music; and Vocal Music. Shortly afterwards, a permanent choir and symphony orchestra were established to support conducting studies.
An Opera Studio was also founded within the Faculty of Vocal Music, becoming the Educational Opera Theatre in 1964.
In 1995, the Conservatoire regained its status as the State Academy of Music and was named after the eminent Bulgarian composer Prof. Pancho Vladigerov. In 2006, it became the National Academy of Music.
PHOTO Facebook /National Music Academy "Prof. Pancho Vladigerov"
Speaking to Radio Bulgaria, Prof. Sava Dimitrov emphasised that the 105th anniversary would be a true celebration of music, reflecting the full breadth of activity across the musical community. The Academy’s major ensembles will take to its stage, including its professional Academic Symphony Orchestra, which has been part of the institution since 1928, its Chamber Choir and its student ensembles.
The National Academy of Music works in partnership with all of Bulgaria’s major musical institutions, from the Sofia Philharmonic and the Sofia Soloists Chamber Ensemble to the orchestras in Ruse, Varna and Burgas, the Vratsa and Vidin Symphony Orchestras, and the ensembles of the country’s opera houses.
The Music Academy is a comprehensive higher education institution offering the full range of specialisations in music and music education, including the essential theoretical disciplines that develop the body of scholarly knowledge relating to Bulgaria’s musical heritage. This is why the anniversary programme also features numerous conferences and academic events, many of them open to the public.
The rector also highlighted the wide range of support available to doctoral students, who represent the third cycle of higher education and are being prepared to become the next generation of academic colleagues and teachers.
“As you know, the law has made a doctoral degree a prerequisite for advancement within the academic hierarchy. I therefore firmly believe that, in this respect, the Academy is exceptionally vibrant and currently ranks among the strongest higher education institutions in the country. I would confidently extend that assessment to Europe as well.”
PHOTO Facebook /National Music Academy "Prof. Pancho Vladigerov"
Today, the Academy’s teaching staff comprises distinguished musicians and researchers whose professional standing is reflected in their presence on the international stage and their active participation in scholarly exchange. Students are given regular opportunities to perform in concerts and stage productions, take part in academic forums and publish their work in the Academy’s print and online publications. Alongside the regular curriculum, numerous masterclasses and special lecture series are organised, led by prominent Bulgarian and international musicians and musicologists.
PHOTO Facebook /National Music Academy "Prof. Pancho Vladigerov"
Asked whether he considers the Academy competitive with other European institutions of higher music education, Prof. Dimitrov replies:
“I believe that we often set an example and offer innovation, combining traditional and modern approaches to education. Naturally, the Music Academy meets all the requirements laid down, first and foremost, by our national legislation. The fact that this legislation is harmonised with European standards is further proof that we operate at the highest standards available.”
Prof. Dimitrov has no doubts about the high quality of education provided by the National Academy of Music:
“You know, we have been talking quite a lot lately about Bulgaria’s concertmasters. A respected colleague of mine, a professor and conductor, took the trouble to calculate that there are as many as 72 Bulgarian concertmasters working in orchestras in the so-called ‘Category A’ group, regarded as the world’s leading professional ensembles. This is not an assessment we are making of ourselves; it is one made by the world. So I can say that, at present, we offer an exceptionally high standard of education, one whose quality is firmly established.”
PHOTO Facebook /National Music Academy "Prof. Pancho Vladigerov"
Today, the Academy’s reputation is carried around the world by musicians such as Pavel Balev, Vesko Eschkenazy, Penka Kouneva and Plamena Mangova. In earlier decades, Bulgaria’s most prestigious higher music institution introduced the world to brilliant opera stars including Todor Mazarov, Hristo Brambarov, Dimitar Uzunov, Nicolai Ghiaurov, Lyubomir Bodurov, Yulia Wiener, Ghena Dimitrova, Raina Kabaivanska, Anna Tomowa-Sintow, Stefka Evstatieva, Kaludi Kaludov, Valeri Popova and Kamen Chanev.
The Academy has also educated generation after generation of Bulgarian composers, among them Filip Kutev, Marin Goleminov, Veselin Stoyanov, Svetoslav Obretenov, Parashkev Hadzhiev, Konstantin Iliev, Lazar Nikolov, Krasimir Kyurkchiyski, Vasil Kazandjiev, Todor Popov, Aleksandar Raichev, Aleksandar Yosifov, Nikolai Kaufman, Aleksandar Vladigerov, Stefan Dragostinov, Simeon Pironkov and Georgi Arnaoudov.
Its distinguished alumni also include conductors Atanas Margaritov, Ivan Marinov, Georgi Robev, Vasil Arnaudov, Georgi Dimitrov, Georgi Notev and Emil Tabakov. Among the leading Bulgarian pianists who graduated from the Academy are Anton Dikov, Nikolai Evrov and Ludmil Angelov, while its outstanding violinist alumni include Petar Hristoskov, Boyan Lechev, Georgi Badev and Mincho Minchev.
We are bringing you our interview with Prof. Sava Dimitrov on 1 November, the Day of the National Enlighteners. What message would the rector of the National Academy of Music like to share with Bulgarians at home and around the world?
“My wish is that they listen to the national spirit as expressed through music, and work to strengthen and promote our national identity around the world.”
