German students rally against cuts and conscription
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:44:20 UTC
14:44:20 KST

AA Photo
More than 100,000 school and university students rallied across Germany on Oct. 31 against government spending cuts and plans to revive military conscription, demanding greater investment in education and public services.
The demonstrations remained largely peaceful through the afternoon. In Berlin, police recorded up to 5,000 participants outside the Brandenburg Gate, half the turnout announced by organizers from the Gen Z Regelt movement.
Students accused the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz of prioritizing military expansion and big business while cutting welfare and social spending. They said years of cuts had left classrooms underfunded and public services strained.
Banners called for Merz to resign and carried messages including “Your austerity policy is costing our future,” “No to cuts and war budgets” and “Invest in people, not war.” Other signs demanded support for education, urged politicians to listen to Gen Z and declared: “Berlin is saving, the rich are laughing.”
Student representatives also criticized the government’s proposed health and pension reforms and its handling of the climate crisis. Demonstrators opposed a new military service law requiring compulsory medical examinations, which they said could pave the way for mandatory conscription.
“We want to show solidarity with France, we want to reclaim our future, we want to fight for educational justice,” university student Michelle told Anadolu Agency.
She said cuts were affecting public services needed to secure a fairer future and called for education funding to take priority over military spending.
Anastasia, 17, said students felt politicians were not listening to them. She opposed compulsory military service and rejected further militarization as a response to conflicts.
“I just don't think that we should send young kids into wars,” she told Anadolu Agency.
Sophie, a 16-year-old student, described teacher shortages, inadequate education budgets and poor school infrastructure. Inspired by demonstrations in France, she said she hoped similar action could bring change in Germany.
“More budget for schools, for example, because our school is very bad, the windows can't even close,” she said.
Several demonstrators wore keffiyehs, while others carried Palestinian flags in support of people in Gaza. Speakers expressed solidarity with student groups worldwide.
Participant Jean-Michel opposed higher defense spending while education remained underfunded. He also expressed solidarity with students in Lebanon, Syria and Palestine whose schools had been bombed, alleging Germany had provided financial, moral and political support for the destruction.
Before the rallies, media reports questioned the movement’s organization and security officials raised concerns about possible violence. Berlin organizers said they were committed to peaceful protest and were directing their criticism at political parties.
“The police are not our focus; we’re here because the political parties are all failing us,” one organizer said.
Berlin police said the Brandenburg Gate rally ended without any serious incident. Participation fell short of expectations in the capital and several other cities after some organizations withdrew their initial support.
The BSK, the largest student organization, and the Jusos, the youth wing of the center-left Social Democratic Party, cited a lack of transparency. They described the movement as a loose online coalition whose organizers were difficult to reach and whose leadership remained unclear. The Greens and the socialist Left Party supported the protests.
The demonstrations followed similar student actions in France, Belgium and Italy. Many participants cited the French protests as an inspiration, arguing large street demonstrations could push politicians to respond.

How do you score 171 out of 170 in a Harvard Exam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:38:04 UTC
14:38:04 KST

In a recent conversation with 
The Times of India
, Impact Catalyst Aruna Lohia Goenka unveiled YASHA
, her five-pillar framework for Viksit Bharat 2047: Yuva, Anna, Shiksha, Hunar and Abundance, shaped by nearly 30 years of engagement in national development.
The 
knowledge series
, under the overarching theme of Viksit Bharat 2047, now takes that conversation further. Across five interviews, Sanjiv Kaura, CEO-CSR, The Times of India, explores the experiences, convictions and ideas behind each pillar of the YASHA framework.
We begin with 
S for Shiksha
.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 As we approach a world in which machines may become more intelligent than human beings, what is the greatest danger facing our children?
Aruna Goenka:
 The danger is not that machines will become more intelligent. It is that humans may stop thinking and become like robots: programmed to respond, but forgetting how to feel, empathise and connect.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 Can you share an example of an educational intervention that reflects this philosophy?
Aruna Goenka:
 In the tribal district of Bastar, Chhattisgarh, we taught children 
how to think, rather than 
what to think. That was in the 1990s. The greatest moment is not when a child says, "I know the answer." It is when the child asks, "But why?" Today, 30 years later, I feel blessed to be associated with the AM/NS India Times Critical Thinking Championship, which reaches 1 million children each year across 28 states and 8 Union Territories in 14 languages. The scale has changed enormously, but the underlying conviction remains the same.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 If AI can become a personal tutor to every child, will we still need teachers?
Aruna Goenka:
 More than ever! AI may explain Einstein’s and Newton's laws, but can it recognise the child who has stopped believing in herself? A machine can deliver a lesson, but a great teacher can change a life. AI should be our children's co-pilot, not their autopilot.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 Are we sometimes confusing marks with intelligence?
Aruna Goenka:
 (Laughs) We give children marks for answering questions correctly. Perhaps we should reward them much more for asking questions nobody else thought of! And who says 100% is the ceiling? Let me tell you a fascinating story. In December 2018, an IIT alum and IAS officer, Ankur Garg, studying at Harvard Kennedy School, scored 171 marks out of 170 in a macroeconomics examination conducted by the world-renowned economist Professor Jeffrey Frankel. Yes, you heard that correctly. 171 out of 170! Now, isn't that wonderful?
For me, that is a beautiful metaphor for education and life. Never allow someone else's definition of the maximum to become the limit of your potential. And why restrict this philosophy to examinations? Whether it is knowledge, kindness, compassion or service, give more than is expected of you. After all, a
100% cent may be the examiner's limit. It need not be the limit of human potential.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 Socrates famously argued that the unexamined life is not worth living. Are we losing sight of that larger purpose of education?
Aruna Goenka:
 Absolutely, Socrates was reminding us that a meaningful life must be examined, not merely lived. For him, the pursuit of wisdom was inseparable from virtue. Compassion, honesty, courage, self-discipline and consciousness are not optional extras in education. They are at its very heart.
And education is not confined to degrees. Think of the extraordinary wisdom ancient Bharat produced: the 
Upanishads
, 
Tirukkural, Yoga Sutras
, 
Charaka Samhita
, and 
Panchatantra
. Consider Gautam Buddha's teachings on compassion and mindfulness; Lord Mahavira's Anekantavada, which reminds us that truth has many facets and no single viewpoint captures its entirety; Kabir's fearless questioning of dogma; Guru Nanak's message of equality and service; Tulsidas's 
Ramcharitmanas
, with its timeless reflections on duty and devotion, and Kahlil Gibran's timeless wisdom on love, self-discovery and nurturing of independent minds across centuries and civilisations, these extraordinary minds explored not merely how much we can know, but how wisely we can live. Their insights continue to inspire humanity even today. I believe we must cultivate the awareness to discover the possibilities present in the Universe; otherwise, surrounded by information and technology, we risk becoming intellectual zombies!
Sanjiv Kaura:
 You come from a family blessed with Lakshmi (prosperity), yet your affection for Saraswati (knowledge) seems just as profound!
Aruna Goenka
: (With a twinkle in her eyes) I come from a family of geniuses and wizards! My elder brother has one of the world's largest collections of handwritten books/manuscripts. Imagine the centuries of knowledge, imagination and wisdom preserved in those pages. I have never seen 
Lakshmi
 and 
Saraswati as rivals but as two complementary forces within us. 
Lakshmi
 symbolises the subconscious mind, where dreams are born, while 
Saraswati represents the conscious mind, which gives direction to the dreams. And remember, 
Lakshmi
 does not stay where 
Saraswati is neglected. Wealth without wisdom never creates lasting abundance.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 We sometimes celebrate the 
silver spoon
. But listening to you, I wonder whether a 
Silva Mind
 is the greater inheritance.
Aruna Goenka:
 (Laughs) Interestingly, I have seen the Silva Mind technique being used by my elder brother for decades – I saw him reading a book about it when he was just fourteen! The power of visualisation fascinated me. I believe it helped him envision extraordinary possibilities and turn them into reality, including the remarkable library he eventually built. But I like your comparison. A silver spoon may feed the body, but a silver mind feeds curiosity. And I must say, there is something wonderful about knowledge. It is perhaps the only inheritance that becomes richer the more you give it away.
Sanjiv Kaura: Which are some of your favourite books?
Aruna Goenka: Oh, Sanjiv, that's like asking a mother to choose her favourite child! (Laughs) But a few have stayed with me. 
Autobiography of a Yogi
 opens our minds to spirituality, consciousness and life's infinite possibilities. Then there is Thoreau's 
Walden
, which reminds us that a rich life need not be a complicated one. And I love Ralph Waldo Emerson's essay 
Self-Reliance
, with its powerful message about trusting one's own judgment rather than blindly following the crowd. Another favourite is 
Critical Thinking
 by Richard Paul. And here's a lovely coincidence! Only recently, I discovered that my younger brother has been reading it since the early 1990s! Imagine - all these years, we have been travelling along similar intellectual paths without even realising it.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 Aruna ji, your closing thoughts?
Aruna Goenka:
 Literacy teaches us to read, education teaches us to understand, and wisdom teaches us to question. Literacy opens the book. Education opens the mind. Wisdom opens the heart. And above all, dream big! But why confine your dreams to the night? Dream during the day, with your eyes wide open, and work to turn those dreams into reality. Imagine 1.4 billion people, each with a dream for Bharat, and each determined to make it happen! When 1.4 billion dreams become 1.4 billion actions, Viksit Bharat 2047 will not be just a vision. It will be our reality!
Disclaimer: This article has been produced on behalf of Aruna Goenka for Times Foundation as part of the Knowledge Sharing Series and published by Times Internet's Spotlight team.

Fat-dissolving claims land FatX Solution in regulatory trouble; CDSCO cancels registration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:37:54 UTC
14:37:54 KST

CDSCO finds over 160 drug samples as 'not of standard quality' for December
NEW DELHI: Promising to dissolve fat cells may sound like an attractive pitch for a slimming product, but it has landed FatX Solution in trouble with the country's drug regulator. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has cancelled the product's registration after finding that it was being promoted with claims that are not permitted for cosmetics.In an order dated October 28, CDSCO said Delhi-based importer Tekno Midas Aesthetics was marketing FatX Solution on its website as a product that could dissolve fat cells and reduce their size. The regulator said these were drug-related claims and did not fit the definition of a cosmetic under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.The action followed a scrutiny of the company's application and website, during which CDSCO found differences between the claims being made online and those mentioned on the approved product label.Under the Cosmetics Rules, 2020, cosmetic products cannot make false or misleading claims. The rules define cosmetics as products meant for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering appearance.
Claims to dissolve fat cells go beyond this definition, the regulator said.CDSCO had issued a show-cause notice to the company on August 10, citing violations of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and the Cosmetics Rules. The company submitted its response on September 1, but the regulator found it inconclusive and unsatisfactory. The firm also requested that its registration certificate be voluntarily surrendered.
Rajan Bhatnagar of Tekno Midas Aesthetics told TOI that the product had been registered as a cosmetic more than four years ago. "At that time, the licence was granted because the product was registered as a cosmetic. The authorities have now changed their interpretation of the category under which the product falls. Earlier, it was considered a cosmetic, but now they say it falls under another category," he said.He said the company had decided not to contest the matter after receiving the notice. "We did not want to get into any dispute or challenge the notification. We voluntarily requested the surrender of the licence, and the authorities cancelled it," he said.The Central Licensing Authority subsequently cancelled the registration certificate, RC/COS-003300, which was issued in July 2022 and was valid until July 14, 2027. The cancellation took effect from October 28.

Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

North Korea tests cluster warhead for tactical ballistic missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:36:51 UTC
14:36:51 KST

North Korea conducted a test of a cluster warhead for a tactical ballistic missile to assess its combat applicability and destructive power, state media reported on Sunday.
The Missile Administration carried out the test on Saturday, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
The test was overseen by General Kim Jong-sik, a member of the Central Military Commission of the ruling Workers' Party of Korea and first deputy director of a department of the party's Central Committee.
North Korea's Ballistic Missile Systems Research Institute and Warhead Research Institute said the test confirmed that the country's "Type-2 standard cluster warhead" could devastate a target area of about 12 to 13 hectares (29 to 32 acres) at what they described as an "ultra-high density."
The head of the Missile Administration said North Korea classifies its cluster warheads into four categories, including special-purpose and standard types.
He said Pyongyang plans to make all four types available to military units by the end of this year, allowing them to select warheads according to operational objectives and the characteristics of targets.
The Missile Administration described the test as part of regular scientific research aimed at increasing the destructive power of its weapons systems.

Two Palestinian babies die in Gaza tent fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:35:57 UTC
14:35:57 KST

Two Palestinian infants have died of severe burns after a fire tears through a displacement tent in Al Mawasi, west of Khan Younis in southern Gaza, as families cook over open flames amid shortages under Israel’s blockade.
Habiba Mohammed Zanoun, two months old, and Aseel Abu Suhayban, seven months old, died on Saturday morning at Nasser Medical Complex, which identifies them. Both are admitted to intensive care after flames break out on Friday afternoon while relatives are gathered at the tent.
Habiba was due for her two-month vaccinations on the day she dies.
Sources tell Anadolu the fire started while food is being cooked inside the tent. They said severe shortages of cooking gas and basic supplies force displaced families to prepare meals over open fires.
Aseel’s mother rushed to save her daughter and suffers burns. She was also taken to hospital.
‘Why is all this happening to us?’
The girls’ grandmother told Anadolu that her daughter had come to visit the family when the fire erupted. Habiba was her daughter’s baby, she said, and neither infant could withstand the severity of her injuries.
“Why is all this happening to us?” she asked. “Every day there are accidents, bombings and fires, and people are dying in so many ways.”
“For three years, we have been living like this, amid displacement, anguish and pain,” she added.
Cooking without safe alternatives
Sources said the blaze is one of three fires reported on Friday in displacement tents in central and southern Gaza.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned in June that cooking inside tents is a leading cause of fires. It said blankets, old fabric, cardboard and plastic sheeting used to reinforce shelters let flames spread rapidly and make fires harder to control.
OCHA also reported that Israeli authorities denied entry on August 26 and September 2 to a previously approved shipment through the Egyptian corridor. The shipment contained 36,960 pieces of timber and 660 emergency shelter kits.
The Gaza Government Media Office previously said more than 800,000 displaced Palestinians live in tents unfit for human habitation. It estimates that 162,000 of Gaza’s 270,000 displacement tents need immediate replacement.

Interview: Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building provides key insights for political parties worldwide, says Tajik expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:35:44 CST
14:35:44 KST

DUSHANBE, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building provides important guidance for political parties in different countries to strengthen their organizational foundations and enhance their governance capacity, a Tajik expert has said.
"Political parties in various countries are facing new risks and challenges in today's world," said Suhrob Raufzoda, editor-in-chief of "People's Tribune," the newspaper of Tajikistan's ruling People's Democratic Party, in an interview with Xinhua.
In his view, steadily strengthening organizational foundations and enhancing governance capacity are important guarantees for a country's long-term stability and development, and the Communist Party of China's (CPC) experience in advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance provides useful guidance for political parties in other countries.
Raufzoda attaches particular importance to China's efforts in personnel training. He said that modern state governance requires high-caliber officials with firm political conviction, professional expertise and a strong sense of responsibility. Therefore, cultivating officials and building such a cadre represent important investments in China's long-term development, he added.
In Raufzoda's view, strengthening the Party's organizational system, advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance, and cultivating high-caliber officials characterized by loyalty, integrity and a sense of responsibility are interconnected and mutually reinforcing.
The Tajik expert believes that an important objective of Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building is to further strengthen the CPC so that it always remains a vibrant Marxist governing party and the strong leadership core of the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
"The experience of the Communist Party of China has attracted the attention of many countries, as it demonstrates practical experience in continuously improving institutional development, strategic planning, the training of highly qualified personnel and mechanisms of state governance," Raufzoda said.
He stressed that every country has its own historical traditions, political system and development path. At the same time, continuously enhancing governance capacity, strengthening institutional development, cultivating highly qualified personnel and building public trust are common tasks facing many countries, he said.
Raufzoda also noted that China's achievements in areas such as poverty alleviation, personnel training, state governance, scientific and technological innovation, and modernization can provide useful guidance for countries of the Global South as they seek development paths suited to their national conditions.
"A deeper study of China's concrete practices can help provide a more objective and comprehensive understanding of the CPC's ideas on state governance and its experience in governance," he said. ■

Ex-LS Speaker Meira Kumar presided over CEC’s public impeachment
NEW DELHI: Former Lok Sabha Speaker Meira Kumar presided over the INDIA bloc's symbolic “public impeachment” of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar on Saturday, seated in a chair steeped in history. The chair was once used by India's first Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru.The information was shared by Congress media and publicity department head Pawan Khera, who was involved in organising the event at the residence of Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge at 10, Rajaji Marg in New Delhi.“The chair on which Meira Kumar sat during today's public impeachment proceedings against the CEC was once occupied by the first prime minister of India, Jawaharlal Nehru, the great-grandfather of Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi,” Khera later said in a post on X.“It was Nehru Ji's chair throughout his tenure as prime minister. It witnessed some of the most consequential decisions in our nation's history and carries the weight of that legacy,” he added.Khera said that Meira Kumar, sitting in the same chair, pronounced Gyanesh Kumar “unfit to continue as the Chief Election Commissioner of India”.“Gyanesh Kumar has been rejected by the people of India. It is only a matter of time before he goes,” he said.
The INDIA bloc organised the symbolic proceedings, accusing the CEC of allegedly facilitating the deletion of voters' names from electoral rolls and demanding that he be tried in court for treason and jailed.Kumar opened the proceedings, saying the opposition had decided to convene the meeting because of alleged wrongful deletions of eligible voters.“When this issue is raised by the INDIA bloc, there is no accountability. So we have decided that the INDIA bloc will hold a meeting and bring a proposal to remove Gyanesh Kumar,” she said.The resolution was moved by Kharge, seconded by Samajwadi Party leader Harendra Malik and supported by Rahul Gandhi and other opposition MPs and civil society representatives. It was adopted unanimously through a show of hands.Kharge alleged that the right to vote was under threat and accused the Election Commission of functioning at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and home minister Amit Shah.Rahul Gandhi described the proceedings as a “political weapon” against those who, he alleged, had colluded to destroy people's votes.

BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra said the opposition was holding a “mock parliament” and took a swipe at Rahul Gandhi.The symbolic proceedings came ahead of the INDIA bloc's November 1 march and rally at Ramlila Maidan, where opposition leaders are seeking to intensify pressure for the CEC's removal and raise concerns over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

‘Like Kashmir’: How a toxic marble dump yard became a tourist spot in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:25:32 UTC
14:25:32 KST

‘Like Kashmir’: How a toxic marble dump yard became a tourist spot in India
The vast ‘snow yard’ in otherwise arid Rajasthan state attracts hundreds of tourists daily, but residents face severe health risks.
Kishangarh, India – As Bagharam Gurjar kneels to pull weeds from his maize field in western India’s Rajasthan state, the sound of his wife coughing nearby makes him restless.
“Everything gets ruined when dust settles on the soil,” says Gurjar, 53, barely looking up.
“May God make everything right,” replies his wife between bouts of chronic cough. “Otherwise, it becomes difficult to grow crops.”
The Gurjars are among nearly 5,000 people living in the vicinity of what has turned out to be one of the most unusual tourist destinations in India.
Their village, Bhogiyawas, is just 6km (4 miles) from Kishangarh, where a 300-acre (121-hectare) marble slurry dumping yard resembles a snow-clad landscape, attracting hundreds of tourists every day in an otherwise arid state.
Locally known as a “Snow Yard”, the landfill in Rajasthan’s Ajmer district is the largest of its kind in Asia. Its pristine white hills and slopes with water-filled pits provide a surreal backdrop for visitors, who get free entry to the site.
Newlyweds pose against the snowy backdrop or the blue artificial lake, while couples soon to get married organise pre-wedding photoshoots. Social media influencers throng the landfill to make reels. Music videos and movies are also frequently shot here.
“Everyone, right from my five-year-old niece to my mother, loves it very much. Their first impression was that this looks like Kashmir,” Salim Shahzada, a businessman from Uttar Pradesh state, told Al Jazeera, referring to Indian-administered Kashmir.
Shahzada said he had visited the place a couple of times and decided to bring his family along this time. But he had no idea about the health and environmental problems linked to the dumping yard.
“I do not have much knowledge about this place or its ill effects. I only know that this is where marble cutting waste is dumped and that the hill itself is made of this waste,” he said.
Kishangarh, a marble and granite hub, is home to nearly 1,200 processing units, with the total daily business estimated at more than 160 million rupees ($1.7m), providing jobs to about 25,000 people, according to the Federation of Indian Granite and Stone Industry.
Every day, nearly 1,000 tankers carry slurry from those units and empty roughly 5,500 tonnes of waste on the government-allotted dump site, which, for the people living nearby, has turned into a health hazard.
Gurjar said the yard has affected residents in at least six villages. “How many problems can I even tell you about? If there were just one or two, we could deal with them,” he said.
“But here, almost everything is going wrong because of the dumping yard. People like me are suffering from chest infections, dental problems and skin allergies. It does not matter whether they are children or elderly people; everyone is suffering.”
Gurjar said he and his wife are forced to take regular medicines for chest infections or skin problems.
Aditi Goyal, a general physician at Ajmer’s Ganga Narayan Hospital, said the residents of Kishangarh face several health risks, mainly respiratory and skin problems. She said the workers in the marble processing units are more vulnerable to chronic illnesses because of prolonged exposure to toxic dust.
“Over the last couple of years, cases of respiratory problems have increased significantly in this area because people are exposed to dust from the dumping yard,” Goyal told Al Jazeera.
“However, dust from industrial waste is not the only issue. People in Kishangarh, who are mostly farmers, also suffer from infections caused by dust coming from the soil,” she said, advising people to wear masks to protect themselves from dust.
The same dust settles on the fields, hardening the soil and making it difficult to grow crops.
A study led by Laxmi Kant Sharma, professor in the department of environmental science at the Central University of Rajasthan, found that the concentration of lead silicate in Kishangarh’s soil was several times higher than normal, indicating extreme contamination.
“Since the waste particles are smaller than 75 micrometres, they can spread far and wide, making the soil infertile,” the study said.
The study also found that the concentration of PM2.5 exceeds the limit of ambient air quality standards. “Several people may be suffering from silicosis. The government needs to take immediate action to prevent the situation from getting out of hand,” it said.
Ugam Singh, another resident of Bhogiyawas, remembers when things were different. The continuous dumping of slurry slowly changed the landscape and the lives of people in Kishangarh, says the 65-year-old.
“Nowadays, the situation has worsened to such an extent that even the groundwater is no longer fit for consumption,” Singh said.
“The fluoride levels in the water are so high that it tastes salty. My teeth have started decaying and my bones have become weak,” he added, pointing to his teeth, which appeared pale, pitted and worn.
Singh said the residents of villages surrounding the dump yard have complained to the authorities, including officials of the Rajasthan State Pollution Control Board (RSPCB). But their requests fell on deaf ears.
“What I have come to understand is that it does not matter which government is in power. No one listens to the poor. To make the rich richer, the government sacrifices the interests of people like us. It feels as though our lives have no value,” Singh said.
“Even today all we want is for this marble slurry dumping to stop so that we can breathe freely again and our fields can become green and productive once again.”
Singh also claims that if residents of all the villages around the dumping yard were properly examined, almost every household would have someone suffering from respiratory problems such as asthma.
Last year, local environmentalist Drupad Malik filed a case before the National Green Tribunal over the harmful health and environmental effects of the Kishangarh dumping yard. The tribunal observed that unregulated dumping of marble slurry was contaminating groundwater and air. It directed the RSPCB to enforce monitoring, conduct sample inspections and penalise the marble processing units violating environmental norms.
Al Jazeera reached out to a senior official at the RSPCB’s regional office in Kishangarh, but she refused to speak on the matter.
Central University’s Sharma said the areas surrounding the Kishangarh dumping yard are unfit for human settlement. He said his research was shared with state authorities, but nothing was done to improve the environmental conditions in the area.
“There is a dire need to shift the dumping yard to another place where there is no human contact. This area has become extremely toxic and vulnerable to severe diseases. I am surprised that people are allowed to visit the site without masks and even have food there,” Sharma told Al Jazeera.
“I have forwarded several suggestions, including installing tile units, as [marble] slurry is used in tile manufacturing. This could, to some extent, help reduce pollution in Kishangarh,” he added.
Meanwhile, Ram Lal, a resident of Tokra village, about a 15-minute drive from Bhogiyawas, appealed to the government to find an alternative site for dumping the marble slurry.
“Kishangarh is full of slurry, and it is time to shift the dumping yard out of here to some other place where no one will suffer for at least two to three decades,” Lal told Al Jazeera.
“We also demand that free medical camps be set up to assess people whose health has declined because of the fine dust particles that have been flying in the air and settling here for years,” he said.
“No one from our village can afford it if someone develops a disease that costs thousands of rupees to treat.”

Israel ready for renewed Iran conflict: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:19:08 UTC
14:19:08 KST

AA Photo
Israel has completed preparations for renewed fighting with Iran, but no decision to resume attacks has been made, Yedioth Ahronoth reported on Oct. 31 as diplomatic contacts continued.
The Israeli military has finalized offensive and defensive preparations, while U.S. Central Command chief Brad Cooper has presented President Donald Trump with options for further strikes, according to the newspaper, cited by Anadolu Agency.
Citing unnamed political sources, the newspaper said the decision rests with Trump as he weighs an agreement with Tehran against renewed attacks coordinated with Israel. Israeli political and military leaders do not control whether another round of fighting begins, the report said.
Preparations have moved beyond planning. The Israeli air force has repeatedly flown dozens of fighter jets and refueling aircraft through Syrian and Iraqi airspace toward Iran’s borders to rehearse potential attack routes, according to the newspaper.
Cooper presented the military options at a meeting attended by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine. The newspaper said no decision to resume combat emerged from the meeting.
Citing media reports, it said 10 U.S. military transport aircraft had arrived at Israeli air bases in recent days, delivering equipment as Washington reinforced its forces in the region and prepared for possible military operations.
The unnamed sources questioned whether Washington had clear strategic objectives for another operation. Strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities, missile systems and other military capabilities would not necessarily bring down its government or change its policies, they said.
The sources suggested Washington could use the threat of force to secure an agreement on more favorable terms. They said any settlement failing to address Israeli concerns about Iran’s nuclear program, missile systems and armament would leave unresolved the threats Israel says it faces.
Another round of fighting could spread to Lebanon if Hezbollah joined, as it had previously, the sources said. Such an escalation could prolong the conflict and put further pressure on Israeli air defenses and stocks of interceptor missiles.
Alongside the military preparations, the newspaper cited reports of progress in indirect contacts between Washington and Tehran through Qatari mediation, aimed at opening direct negotiations.
Those talks would cover Iran’s nuclear program, the Strait of Hormuz and economic incentives for Tehran, with China and Russia potentially acting as guarantors of an agreement, according to the report.
The newspaper argued Israel’s challenge was to ensure any military action served its long-term security interests, with clear objectives, intended outcomes and conditions for ending hostilities.
The war began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28. An April ceasefire halted the fighting before hostilities between Washington and Tehran resumed in July as negotiations stalled.

Lebanese artist turns Israeli war remnants into ‘silent witnesses’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:14:21 UTC
14:14:21 KST

AA Photo
A Lebanese visual artist is transforming shrapnel, metal and other debris collected from buildings hit by Israeli attacks into sculptures and art objects, preserving the remnants as silent witnesses to the destruction and displacement caused by war.
Lina Jouni began working with the materials after returning home following Israel’s 2024 attacks on Lebanon. While sorting through the rubble around her home, including broken glass, stones, metal and cables, she realized the debris carried traces of a period that should not be forgotten.
After initially experimenting with glass, she turned to shrapnel, preserving its rust, curves and marks while making minimal alterations. The fragments have since become her artistic tools, taking the shape of faces, hands and abstract figures.
Some of the materials are collected by Jouni herself, while others are brought to her by people in the community. Through her work, she documents the destruction caused by Israeli attacks and preserve the memory of events, including the killings in Nabatieh, the 2024 pager explosions and attacks on vehicles. “I approached shrapnel as something capable of carrying history,” Jouni said. “I turned these pieces, which symbolize destruction, into instruments of life that tell the story of our survival.”
She said collecting the materials remained difficult, as some areas hit during the 2024 war were still inaccessible due to security risks and the presence of drones.
Describing reconstruction and the restoration of life as the central themes of her work, she said: “We experienced war and displacement, and we suffered. We need life again. Rebuilding means bringing life back.”
“We have materials, land and labor. We can build a new life and reconstruct at a lower cost,” she added.

Bulgaria heads to presidential runoff amid political instability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:11:22 UTC
14:11:22 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
Bulgarians will return to the polls Sunday to elect their president in a runoff between acting President Iliana Yotova and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov after neither candidate secured a majority in the first round.
Yotova and her running mate, Kiril Valchev, received 34.8% of the vote, while Gyurov and Georgi Kandev secured 32%, according to the Central Election Commission.
Turnout in the Oct. 25 vote stood at around 22.5%, the lowest recorded in the country's post-communist history.
A total of 27 candidates contested the first round.
A candidate must receive more than half of the valid votes, with turnout exceeding 50% of registered voters, to win in the first round under electoral rules. If those conditions are not met, the two leading candidates advance to a runoff.
The vote comes amid political instability in Bulgaria, which has held eight parliamentary elections since April 2021, including seven early elections.
The repeated parliamentary votes followed difficulties among political parties in securing the support needed to form stable governments.
Disagreements over coalition arrangements led to the collapse of successive attempts to establish regular governments, resulting in caretaker Cabinets and further early elections.
The latest parliamentary election, held in April, saw Progressive Bulgaria, led by former President Rumen Radev, win 131 of the National Assembly's 240 seats, giving the party an outright majority.
Yotova, who served as Radev's vice president, assumed the presidency after he resigned in January. Backed by Radev's Progressive Bulgaria party, she is seeking a full presidential mandate.
A victory would make Yotova Bulgaria's first elected female president, whose duties include representing the country, serving as commander-in-chief of the armed forces and exercising a veto on legislation.
Gyurov, an economist and former deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, served as caretaker prime minister before the parliamentary elections in April. He is backed by opposition parties.
The campaign has included debate about Bulgaria's foreign policy and its relations with Russia, Ukraine and Western allies.
Polling stations are scheduled to open at 7 am (0500GMT) and close at 8 pm (1800GMT).

Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest retreat was torched in an arson attack. Should it be rebuilt?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:00:04 UTC
14:00:04 KST

One of the last structural relics of Adolf Hitler’s dictatorship was conceived to project indomitable power. Last month it was destroyed in a suspected arson attack. Will it, and should it, be rebuilt?
The historic Nazi mountaintop retreat known as the Eagle’s Nest is perched on an Alpine peak at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000ft), with stunning views over southern Germany and Austria. In German, its design is known as Überwältigungsarchitektur, intended to overwhelm and intimidate.
Now, despite the efforts of 200 firefighters battling through the night, only charred ruins remain of the former guest lodge, tourist magnet and remembrance site destroyed in the blaze which started on 23 October. It is closed indefinitely.
“Even if a British air force bomb had struck the building on 25 April 1945, as it did most of the other structures in what was then the ‘Führer’s no-go zone’ on the Obersalzberg near Berchtesgaden, Hitler’s former tea house … could scarcely have been more severely damaged than it was by the fire,” Munich’s Süddeutsche newspaper said.
The fire has triggered a debate about whether, and how, to rebuild at the toxic site for the next generation of visitors, while mitigating the never-quite-banished risk of creating a shrine for neo-Nazis.
While the places associated with Hitler’s victims, including the former concentration camps, are preserved in perpetuity, the question of how to treat the perpetrators’ artefacts remains fraught, particularly given the resurgence of the far right in Germany and in Europe more broadly.
Local authorities believe the fire was deliberately started by a 33-year-old suspect with a history of mental illness. The site, which is owned by the German state of Bavaria, attracts more than 300,000 people each year but was closed to visitors that day. No one was injured.
Bavarian state culture minister Markus Blume has said a commission of experts in heritage conservation, construction and Germany’s culture of Holocaust remembrance would be enlisted to help determine the future of the Eagle’s Nest.
Given the building’s inextricable links to the Nazi regime and its crimes, Blume said, “any reconstruction must do justice to this historical responsibility”.
The marvel of Alpine engineering, which took 3,800 workers just over a year to build, is known more prosaically in German as the Kehlsteinhaus, for the mountain it rests on.
After a coach ride on serpentine roads through five tunnels, visitors rode a brass-plated lift, built into the rock, for 41 seconds to reach its portal.
“The prestige project and the road leading to it cost about 30 million Reichsmarks, equivalent to about 130 million British pounds today,” said Nazi-era historian Felix Bohr, author of Before the Downfall: Hitler’s Years in the Wolf’s Lair, which is being published in the UK in November.
“Hitler loved architecture that made other people look small. He insisted on being involved in the planning and construction of propaganda buildings.”
The lodge was completed in 1938, and mainly used to welcome and impress state guests, diplomats and select foreign journalists.
Just a short distance down the mountain at the Obersalzberg complex was Hitler’s own residence, the Berghof, where he spent about a quarter of his 12 years in office.
“Important decisions about prosecution and crime, about war and genocide were taken there,” said Sven Keller, director of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, an educational facility at the site.
“The surrounding mountain scenery was used as a backdrop for the construction of Hitler’s ‘Führer’ image. It offered spectacular, awe-inspiring views, and demonstrated technical prowess to subjugate even this rough natural environment.”
Inside, it had many of the trappings of Nazi bling, including Untersberg marble donated by Mussolini, Venetian mirrors and plump green leather armchairs recalling an English country manor house.
Hitler is known to have visited the Eagle’s Nest only 14 times until 1939 and then never again due to the second world war’s outbreak, when the tea house no longer matched the warrior-statesman image he wished to project, Bohr said. Close associates including his companion Eva Braun still used it regularly, however.
After the war, Obersalzberg became a recreation centre for occupying US troops, but the last vestiges of the Berghof were torn down and hundreds of trees were planted in its place – a fateful decision that has served as a cautionary tale.
“The Americans and the Bavarian state tried to prevent it from becoming a pilgrimage site for old Nazis and Hitler admirers. It didn’t work. If anything, a hidden site in the woods is even more interesting and mysterious,” Keller said. Nazi swastikas were often found carved into the tree bark.
He said a 180-degree pivot toward clearly marking the site and exposing its history, including how it fit into the Nazi power apparatus, proved the healthier approach.
“Public accessibility creates transparency whereas barriers or fences encourage rumours and legends,” Keller said. “Today, a popular public trail crosses the site, and mundane activities such as hiking keep it from becoming a sacred space (for neo-Nazis).”
Keller said transparency should be the watchword going forward.
“I cannot imagine that those responsible would opt for [a] simple reproduction of Nazi architecture, but it also can’t be left as a ruin – those tend to be even more fascinating,” he said.
“Instead, we should find ways to integrate the material remains and new information and education, showing the temporal layers, including the use as a tourist destination since the 1950s. The fire added a new layer to the history to Obersalzberg, and this should be visible too.”
New political realities in Germany and Austria, where the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) and Freedom Party lead the respective national polls, will have to be taken into account as well, he said.
Bohr said that troubling context led him to oppose any reconstruction of the Eagle’s Nest. “Hitler’s megalomania should remain a ruin. My suggestion would be to secure the remaining structure as far as possible and to use it to convey the history of the site,” he said.
“Particularly in view of the strength of the AfD and the rise of right-wing extremism in Germany, the focus should be on coming to terms with Nazi ideology, not on restoring its stage sets.”

What kind of prepper are you?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:00:04 UTC
14:00:04 KST

Perhaps, almost seven years later, there are aspects of the Covid lockdown some are nostalgic about, but it’s doubtful the great loo-roll hoarding of 2020 is one of them. And yet, here we appear to be again. Well, nearly.
Some shops sold out of baked beans and water this week, after government advice that we should stockpile supplies to prepare for emergencies “ranging from severe weather to cyber-attacks”. We must Be Ready – which is the name of the campaign that has launched. Security minister Dan Jarvis said that “those who can follow this advice should follow this advice”.
So, what’s your prepper style? Panic? Denial? Ambivalence? I’ve been asking everyone I come into contact with since the news of Be Ready broke. Their reaction to it has, each time, confirmed everything I already knew about who they were.
I’ve been mass interrogating because my prepper style is anxiety-tinged delusion. I’m nervous, but if enough people roll their eyes while saying the government is merely being dramatic, I will be completely reassured and unquestioningly believe them – ill-informed, both generally and precisely, members of the public – over experts armed with classified inside knowledge whose job it is to ensure the safety of the nation. This is ultimately because I’m lazy, and hate supermarkets, but also because I know who I am, and that is somebody who will not survive any kind of serious adversity. Worse, I won’t even try to, I’ll just immediately give up. I never understand why people attempt to get away in zombie apocalypse movies – let them eat your brain and be done with it. I despise running, and what would it be like even if humans did somehow triumph in the end? It would make that time when all the pubs and hairdressers closed in Covid and we were miserable and looked a proper state seem like a picnic.
My husband is the king of it’s-not-just-a-river-in-Egypt, and he is the only person I take no comfort from, when he says that Be Ready is a fuss over nothing. Entirely on brand, he is acting as though I heard about this campaign from some obscure conspiracy-theory site via the dark web, rather than literally the government of our country. He says he doesn’t need to prep because he is a natural hunter-gatherer, an optimist who always makes it work. He’ll catch a squirrel for dinner and roast it over the fire of sheer determination in his soul, totally in his element, ready to insist that it’s actually delicious and we should have tried it years ago. This is a man who would enjoy the challenge of a zombie apocalypse, thrive in it, not least because his hair is never that great anyway.
Slightly further from home, my most suspicious friend is about to get large amounts of cash out to hide around her home, and only hasn’t done so yet because she’s worried about general break-ins – and the eventual looting and pillaging. As soon as she decides whether she trusts the internet or humankind least, she will spring into action. Some particularly right-on, calm, efficient friends already have everything on the checklist in stock, and have since before Be Ready was a twinkle in Wes Streeting’s eye, you know, just in case. Mates at the other end of the organisational spectrum keep meaning to buy the stuff on the list, but have forgotten the list every time they’ve been shopping. My most head-in-the-sand pal, as expected, had absolutely no idea what I was on about when I asked for her thoughts, and told me to shut up when I tried to explain.
What we’re really talking about here is the way we deal with fear. How we manage to keep calm and carry on, go about our business as normal, despite our defence secretary using terms like “state-sponsored terrorism” and saying sentences such as, “in the face of those threats, which are not hypothetical but real, and not somewhere else but increasingly here, we have to step up and take seriously our national resilience as well as our national defence.” We all have our methods for trying to maintain the illusion we have any control.
The fact that everybody is behaving in a manner so true to form does make me wonder about the future of civilisation if something terrible goes down, and I, and all those like me, are wiped out. The world will then be made up of a very specific type of human being. And my husband, of course, resplendent in a squirrel loincloth.
Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

Are the US midterms going to see a blue wave of Democrats winning seats – or a blue flood?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

He spoke admiringly of a senator’s posterior. He baselessly accused a Muslim candidate of being a terrorist. He boasted about his renovations of the White House. He quipped that his own supporters couldn’t afford a hamburger at his Mar-a-Lago club. Every now and then, he spoke about the cost of living, and other everyday concerns of voters.
Donald Trump has held dozens of campaign rallies before next week’s US midterm elections. The 80-year-old remains convinced that he can prove the doubters wrong again and help Republicans retain control of the US Congress. But it was five words he uttered at this summer’s Republican convention in Dallas that could seal his party’s fate: “Pretend I’m on the ticket.”
That plea was music to the ears of Democrats. It helped ensure that the midterms will deliver a national verdict on Trump’s second term in the White House. And opinion polls suggest that the judgment will be damning, piercing his aura of invincibility, reshaping the final two years of his presidency and setting the stage for a fierce battle to succeed him.
“Donald Trump nationalised these races, and now they’ll lose seats because of it,” said Michael Steele, a former chair of the Republican National Committee. “He made himself the referendum. Individual candidates wanted to run their individual races but he told them: ‘Put me on the ballot.’ He has political instincts for himself, but no political instincts for the party.”
Pain is the norm for White House incumbents when the midterms roll around. In 1994, Bill Clinton suffered a 54-seat setback in the House of Representatives; in 2010, Barack Obama lost 63; in 2018, Trump himself lost 40. He seems unlikely to defy history this time. Trump goes into the elections with the lowest approval rating of any president before the midterms since Harry Truman’s Democrats were crushed 80 years ago.
The coalition that in 2024 powered Trump to the greatest comeback in modern political history has suffered blow after blow: his failure to fully release the Jeffrey Epstein files detailing ties of the elite to the child sex offender; the growth of datacentres in rural communities; an eight-month-old war in Iran that he promised would be over in weeks; a relentless rise in the cost of fuel and food.
The anger over Trump’s broken promises has been compounded by a whiff of corruption, and the perception that he is using the presidency to enrich himself and his family. He accepted a plane from Qatar to use as Air Force One, decorated the Oval Office in gold, demolished the White House East Wing to make way for a $400m ballroom and is planning a triumphal arch in Washington. His personal fortune meanwhile has surged – from $2.3bn in 2024 to $6.5bn, according to Forbes.
‘Much more macro than Maga’
With Republicans clinging to a paper-thin 218–214 margin in the House and 53–47 lead in the Senate, opinion polls indicate a rising “blue wave”. A recent Reuters/Ipsos survey gave Democrats an 11-point lead, 47% to 36%, on the generic congressional ballot, while Trump’s approval rating stood at 32%. Voters will also choose governors in 36 states and three US territories, and decide thousands of state legislative contests.
Tens of millions of early votes have already been cast, with habitual Republican turnout lagging behind Democratic participation in critical battlegrounds. So dire is the environment for Republicans that conservative Super Pacs backed by billionaire Elon Musk, who has poured $366m into saving Republican candidates, are being forced to dump emergency funds into strongholds like Kansas, Iowa and Texas.
Trump won the presidency in 2024 after promising to curb inflation and lower prices; instead, the opposite has happened. Across the country, voters are confronting an affordability crisis exacerbated by two defining choices of Trump’s second term: a sweeping regime of foreign tariffs and the fateful decision to launch airstrikes on Iran in February.
Chris Matthews, a political commentator and former presidential speechwriter and congressional aide, said: “He’s losing on cost of living and affordability. Older people on limited incomes are focusing on what it costs to live each month. It’s much more macro than Maga. No matter what he does for Maga people, the power of macroeconomics is much stronger and people are going to vote against him.”
The economic fallout of the Iran war, which Trump frequently downplays as a “little detour”, has reverberated across global energy markets. Diesel prices have soared, sending shock waves through agriculture and freight transport from the Central valley of California to the grain belts of Iowa and Ohio.
Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and former official in the Clinton White House, points out that voters can directly attribute their economic misery to the president. “There’s a very clear line between his actions and the things people don’t like,” she said.
“It’s going to be the tariffs and it’s going to be the war: both self-inflicted wounds. He didn’t have to raise tariffs; that was his theory of the world, which turned out to be wrong. Bombing nuclear sites in Iran was one thing, but going to all-out war turned out to be a mistake. Voters connect his actions to things they don’t like.”
This frustration is fuelling an energetic mobilisation among Democratic candidates, particularly women running in districts that once seemed out of reach. Jessica Mackler, the president of Emilys List, which is backing 247 female candidates this cycle, notes that voters feel the economic system is actively stacked against them.
“Voters understand that the corruption coming out of Washington is directly linked to why they can’t get ahead, and why they find it so hard to make ends meet,” Mackler said. “Cost of living is a huge driver but voters are desperate for new leadership who have lived their pain and understand it.”
A ‘devastating referendum’ on Trump
For months, Republican strategists urged their candidates in tight suburban races to keep national politics at arm’s length, and focus on local accomplishments, perhaps hoping that Trump might quietly concentrate on his day job in Washington. Instead, the president has embarked on a whirlwind tour across the country, denouncing Democrats as “communists” while touting a strong economy, secure border and historic drop in violent crime.
But Steele, a co-host of the MS Now network’s the Weeknight, argues that core conservative voters feel increasingly betrayed by a president who promised to avoid foreign entanglements and bring down costs. “Donald Trump lied to his tribe … He said he wouldn’t engage us in foreign wars; we’re now turning the corner into a year of a war he started and people are saying: ‘I can’t even afford to put gas in my car.’”
Perhaps no development in the 2026 midterms is more alarming to Republican strategists than the dramatic erosion of support among Latino voters. In 2024, Trump made historic inroads with Latino men, sparking triumphant declarations of a permanent multiethnic, working-class coalition.
Yet no sooner had he taken the oath of office than he unleashed an aggressive, high-visibility deportation campaign featuring heavily armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids in cities and agricultural hubs.
Larry Jacobs, founder and director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota, said: “Donald Trump launched his radical deportation strategy and it has powerfully alienated the fastest-growing part of the electorate.
“A year ago, Republicans thought they had established a new Hispanic coalition that would guarantee five new seats in Texas alone. They may lose all of them. Economics is a driving factor, but opposition to Trump’s deportation policies has contributed massively to the magnitude of the defections.”
Henry Olsen, a senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center thinktank in Washington, notes that the Latino shift is visible across public polling and state-level data, saying: “Whether it’s a 15-point shift or a 30-point shift, it’s a big deal. Unless every piece of evidence we have is wrong, Latino voters are having serious buyers’ remorse.”
This dynamic is evident in Texas, where no Democrat has won statewide office since 1994. James Talarico, a 37-year-old state representative and former public school teacher who preaches a gospel of social justice, is taking on Republican state attorney general Ken Paxton in the most expensive Senate race in history.
Paxton, a staunch Trump ally, has been bogged down by years of corruption allegations, personal scandal and securities fraud charges. Despite $300m in outside Republican spending, led by Musk, Talarico has a narrow lead in most polls.
Jacobs views Texas as a bellwether for the post-Trump Republican party. “If Paxton loses, it’s going to send a very powerful signal to future Republican leaders about how they handle immigration,” he said. “It proves that attacking the fastest-growing part of the electorate is political suicide. Texas is a devastating referendum on Donald Trump.”
A test for Democrats
While Democrats appear heavily favoured to pick up the four net seats required to capture the House of Representatives, their path to taking the Senate is a steeper climb. Yet because of Trump’s dismal approval ratings and the economic shock of the Iran war, the Senate battlefield has expanded into states that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024.
In Ohio, former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown is mounting a comeback bid against incumbent Republican Jon Husted. Brown, a grizzled populist with deep ties to organised labour, has capitalised on working-class anger over fuel prices and plant closures, as well as local opposition to datacentres. In a peculiar recurring feature of his rallies in the state, Trump has frequently veered off-script to praise Husted’s physique. (“His ass was like a big piece of muscle,” according to the president.)
In Michigan, Republican Mike Rogers is up against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a 41-year-old doctor and former Detroit health director bidding to become the first Muslim senator in the US. Republicans have aggressively targeted El-Sayed over past foreign policy statements, while pro-Israel Super Pacs have poured millions of dollars into the state to defeat him. Trump has launched Islamophobic tirades, calling El-Sayed a “jihadist”.
Olsen said: “El-Sayed is the biggest test for progressives. If he wins stateside in an industrial heartland state like Michigan, progressives will argue they have the upper hand heading into 2028.”
However, Kamarck cautions against over-interpreting progressive strength. She insisted: “The progressives are a minuscule portion of the Democratic party. This is an overblown story. The moderates are winning the vast majority of these races across the country.”
In Maine, veteran Republican senator Susan Collins is fighting for her political life against Democrat Troy Jackson, a lumberjack and former president of the state senate. Collins has attempted to distance herself from Trump, appearing on the trail with independent former senator Joe Manchin, but Democrats have relentlessly hammered her votes for conservative supreme court justices and other Trump priorities.
In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola is mounting a challenge to Republican senator Dan Sullivan. The contest has become embroiled in a legal dispute after the justice department sought to block certification of a possible Peltola victory. Her allies reportedly helped recruit a decoy candidate with the name Dan Sullivan to confuse voters. Peltola’s campaign denies involvement.
‘He’ll do anything’
Election integrity remains a broader national concern. Trump’s repeated, unsubstantiated claims of election fraud have prompted Democrats and voting-rights organisations to prepare legal teams and observers for disputes or federal interference. The administration says federal election monitors will follow the law, and has denied plans to send troops or immigration agents to polling stations.
Tara Setmayer, a co-founder and chief executive of the Seneca Project, a women-led political action committee, said: “I am extremely worried. We have seen what Donald Trump has done when he had guardrails; now he has none. He has power and people who are aligned with him in the attack on our election integrity in positions of power.
“This is a great concern to me because Trump is looking at the sun setting on his presidency and we all know that he is deathly afraid of being out of power. He’ll do anything to stay in power, even if that means creating another constitutional crisis to try to stop Congress from being seated. We cannot suffer from a lack of imagination of what these people are capable of.”
A Democratic victory in either chamber will effectively stall Trump’s domestic legislative agenda, leaving his administration to rely on executive orders. Hakeem Jeffries, who would likely become the first Black speaker of the House, has pledged to immediately unleash subpoena power to investigate administration corruption, foreign policy decisions in Iran, and the personal financial enrichment of the Trump family.
Jacobs said: “It’s going to be a fistfight. I’m not expecting major legislation to pass. I think there will be extensive investigations of Donald Trump and his cabinet, and that’s what we’re going to get for two years.”
Steele believes that a Democratic House will immediately assert control over federal purse strings. “Congress will freeze money on projects like tearing down the East Wing for Trump’s ballroom, and they’ll reassert oversight over the Kennedy Center,” he said, referring to the national arts complex and living memorial to the 35th president. “Trump is effectively a lame duck now. The rest of the country knows his time is coming to an end.”
Indeed, before the last vote is counted, attention will likely turn to the presidential contest in 2028. For Republicans, a crushing midterm loss could accelerate the race to a post-Trump future. JD Vance is currently positioned as the heir apparent to the Maga movement, but figures such as the senator Ted Cruz of Texas and the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, could also be in contention.
Steele commented: “Republicans need to recognise that the future of the party does not rest solely with the Maga base. It rests with winning back the suburban, moderate and Hispanic voters this administration has isolated.”
Under pressure from a restive base, Democrats will also be preparing for a sprawling contest to decide the future direction of their party – and how it can turn the page on the Trump era. The next Democratic presidential candidate is equally uncertain, with outgoing California governor Gavin Newsom, Georgia senator Jon Ossoff, New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and even former vice-president and 2020 nominee Kamala Harris among those regularly mentioned.
Bill Whalen, a research fellow at the Hoover Institution thinktank in Stanford, California, said: “Voters are tired. When you combine high prices, the endless argument and the constant noise of Donald Trump, people want a change from the status quo.”
“On November 3, the voters are going to speak – and Donald Trump is not going to like what they have to say,” he predicted.

Piles of rubbish, power cuts and potholes: anger grows over Johannesburg’s run-down infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

One week before the local elections in South Africa, the pavements and roads of the Johannesburg township Alexandra were filled with piles of rubbish, rotting in the heat. At the Jukskei River, its banks choked with rubble and litter, foul-smelling brown water flowed out of a culvert.
“We’ve got way too many challenges,” said Semadi Manganye, the chief executive of Alexandra Water Warriors, an environmental NGO that organises clean-ups of the river and plants trees on its banks. “If it’s not electricity, it’s water. If it’s not water, it’s waste.”
Manganye acknowledged the challenges of providing public services in a city whose population grew by 10% to 4.8 million between the 2011 and 2022 censuses. “I have an understanding of why they’re failing,” he said. “But we’ve got to mitigate against this – we knew that it was going to happen.”
On 4 November, up to 29 million South African voters will go to the polls for local elections amid deep discontent with the water cuts, power outages and potholes that plague the country’s 257 municipalities. Their problems are so deep that even the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, has admitted: “Too many of our municipalities are failing to meet the needs and expectations of the people they are meant to serve.”
In the last financial year (2024-25), only 39 local governments, 15% of the total, received a “clean” audit from the country’s auditor general. Two-thirds are “financially distressed”, according to a parliamentary budget office report.
Nowhere are the problems more pressing than in Johannesburg, South Africa’s largest city and commercial capital. The city has been ruled by a series of unstable coalitions, with 10 changes of mayor in the past decade. Authorities have admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog. It is estimated that a quarter of the water bought by the municipal water body Johannesburg Water is lost to leaks.
At a public meeting in Rabie Ridge, a township in the city’s north-east, about 400 people berated the incumbent mayor, Dada Morero, and executives from Johannesburg’s electricity utility, City Power.
One person said she had had no power for six months. Another said her mother had been forced to turn to loan sharks after receiving energy bills as high as 6,000 rand a month when her monthly pension was 2,000 rand.
“If there is any organisation that is dysfunctional it is this organisation … it is failing,” one man said, drawing huge cheers from the audience.
Even some affluent northern suburbs are going without piped water for weeks at a time. After a month-long outage about six months ago, people in parts of Melville and Westdene have been unable to predict when they will get water since September.
“The word I’d use is desperate, because literally there’s been almost no water at all,” said Kate Spiller, a semi-retired management consultant. “During the day, there’s dribs and drabs. And then sometimes in the middle of night, my husband’s been able to fill a couple of five-litre bottles and then it’s gone dry again.”
Spiller and her husband drive 10 minutes almost daily to a mosque that has a borehole to fill up about a dozen five-litre bottles, which they use to take bucket showers. “It’s incapacitating … you’re always planning, you’re always thinking: ‘We need to get water, we’d better make a plan,’” she said.
“Overall, Johannesburg is providing the necessary services to our communities,” Morero said in an interview after the Rabie Ridge meeting. “Isolated areas where they don’t have [services], we are focusing on right now.”
He acknowledged parts of the inner city were without power, due to a “collapsed” substation, but blamed “vandalism” and criminals. “From time to time, with the JPMD [Johannesburg Metropolitan police department] we try to push back, but there are also syndicates who are also organised and affecting our infrastructure,” he said.
However, experts have said many city politicians and officials are themselves corrupt. An October report by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime said: “Governance failure in the CoJ [city of Johannesburg] has given birth to a criminal ecosystem.”
“People in charge of the supply chain system can easily get backhanders,” said Rashid Seedat, a former city official and the executive director of the Gauteng City-Region Observatory, a research organisation.
“Of course, corruption is the metro police officer taking a bribe of 200 rand [and] a 200m rand tender. It’s across the board and endemic in the entire system and acceptable.”
The Democratic Alliance, South Africa’s second-largest political party, has mounted an energetic campaign in Johannesburg, under the 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor Helen Zille, to try to unseat the African National Congress (ANC) and its coalition partners, the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) and the populist Patriotic Alliance.
Zille, who is white, has previously caused controversy, particularly among black voters, including for tweets in 2017 that said colonialism was not completely negative. However, viral stunts that have drawn attention to Johannesburg’s infrastructure issues, such as Zille snorkelling in an enormous flooded pothole, have helped to put the DA ahead of the ANC in the polls (voters choose parties and councillors, who in turn elect the mayor).
The DA has polled between 29% and 36% in October, compared with 22% to 27% for the ANC, which is fielding three possible mayoral candidates amid factional infighting. However, this may not be enough for Zille to form a coalition, analysts say.
“In order to understand Joburg, you actually have to zoom out a bit and look at all of Gauteng [province],” said Ziyanda Stuurman of Africa Practice, a consultancy. “Over the last decade, and especially since 2021, there’s been this very clear working relationship between the ANC, EFF and ActionSA across the three municipalities [Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni].
“Once in-principle coalition arrangements are agreed to, you’ve seen the EFF back ANC and ActionSA mayors across all three cities and there’s been a negotiation keeping in mind all three.”
Stuurman said a coalition similar to recent ones could lead to five more years of decline in Johannesburg. “It’s been much more horse-trading than it actually has been about the city’s best interests.”

Ukraine-Skeptic Faces Challenge in Bulgarian Vote: What to Watch

Why 1 November holds a special place in Bulgaria's calendar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
04:59:26 UTC
13:59:26 KST

Author
Katerina Hapsali
National Awakeners Day
Why 1 November holds a special place in Bulgaria's calendar
Sunday 1 November 2026 06:35
Sunday, 1 November 2026, 06:35
PHOTO BTA Archive
Font size
Some dates have a special place in the hearts of Bulgarians. They bring people together, inspire pride and offer a welcome respite from the arguments and divisions of everyday life. One of them is 1 November – National Awakeners Day, a distinctly Bulgarian holiday whose meaning goes beyond honouring the achievements of the past.
The day was originally dedicated to the educators, writers, revolutionaries and spiritual leaders who worked for the freedom and advancement of the Bulgarian people during the National Revival, when Bulgarian lands were still under Ottoman rule.
Today, their names are familiar to every Bulgarian. Among them are the monk Paisius of Hilendar, Bishop Sofroniy of Vratsa, the educator Neofit Rilski, Petar Beron, author of the first modern Bulgarian textbook, the revolutionaries Georgi Sava Rakovski, Hristo Botev and Vasil Levski, and Ivan Vazov, author of the first Bulgarian novel.
PHOTO BNR Archive
These are just some of the writers, thinkers and revolutionaries who helped sustain a sense of Bulgarian identity and encouraged the struggle for freedom and national progress before the country’s liberation in 1878.
But Bulgaria’s national awakeners did more than inspire admiration. Encouraging people to question the status quo and stand up for their beliefs takes more than persuasion and personal example. It takes passion, honesty and sometimes a willingness to challenge and provoke.
Many addressed their fellow Bulgarians directly, often in uncompromising terms. They appealed to their conscience, challenged their complacency and refused to let them remain indifferent. They were a necessary thorn in society’s side – an uncomfortable presence that helped it move forward.
Writer and poet Ivan Vazov, author of the first Bulgarian novel.
PHOTO archives.government.bg
Every nation needs people who challenge it to think, question and resist indifference. Bulgaria has a holiday dedicated to just such people.
National Awakeners Day was first celebrated in Plovdiv on 1 November 1909, the feast day of St John of Rila, Bulgaria’s patron saint, according to the old calendar. It became an official holiday in 1922 at the initiative of Stoyan Omarchevski, then Minister of Public Education.
Omarchevski believed that their achievements should remain part of the nation’s collective memory. Their example, he argued, could continue to inspire future generations and sustain a sense of national purpose.
The holiday was observed until 1945, when it was abolished by the communist regime. It was officially reinstated in 1992. Since then, the meaning of the Bulgarian word "buditel", usually translated as "awakener", has gradually expanded. Today, it can refer to anyone who helps keep a society intellectually, culturally or morally awake, regardless of the period in which they live.
Poet and revolutionary Hristo Botev.
PHOTO Facebook/ Hristo Botev National museum
This year, 1 November coincides with the second round of Bulgaria’s presidential election. Some will see symbolism in that coincidence, others irony. But perhaps it serves above all as a reminder of the people who once inspired Bulgarians to look beyond their immediate concerns – and of how much the country still needs leaders with the courage, integrity and vision to do the same.
Recognising that need may itself be a form of awakening.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) expressed support for the LGBTQ+ community ahead of the 24th Taiwan Pride, praising those who have spoken out about their experiences and calling for greater understanding and respect.
In a Facebook post, Lai said a truly free society requires not only the right to speak but also a willingness to listen to people's concerns and experiences. He said this was the central message of this year's parade, themed "Our Voices, Our Journey."
Lai acknowledged that many members of the LGBTQ+ community have faced prejudice, harassment, and other challenges while growing up. Referring to recent controversy over heavy-handed law enforcement in recent days, he expressed concern that the understanding and respect the community had worked hard to achieve could be undermined.
He said the parade brings together participants from Taiwan and around the world, allowing people with different backgrounds and life experiences to express themselves freely and appreciate one another's perspectives. He offered his support to everyone taking part and said their voices deserved to be heard and respected.
Lai noted that Taiwan became the first country in Asia to legalize same-sex marriage in 2019, following years of advocacy and public debate. The change gave same-sex couples the legal right to marry and establish families, per UDN.
“Seven years ago, Taiwan became the first country in Asia to legalize same-sex marriage. This is the result of many years of hard work, giving those who love each other the right to start a family. Equality cannot be reversed; to ensure everyone can truly live in peace, we still need to continue our efforts in our daily lives,” said Lai.
As president, Lai said the government must protect everyone's dignity, regardless of gender, sexual orientation, or gender identity, and ensure equal opportunities and the freedom to pursue happiness.
He added that respect for these principles extends to the exercise of public authority. Law enforcement agencies should act within the law, respect privacy, and treat everyone equally so that no one is intimidated or targeted because of their identity.
Lai said the world sees Taiwan's rainbow and how its people use democracy and freedom to bring different voices together in public spaces. He said Taiwanese people cherish these freedoms and should take seriously every voice reminding them that the country can do better.
