'My husband made me feel like a nymphomaniac': Rediscovering sexuality after divorce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
04:49:41 UTC
13:49:41 KST

"When I was married, there was a lot of criticism directed at me about our sexuality within the marriage. As far as my husband was concerned, I was some kind of nymphomaniac, and I remember how I really had to silence the passionate, sexual woman I was.
"So when I entered the dating world as a divorced woman, I carried that inner voice with me for a long time, a belittling voice telling me to keep a low profile. I also come from the religious-Zionist community, and for many years I worked as a sex counselor under the radar because I was afraid my profession wouldn't be accepted by my children's educational institutions," says Eden Ziv, a sex and relationship counselor trained in sex and couples therapy who helps individuals and couples reconnect with their bodies, desire, pleasure and love.
Ziv lectures on sexuality, relationships and personal empowerment, and facilitates women's and men's discussion groups. She joined the "Sex Appeal" podcast to discuss the journey divorced men and women go through as they rediscover their sexuality after marriage.
'People thought I'd lost my mind'
"I got divorced 27 years ago, after seven years of marriage and two wonderful children. One of the reasons I divorced was that the sex and the relationship weren't working," she admits. "I was 28, very young, and I felt tremendous guilt about having failed. For me, not being able to keep a family together over time felt like a terrible failure.
"On the other hand, it was also the moment when I told myself it was time to choose myself. I wasn't willing to continue that intergenerational pattern of being a submissive, diminished woman in a position of weakness. I wanted to start doing things for myself."
How did people react to your decision to divorce?
"Naturally, I encountered plenty of raised eyebrows. People thought I'd lost my mind, that I was going through some kind of rebellion and would soon come to my senses. But I didn't. And that's something many people who decide to divorce have in common: the realization that it's time to choose themselves, that it's not too late and that there's a wonderful opportunity for something new.
"I'm certainly not saying this to encourage people to end their relationships and get divorced. But I do think it's important for people to reach a place where they're capable of choosing themselves. And I chose myself. Once I did, I began exploring workshops, tantra and sexuality education because I knew they would help me live a life filled with pleasure."
What challenges might someone face after ending a marriage?
"The first challenge is the physical changes we experience, especially women. Most of us have been through pregnancies and childbirth. Our bodies aren't what they used to be. There are stretch marks, veins, cellulite, our breasts have changed. Then you enter the dating world as a newly divorced woman and start meeting new men, and suddenly there's a lot of anxiety about body image.
"How will they react to my stomach, my breasts, the marks on my body, the fat, the changes in my weight? Things have changed. I'm not the same Eden I was when I got married all those years ago.
"This is something I hear constantly in the women's groups I lead: the fear surrounding their changed bodies. Men have similar concerns, including weight gain and hair loss. We're supposed to start something new, but we're already people with life experience, emotional baggage, past experiences, pain and inhibitions. And in the middle of all that, we're supposed to meet someone else who brings their own baggage.
"For example, a man once came to me for therapy because he was absolutely terrified. He believed his penis was small because that was what his wife had repeatedly told him. She constantly belittled him, saying: 'You have a small dick,' 'Your dick is worthless,' 'Your dick is so small I can't even feel it.'
"He was such a sweet man, but he was frightened of everything. He said to me, 'Eden, how am I even supposed to take that step? How do I meet new women after what I've been through?'"
Wow. So what did you do?
"We started working on his self-image, his connection to his penis and his relationship with his body. We worked on helping him connect with his penis in all its different states. It was incredibly moving to see the transformation that took place. It wasn't an easy process for him, but it was deeply meaningful.
"The words we carry with us, and the beliefs that others instill in us alongside them, affect people of every gender. They can influence us and our sexual performance for years."
Words can leave deeper scars than physical blows. They can echo in people's minds for decades.
"Exactly. Those words were still there, very present. I was deeply moved that he was able to come to therapy and that he specifically chose to go through this process with a woman to reconnect with that part of himself."
What does that kind of therapeutic process actually involve?
"First, it's about understanding what he thinks about himself and normalizing a lot of things. I talk with him about his personal experiences, about how he experiences his body. We discuss beginning to get to know his body differently.
"We also talk about self-pleasure, not simply masturbation. It's about exploring the body as a whole, not just the genitals. As a society, we place an enormous amount of importance on our genitals when it comes to sexuality, but our sexuality doesn't exist only in our genitals.
"Another part of the work was reducing his need for validation from others. We don't ignore what happened because we heard those words, and I can't erase that past experience. It happened. The words were spoken and heard. But the goal is to stop drawing your sense of worth from that experience or allowing it to control you.
"It's about understanding that the experience doesn't define you. I explained to him how incredibly important it was for him to build a strong sense of self for his own sake, not for anyone else's."
'They realize they have a problem with sex, and they don't want to carry it into a new relationship'
"That was his experience, but you also asked what else people bring with them into the dating world after divorce," Ziv continues. "Beyond low self-esteem, they bring a great deal from their previous relationships.
"Women have told me in my clinic that they used to have sex just to check it off a list, that they didn't enjoy the sex they had with their husbands. Some experienced actual pain during intercourse because they weren't even lubricated. They come to me because they recognize that something isn't working in their sexuality, and they don't want to carry that problem into their future relationships.
"Sometimes they've been told they're 'frigid,' that they're not sexual at all, that they don't know how to have sex, that they're bad in bed, worthless, clueless or uninterested. They hear things like, 'Who would even want you?' Those cruel words continue to echo inside them. They tell me, 'Who would even want me? He said I was terrible, that I was awful, so why would anyone else want me?'
"And I tell them, we're going to go through a process that has nothing to do with the next man who comes along, or any of the men who might come after him. This is about you. It's a gift you're giving yourself because you deserve it.
"I believe we need to truly live our lives, not just exist on the sidelines. I don't want to live someone else's life. I don't want someone else defining my life. I want to live this life as fully as I possibly can, with complete presence, purpose and intention."
There's a stereotype that people become extremely sexually adventurous after divorce. People talk about divorced women wearing leopard print and going to sex parties. How much truth is there to that stereotype?
"The red lipstick and leopard-print clothing are such stereotypes, although I wore red lipstick and had red nails for years myself," she says, laughing. "I think it really depends on what stage of life you're at when you divorce. But some people develop this enormous appetite for life. At least initially, they want to devour the world, especially if they experienced almost nothing sexually during their marriage.
"And often, what drives that is the need for validation from someone else. To feel that I'm worthy, desirable, good in bed or wanted, I might try to have as many sexual conquests as possible. Those experiences aren't always balanced or beneficial, but there's also genuine curiosity involved."
So a lot of it comes from a sense of something missing? Because I feel terrible and I'm grieving my previous relationship, I want to prove to myself that I can attract anyone, that I can seduce people?
"Exactly. And that can lead to less positive experiences in those sexual encounters because when people approach them from a place of emptiness, things tend not to go as well."
For example?
"First, we expect the other person to fill that emptiness. But the other person isn't responsible for our orgasms, or for filling any emotional void we have. We need to do what I call working 'from the inside out.' We need to create that internal connection and then carry it outward.
"That means doing the work on ourselves first, connecting with our sexuality, our bodies, our pleasure, desires and fantasies, but also with our boundaries.
"We need to reach a place where we know what we want and what genuinely feels good for us, men and women alike. Only then can we enter experiences that are much more appropriate for us and encounter things that are truly empowering and healthy.
"But as long as we're being guided by other people's voices, including the voices saying, 'Go screw everyone, this is your time to go wild,' which are things divorced people say to one another, we may end up having experiences that aren't actually right for us."
That makes a lot of sense. Otherwise, sex becomes something you check off a list to prove you've done it and experienced it, rather than allowing yourself to be truly present.
"That's exactly it. Sex becomes mechanical, and people can come away from those experiences feeling hurt. There's also an enormous fear of being alone, a fear that nobody will want me. So when someone comes along who does want me, especially if they're pursuing us a little and showing interest beyond sex, we might say, 'Well, maybe I should give this a chance,' even if the person isn't actually right for us.
"And then we find ourselves in a situation that isn't necessarily good for us, one that doesn't always help us move forward."
What's the most common fear you've encountered in your clinic among divorced men and women returning to the dating scene?
"For men, it's mainly concerns about sexual performance. If they've experienced erectile difficulties or premature ejaculation, they're afraid those problems will happen again. Sometimes performance anxiety develops simply because they're so excited or nervous about meeting someone new. For these men, the need to perform becomes something that controls them. But what if I don't feel like having sex? What if I'm tired? Does that mean I'm not good enough? That I'm not sexual enough? That I don't want her? The meanings men attach to these situations can be incredibly restrictive.
"I led a men's discussion group some time ago, and there was one divorced man who was very macho. For almost the entire evening, he boasted about how great he was in bed, how successful he was with women and how he refused to commit to a relationship because that was the only way he could enjoy everything life had to offer. But as the evening went on, a different voice suddenly emerged. He became very vulnerable and began talking about his performance anxiety and the fact that he didn't always get an erection, something that frightened him.
"It was as though layers were being peeled away. You wouldn't believe what happened in that room. It was a defining moment, and it was incredibly moving. I paused for a moment and allowed some silence. Then I told him how moving it was to see him bring that vulnerability into the room because suddenly he didn't have to prove how macho he was. Suddenly, something genuine emerged. A vulnerable man showing his sensitivity is, in my eyes, one of the most powerful things there is."
How can people deal with sexual trauma or negative experiences from the past without allowing them to control a new relationship?
"I think the first thing is communication. Communication is the key, and it's one of the hardest things for us to do. We find it incredibly difficult to communicate what we truly need and want, and to talk about our difficulties and struggles.
"Performance anxiety, for example, often becomes a vicious cycle. Someone experiences it once in one relationship and then carries it into future relationships because the experience keeps echoing in their mind. That's where good therapy can really help heal the emotional wounds left by the past."

UN demands investigation after staffer’s death in Houthi custody in Yemen
Mohammad el-Shami had been held since June 2024, when he and many other UN and NGO workers were accused of being spies.
The United Nations has demanded an investigation into the death of an employee in Houthi detention in Yemen.
Mohammad el-Shami, a staff member of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) in Yemen, died more than a month ago, but his family was only recently informed, the UN said in a statement on Saturday.
The Houthis did not say how he died, but his family “deserve to know the truth”, said UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk.
The human rights chief also demanded “full transparency” from the Houthi authorities and an “urgent, independent and thorough investigation” into el-Shami’s death.
El-Shami had been arbitrarily held in Houthi custody since June 2024, when he and more than 60 people working with the UN and other NGOs were detained and accused of being part of an “American-Israeli spy network”.
“I am also gravely concerned” for the seven other OHCHR personnel who were detained alongside el-Shami and are still being held, Turk said. “I appeal again for their immediate and unconditional release.”
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a separate statement on Saturday that he was “appalled” by el-Shami’s death and echoed Turk’s calls for an investigation.
The UN is “urgently seeking answers” from the group about the circumstances of his death, Guterres added.
El-Shami is the second UN staff member to die in Houthi detention, following the death of a World Food Programme staffer in February 2025.
A total of 72 UN staffers and NGO workers, including el-Shami, have been detained by the Houthis.
The UN paused operations in parts of Houthi-held Yemen in February 2025 over concerns for the safety of its employees.
The rebel group has previously paraded some detainees on television channels, presenting them as collaborators with Western intelligence agencies and Israel.
On October 6, the UN announced that a World Food Programme employee had been released after being “arbitrarily detained” by the Iran-backed group.

Awad Rjoob and Tarek Chouiref
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
Israeli authorities have issued 9,518 demolition or stop-work notices against Palestinian structures in the occupied West Bank since the start of 2015, a Palestinian government commission said Saturday.
The Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said the notices halted construction and left properties under threat, disrupting the lives of families and limiting ability of communities to build homes, expand services and sustain livelihoods.
The report, obtained by Anadolu, documented 9,174 notices between 2015 and 2025 and another 344 in the first nine months of 2026.
The commission cautioned that its figures did not necessarily capture every notice issued by Israeli authorities. The tally was based on cases documented by the commission and partner legal organizations, including the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center and the Society of St. Yves.
Hebron accounted for the largest share, with 2,697 notices, followed by Bethlehem with 1,310, Ramallah and al-Bireh with 1,118, and Jerusalem with 929.
The annual total peaked at 1,333 in 2023, compared with 701 in 2015.
Separately, data from the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) showed that nearly 12,000 structures were demolished during the same period, including 1,698 funded by donors.
The demolitions displaced more than 18,000 Palestinians and affected approximately 843,000, according to OCHA.
The UN office records demolitions carried out on grounds including the lack of Israeli-issued building permits, as punitive measures or during military operations.

China Focus: China's new rules to protect children's health, safety take effect
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:41:41 CST
13:41:41 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Four new or revised mandatory national standards and regulations to better protect children's health and safety took effect in China on Sunday, covering classroom lighting, youth sports training, and children's products and toys.
The rules aim to reduce health and safety risks in children's daily learning, physical activities and play, with a greater emphasis on prevention and clearer safety requirements.
BETTER LIGHTING TO PROTECT EYESIGHT
A revised national standard on classroom lighting and daylighting sets stricter requirements for the lighting environment in primary and secondary schools, as China steps up efforts to curb myopia among children and adolescents.
The standard addresses aspects such as natural light, lighting uniformity, blue-light hazards and flicker, aiming to enhance the comfort of classrooms for students who spend long hours reading and writing. It also calls for regular inspections and upkeep of lighting equipment.
The revised standard will also apply to secondary vocational schools, while extracurricular training institutions serving school-age children are encouraged to follow its requirements.
Liu Yiwei, a lecturer at Capital Normal University, said the new standard sets more detailed mandatory requirements for classroom lighting, providing a measurable and enforceable framework to support efforts to prevent myopia among young students.
It incorporates the principle of putting health first into educational settings and places greater emphasis on preventing myopia before it develops, Liu added.
MORE STANDARDIZED SPORTS TRAINING
A new code of conduct for youth sports training sets requirements for training venues, class sizes, instructor qualifications and safety management, addressing concerns over unsafe facilities and uneven coaching standards in a rapidly growing market.
It is essential for training providers to tailor courses to align with the ages, physical conditions, and varying levels of athletic ability of children. Instructors must hold recognized qualifications, while people with specified criminal records, including those involving sexual abuse or physical assault, are prohibited from working in the sector.
The rules also establish limits on class sizes and require additional first-aid support for high-risk sports, helping create safer conditions for children to participate in physical activities.
Huang Haiyan, dean of the School of Management at Beijing Sport University, noted that the code upgrades the regulatory framework and is a necessary step toward higher-quality development of the industry.
The code should serve as a basis for further clarifying the respective oversight responsibilities of education, market regulation and public security authorities, helping improve the overall governance of the industry, Huang said.
SAFER CHILDREN'S PRODUCTS, TOYS
A new mandatory national standard on the general safety of children's products establishes baseline requirements for products used, worn or played with by children under 14, covering product categories that previously lacked mandatory safety standards.
The standard covers risks such as sharp edges, detachable small parts that could cause choking, and cords that could pose strangulation hazards. It also sets limits on potentially harmful chemicals, including heavy metals and formaldehyde.
Meanwhile, revised mandatory toy safety standards expand controls on hazardous substances and strengthen requirements concerning physical safety and fire risks.
The revisions pay particular attention to products that have drawn public concern, including popular novelty toys such as squishy toys and slime. They introduce additional limits on substances such as formaldehyde, plasticizers and boron, helping reduce the risk of harmful chemical exposure.
Together, the new requirements are the country's latest move to fill the safety gaps for certain products used in children's everyday lives, making safety standards more comprehensive as the range of children's goods continues to expand. ■

Roundup: Another wave of protests sweeps Europe over various grievances
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:41:38 CST
13:41:38 KST

MADRID, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Another wave of protests swept across major European cities on Saturday, with demonstrators voicing grievances over issues ranging from living conditions to disputes involving public institutions. Meanwhile, calls for gatherings on social media prompted police to step up security in several cities.
Public services, the cost of living and housing affordability remained key concerns in many of the protests. In France, around 320,000 people took part in a new round of protests on Saturday, including about 70,000 in Paris, according to Interior Ministry figures. Organizers put the nationwide turnout at nearly 500,000, including 200,000 in the capital.
Around 70,000 police officers and gendarmes were deployed nationwide. Most marches passed off peacefully, although clashes with police and other disturbances were reported in several cities. French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters that, according to a preliminary tally, 422 people had been arrested nationwide.
In Germany, demonstrations took place in more than 30 cities on Saturday. Protesters called for greater investment in public services, measures to address the rising cost of living, and opposed compulsory military service. By late afternoon, organizers reported more than 68,000 participants, based on figures from 12 cities.
As in France, the demonstrations in Germany were largely peaceful, but clashes broke out in several cities in the evening. German news agency dpa reported that police officers were injured in Frankfurt, barricades were set ablaze in Hamburg, and officers came under attack in Bremen.
In Italy, protesters remained camped near Rome's Colosseum on Saturday following nationwide demonstrations over living costs and public services. Workers and other groups had joined rallies in more than 60 cities on Friday during a general strike called by Unione Sindacale di Base (USB), Italian news agency ANSA reported. The union estimated 1.5 million people took part, while the Interior Ministry put the figure at about 255,000.
In Portugal, housing protests drew more than 1,000 people each in Lisbon and Porto on Saturday. In Lisbon, demonstrators marched toward Rossio Square, where they planned to camp overnight. Police had dispersed protest encampments in both cities on Oct. 25.
Political grievances also dominated protests in various countries. In Albania, protests demanding better education, improved living conditions and Prime Minister Edi Rama's resignation continued for a 19th consecutive day in Tirana on Saturday, according to the Albanian Telegraphic Agency. Some protesters threw stones and Molotov cocktails at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons. The opposition Democratic Party backed the movement.
In Poland, an escalating dispute over the composition and leadership of the Constitutional Tribunal brought demonstrators onto the streets of Warsaw. Protestors gathered outside Warsaw's Constitutional Tribunal from Friday evening into Saturday, with police reporting four detained during overnight operations around the building, local media reported. Polish President Karol Nawrocki returned early from a foreign trip and announced urgent political consultations.
Elsewhere, social media calls for gatherings prompted heightened security measures. In the Netherlands, police dispersed a crowd near The Hague Central Station on Saturday afternoon and urged the public to avoid the city center. Local police reported 34 arrests during the day.
The gathering followed online calls for demonstrations in several Dutch cities, some of which encouraged looting and vandalism. Some businesses boarded up their storefronts ahead of the planned gatherings.
In Spain, police stepped up security in cities including Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia on Saturday following online calls for gatherings, local media reported.
The deployments aimed to prevent a repeat of the previous weekend's unrest in Barcelona, which left 15 officers injured and led to 128 arrests. Spanish news agency EFE reported on Friday that police had arrested 10 people nationwide on suspicion of inciting unrest and violence through online channels. ■

NEW DELHI, Nov 1 (Reuters) - Indian security personnel carrying batons and shields and accompanied by riot control vehicles surrounded the site of a planned opposition protest in Delhi on Sunday that is set to demand the resignation of the country’s election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Authorities warned of traffic diversions ahead of the protest march and rally that will be led by Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi. The opposition says it expects hundreds of thousands of people to participate in what it says will be a major challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Opposition parties, student organisations and the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party have held near-daily demonstrations since last month demanding that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar step down over the voter list revision that critics say favour the BJP.
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol, while the BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014. But his government remains stable and the next general election is not due until 2029.
The opposition parties have announced they will hold a nearly 1.5 km (1 mile) march on Sunday from Central Delhi to the Ramlila Maidan, a ground that is the designated site for their protest rally.
Visuals from news agency ANI showed riot control vehicles and dozens of security personnel armed with batons and shields outside the rally venue, where announcements were being made urging people to ensure smooth traffic movement and cooperate with police officials.
Delhi Traffic Police said “a large gathering” was expected at the venue, and traffic regulations and diversions would be implemented “as required”.
“People have started coming to participate in this rally…we have ensured proper arrangements at the venue, and arrangements are also planned on the route of the march that will happen in a few hours from now,” senior police officer Rohit Rajbir told ANI.
The protests demanding Kumar’s resignation erupted after The Indian Express newspaper reported in September that his two deputies had raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures, and digital systems.
The change, which began last year, removed over 130 million names - more than the population of Japan- from voter lists, including 28 million who died, 63 million who relocated, and 30 million who could not be traced.
Opposition parties allege the deletions disproportionately affect Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party — allegations the poll panel and BJP reject.

North Korea tests tactical ballistic missile cluster warhead

13:39:50 KST

Seyit Kurt
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
North Korea conducted a test of a cluster warhead for a tactical ballistic missile to assess its combat applicability and destructive power, state media reported Sunday.
The Missile Administration carried out the test Saturday, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
The test was overseen by Gen. Kim Jong Sik, a member of the Central Military Commission of the ruling Workers' Party of Korea and first deputy director of a department of the party's Central Committee.
North Korea's Ballistic Missile Systems Research Institute and Warhead Research Institute said the test confirmed that the country's "Type-2 standard cluster warhead" could devastate a target area of about 12 to 13 hectares (29 to 32 acres) at what they described as an "ultra-high density."
The head of the Missile Administration said North Korea classifies its cluster warheads into four categories, including special-purpose and standard types.
He said Pyongyang plans to make all four types available to military units by the end of this year, allowing them to select warheads according to operational objectives and the characteristics of targets.
The Missile Administration described the test as part of regular scientific research aimed at increasing the destructive power of its weapons systems.

Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
04:33:36 UTC
13:33:36 KST

Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of Southampton
- Summary:
- A mysterious particle overlooked for decades may hold the key to why matter survived the Big Bang, allowing stars, planets, and life to exist. Scientists believe this forgotten neutrino reshaped the early universe and may have left detectable gravitational wave signals that could help unlock the cosmos’s deepest mysteries.
- Share:
Scientists have proposed a surprising new explanation for why the universe exists, and it centers on a mysterious particle that physicists have largely overlooked for decades. Their theory suggests this forgotten particle may have played a crucial role in shaping the early cosmos and allowing matter to survive after the Big Bang.
The research addresses one of the most fundamental mysteries in physics: why does the universe contain matter instead of nothing at all? Scientists believe matter and antimatter were produced in nearly equal amounts in the early universe. When these opposites encounter one another, they annihilate and release energy. If they had existed in perfectly equal quantities, virtually all matter could have disappeared, leaving no material to form stars, planets, or life.
Now, researchers from the University of Southampton and the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur believe they may have found an important piece of the puzzle. Their explanation involves a little-understood relative of the neutrino, an extremely lightweight particle that rarely interacts with ordinary matter.
A Forgotten Particle With a Powerful Role in the Early Universe
The team focused on a type of particle known as a 'decoupled' heavy neutrino. Unlike ordinary neutrinos, this hypothetical heavier relative has generally been considered too weakly connected to other particles to significantly influence the universe.
However, the researchers found that its unusually long lifetime could have made it far more important than previously thought. According to their calculations, the particle may have survived long enough to temporarily dominate the universe's energy density as the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang.
That brief period of dominance could have altered how the early universe evolved, influencing the conditions that ultimately allowed matter to outnumber antimatter.
Dr. Rishav Roshan of the University of Southampton, an author of the study, explained:
"This decoupled heavy neutrino has long been dismissed as an irrelevant background detail in particle physics.
"However, it decays incredibly slowly. As the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang, the particle lived long enough that it temporarily took over the energy density of the universe and triggered a matter-dominated period."
The findings were published in Physical Review Letters, a scientific journal of the American Physical Society.
How a Heavy Neutrino Could Explain Why Matter Survived
Previous attempts to explain why matter prevailed over antimatter generally left out the decoupled heavy neutrino. Because it interacts so weakly with other particles, scientists assumed it would have little influence on the processes responsible for creating the imbalance.
The new research challenges that assumption. The team found that even a particle with extremely weak interactions could indirectly affect the conditions under which matter gained its crucial advantage.
This imbalance, known as matter and antimatter asymmetry, is essential to understanding our existence. For reasons physicists are still trying to explain, the early universe ended up with slightly more matter than antimatter. That small difference allowed some matter to remain after most particles and their antiparticles annihilated one another.
"The fact that we are here at all proves that an asymmetry between matter and antimatter occurred," added Dr. Roshan.
"The decoupled neutrino shifted the temperature in the early universe at which fundamental particles - like electrons and other leptons - interacted with their anti-particles with the help of Standard Model Higgs boson.
"This temperature acts like a switch that shapes how the matter-antimatter imbalance was built up."
The Higgs boson is a fundamental particle associated with the mechanism that gives many elementary particles their mass. In the researchers' proposed scenario, the heavy neutrino changed the temperature conditions governing important particle interactions involving the Higgs boson.
By shifting when these interactions occurred, the particle could have influenced how the imbalance between matter and antimatter developed. In other words, something long considered insignificant may have helped determine why the universe contains matter at all.
Ancient Gravitational Waves Could Reveal the Answer
The theory could also have important implications for understanding how the universe expanded in its earliest stages.
Study co-author Dr. Sudipta Show of the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur said the findings suggest that the forgotten particle may have dramatically altered the expansion history of the young cosmos.
He added: "It offers us a new explanation for how matter won.
"The dramatic shift in the early expansion of the cosmos leaves distinct but detectable imprints of changes, for example on primordial gravitational waves.
"These gravitational wave signatures open up new avenues for us to unravel the evolution of the early universe after the Big Bang."
Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of space and time. Scientists believe processes in the extremely early universe may have generated primordial gravitational waves that carry information about conditions from that distant era.
According to the new theory, the temporary dominance of the heavy neutrino could have left recognizable signatures in those ancient signals. Detecting such patterns could eventually provide a way to investigate whether the proposed particle really influenced the universe's earliest evolution.
For now, the explanation remains theoretical. But it offers physicists a new possibility for solving one of cosmology's deepest mysteries: how matter survived when its encounter with antimatter could have left the universe almost entirely empty.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Southampton. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Rishav Roshan, Sudipta Show. Delayed Charged Lepton Yukawa Equilibration in Minimal Seesaw. Physical Review Letters, 2026; 137 (11) DOI: 10.1103/nfkx-q6z7

‘People are dying in so many ways’: Tent fire kills 2 infant girls in Gaza

Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01

Ramzi Mahmud and Tarek Chouiref
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
Habiba was due for her two-month vaccinations on Saturday. Instead, her family mourned her death alongside that of seven-month-old Aseel after a fire tore through the tent where their relatives had gathered in the southern Gaza Strip.
The family’s visit in al-Mawasi, west of Khan Younis, ended in a desperate attempt to save the two infants when flames broke out Friday afternoon.
Both suffered severe burns and were admitted to intensive care. They died Saturday morning.
Nasser Medical Complex identified them as Habiba Mohammed Zanoun, two months old, and Aseel Abu Suhayban, seven months old.
Sources told Anadolu that the fire started while food was being cooked inside the tent. Severe shortages of cooking gas and basic supplies under Israel’s blockade have forced displaced families to prepare meals over open flames, they said.
'Why is all this happening to us?'
The girls’ grandmother, who did not give her name, told Anadolu that her daughter had come to visit the family at their tent when the fire suddenly broke out.
Habiba was her daughter’s baby, she said. The infant died on the day she was supposed to receive her two-month vaccinations.
Aseel’s mother rushed to rescue her daughter and suffered burns. She, too, was taken to hospital.
The grandmother said neither infant could withstand the severity of her injuries.
“Why is all this happening to us?” she asked. “Every day there are accidents, bombings and fires, and people are dying in so many ways.”
“For three years, we have been living like this, amid displacement, anguish and pain.”
Cooking without safe alternatives
The blaze was one of three fires reported Friday in displacement tents in central and southern Gaza, according to sources.
With cooking gas scarce, families have resorted to makeshift fires to prepare food. Inside crowded shelters built from flammable materials, an everyday necessity can put lives at risk.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned in June that cooking inside displacement tents was a leading cause of fires.
Blankets, old fabric, cardboard and plastic sheeting used to reinforce shelters allow flames to spread rapidly and make fires harder to control, it said.
Fire is one of several dangers facing families in deteriorating tents that offer little protection from the weather.
OCHA also reported that Israeli authorities denied entry on Aug. 26 and Sept. 2 to a previously approved shipment through the Egyptian corridor containing 36,960 pieces of timber and 660 emergency shelter kits.
The Gaza Government Media Office previously reported that more than 800,000 displaced Palestinians were living in tents unfit for human habitation. It estimated that 162,000 of Gaza’s 270,000 displacement tents needed immediate replacement.
The grandmother, mourning the loss of two grandchildren, appealed to the world to pay attention to Gaza’s displaced families and help end their suffering.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk sought to offer assurances that the country's Constitutional Tribunal will operate in accordance with the law, after President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of the previous hard-right government, accused him of staging a forced takeover of the court.
Late on Friday, the Constitutional Tribunal said its longest-serving judge, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, had suspended Bogdan Swieczkowski, the tribunal's president and an appointee of Tusk's nationalist predecessor, and was now in charge of the court.
The move escalated a battle between Nawrocki and Tusk's pro-European government over control of the judiciary.
"I am certain that the Constitutional Tribunal will function as it should. Also, independently of me and in line with the constitution," Tusk said in a televised speech.
"The task of the executive branch, and therefore mine, is to ensure its safety and working conditions, and I intend to fulfill my duty."
Nawrocki calls off flight mid-air
In a dramatic move, Nawrocki turned back his plane, which he was heading to Senegal on, late on Friday and headed for the court headquarters in central Warsaw, following Swieczkowski's suspension.
Riot police have been guarding the court since Friday afternoon, with several hundred protesters gathered to demand Swieczkowski's reinstatement.
"Tonight, there was a breach of public order in the Republic of Poland and a forcible takeover of a constitutional body," Nawrocki said in a statement read by an aide outside the court early on Saturday.
Nawrocki held political consultations throughout Saturday.
Tusk, writing on X, said his government was seeking to restore the rule of law, which the European Union had accused his predecessors - the Law and Justice Party - of subverting.
"This process is difficult, at times even painful, and requires decisive action. There is no other way," he said.
Long-running political dispute
A long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralyzed the institution, with the pro-European government and the nationalist president refusing to recognize appointees put forward by the other side.
The dispute dates back to 2015, when Law and Justice sought to appoint judges to seats already filled by the previous government.
Its nominees gained a majority on the Constitutional Tribunal, while critics at home and abroad said the court no longer met the standards of an independent and impartial tribunal established by law.
After Tusk's coalition took office in 2023, it pledged to restore the rule of law and reform the court, but Law and Justice ally Nawrocki has acted to thwart those efforts since his election as president in 2025.
Earlier this year, Nawrocki refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, while Swieczkowski, a former deputy justice minister in the Law and Justice administration, declined to seat judges elected by the current parliamentary majority.
Last month, parliament appointed Tusk ally Maciej Berek to the tribunal, which critics said undermined the government's stated goal of restoring checks and balances.

The strong showing of the Arab parties in last week’s election was one of the only bright lights to emerge from the frustrating stalemate that the results produced.

There are only slim options available to break the deadlock and prevent another round of elections – a minority opposition government or a centrist unity government.
Arab parties can not be lumped together as monolith
The movement calling for the opposition parties to push for a minority government with its 48 seats, propped up from the outside by the Arab parties’ 19 seats, is highly problematic. What that push doesn’t acknowledge is that just like all the Jewish parties can’t be lumped together, neither can the Arab ones.
Ra’am, which was already part of a government coalition in 2021 and features a Jewish member, Yoav Segalovitz, in its second slot, argues that Arab citizens can use political participation and coalition negotiations to improve their communities and combat the horrific crime level.
The Joint List – consisting of Balad, Ta’al and Hadash – includes anti-Israel extremists, with the parties themselves focused on Palestinian nationalism and calling for a democratic bi-national state to replace Israel. They should never be part of an Israeli government, on the inside or from the outside.
Even if Golan could convince Eisenkot and, somehow, B’Yahad’s Naftali Bennet and Yisrael Beiteinu’s Avigdor Liberman – who have adamantly stated they would not form a coalition with the Arab parties – to agree to bringing in Ra’am, it would only raise the numbers to 56: clearly a non-starter.
Ra’am’s time may come, but in the current constellation, there’s not a place for that party in the government.
That leaves the specter of a unity government. Intense pressure is going to be placed on Netanyahu, Eisenkot, and B’Yahad’s Bennett and Yair Lapid (with 12 seats) to join forces and form a coalition that can agree on most issues.
It would be a bitter pill to swallow for all involved, albeit one that the country desperately needs to prevent another election.
They would be supported from the outside by Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beteinu (with seven seats), creating a stable 67-seat coalition.
There are plenty of obstacles. Netanyahu may think that another election round would tip in his favor, with a smaller turnout and fewer expatriate votes.
Unity government would force Netanyahu to sever alliances with haredi, far-right parties
A unity government would also mean that Netanyahu would have to sever his alliances with the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties and with the far-right parties of Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, whom he last week pledged to keep in a future coalition. He would also have to accept the formation of a state commission of inquiry into October 7.
For their part, Eisenkot and Bennett would have to break campaign promises not to sit with Netanyahu and, for the good of the country, concede that unity is the only way to move forward. Their natural distrust of Netanyahu is warranted, but an arrangement could be worked out that plays to all of the members’ strengths.
Netanyahu, as prime minister, could continue to focus on Israel’s security and the threats emanating from Iran, Hamas, and Hezbollah, and be in charge of foreign policy. There’s not much daylight between any of the parties in regard to that.
Eisenkot and Bennett, in turn, would receive the other vital ministries – Justice, Education, Interior, Internal Security – and begin restoring order to the chaos swirling in the country.
Now is the time for fresh thinking and bold moves. The voters have spoken and given Netanyahu, Eisenkot, and Bennett 60 seats. For the greater good, these leaders must put personalities and egos aside to lead the country into a stable future.

Bolivia declares state of emergency over El Nino weather pattern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
04:04:40 UTC
13:04:40 KST

Bolivia declares state of emergency over El Nino weather pattern
Drought is affecting 78,000 families, and has led to the loss of more than 75,000 cattle, as El Nino is due to peak in late 2026.
Bolivia has declared a nationwide state of emergency to free up resources to deal with the effects of the El Nino weather phenomenon.
Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz signed the decree on Saturday, which also called for further deployments of rescue teams in areas of the country hard hit by flooding and drought.
El Nino will have “very severe impacts in terms of drought and floods”, Paz said, adding that Bolivia needs “the cooperation of all institutions”.
Drought is now affecting 78,000 families in six of Bolivia’s nine departments and has led to the loss of more than 75,000 cattle, according to a government report this week.
Bolivia is also prone to flooding. In December 2025, floods in the Santa Cruz region killed dozens of people.
Neighbouring Chile’s capital, Santiago, recorded the rainiest October ever, while wildfires in Peru killed at least 12 people last month.
El Nino, a global climate phenomenon that occurs roughly every two to seven years, is part of the planet’s natural weather cycle.
During this climate event, warming in the Pacific Ocean brings worldwide changes in winds, pressure, and rainfall patterns, often causing extreme weather.
El Nino’s intensity varies, and its impact changes based on geographic location, but this cycle could be the strongest in recorded history. It is due to peak at the end of 2026, but its impacts could continue well into 2027.
Scientists predict El Nino could cause more than 450,000 deaths globally, with the poorest countries worst impacted.
In early September, the World Meteorological Organization reported a nearly 100 percent likelihood that El Nino will continue through February 2027.

Guangzhou reclaims crown as China’s busiest airport after US$8 billion mega expansion
A new terminal, runway and links with major international trading partners have helped it overtake Shanghai in passenger numbers
Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport has reclaimed its position as China’s busiest airport, handling more than 67 million passenger trips in the first nine months of 2026 following a major expansion last year, the municipal government announced.
The airport overtook Shanghai Pudong International Airport, which handled 66.58 million passenger trips during the same period, official data showed. Baiyun had fallen behind Pudong in 2024 and 2025.
The expansion took half a decade to complete and includes a new third terminal and fifth runway. It cost 53.77 billion yuan (US$8.1 billion) and broke long-standing bottlenecks by increasing Baiyun’s annual passenger capacity to 120 million, the municipal government said on its official WeChat account. Authorities projected it would handle 90 million passenger trips this year.

AI-designed virus given to a human patient for the first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

AI-designed virus given to a human patient for the first time
The viruses, known as bacteriophages, infect and kill bacteria. Unlike antibiotics, they can target specific bacteria while leaving beneficial bacteria largely untouched.
The treatment was developed by Radical Numerics, a company that uses AI to study and design biological systems. Its AI model, Omnii-1, helped create virus variants selected to target the bacteria causing the patient's infection.
Laboratory tests showed that a mixture of the AI-designed viruses eliminated the patient's bacteria. Doctors then administered the experimental treatment under a special permission process for patients with serious conditions who have no satisfactory treatment alternatives.
The company has not disclosed the patient's condition after treatment or other clinical details to protect their privacy. It also stressed that the treatment has not been approved for wider medical use and that one patient's case cannot establish its safety or effectiveness.
The approach could offer another option for patients whose infections no longer respond to antibiotics. However, researchers must still develop reliable ways to design and test treatments for individual infections before the method can become more widely available.

HANOI, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Vietnam has reduced the special consumption tax on all types of gasoline to zero percent from Sunday through March 31, 2027, under a new government resolution issued on Saturday, local daily VnExpress reported.
Under the special consumption tax law, which took effect on July 1 this year, the tax rates are set at 10 percent for regular gasoline, 8 percent for E5 biofuel and 7 percent for E10 biofuel.
The tax was previously reduced to zero percent from late March to June 2026 to help stabilize the domestic market.
Meanwhile, the environmental protection tax on gasoline and oil products remains at zero Vietnamese dong per liter.
These products are also exempt from value-added tax declaration and payment under a policy extended through the end of 2026, the report said. ■

3 Hong Kong Chinese-language newspapers raise retail prices by HK$3
Ming Pao, Hong Kong Economic Times and Hong Kong Economic Journal adjust prices by 20 to 25 per cent
1-MIN READ1-MIN
1
 Listen
Three Chinese-language newspapers in Hong Kong have raised their retail prices by HK$3 (40 US cents) this month, marking the first sector-wide adjustment in two years.
Ming Pao’s increase took effect on Sunday, raising its single-copy price from HK$12 to HK$15, up 25 per cent.
Two financial broadsheets will follow suit on Monday. The Hong Kong Economic Times (HKET) will raise its price from HK$12 to HK$15, while the Hong Kong Economic Journal (HKEJ) will increase its price by 20 per cent from HK$15 to HK$18.

Ukrainian evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky reunite with family
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
03:37:23 UTC
12:37:23 KST

Ukrainian evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky reunite with family
Starved and exhausted residents of Oleshky arrive in Ukraine after months of isolation, but some stay behind.
Starved and exhausted residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky have crossed into Ukraine in a major evacuation operation of civilians, under the first humanitarian truce of its kind in more than four years of Moscow’s war.
The six-day ceasefire covering the town was reached with mediation efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump and help from Pope Leo XIV. It is the longest local pause in fighting since Russia’s full-scale invasion of its neighbour in 2022.
“Ukrainian citizens from Oleshky have crossed the Ukrainian border in the Chernihiv region. All of them will receive the assistance they need,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X, thanking the United States and the first lady for mediating.
“Further steps toward de-escalation and real progress toward peace are also needed,” he added.
Evacuees wrapped in blue and yellow Ukrainian flags stepped off buses at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border and reunited with family members.
Ukrainian officials met the evacuees with posters reading “You’re not alone” and “We embrace with our hearts”, while residents from nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and flashlights to greet them.
Forced to eat grass
Supply routes to Oleshky had been disrupted by fighting and drones. According to some residents, food deliveries were stopped in May, pushing hundreds of people into starvation.
One evacuee, an elderly man in a wheelchair, told the Reuters news agency that he had lost 20kg (44lbs) over the past year, becoming so weak he required hospital treatment.
Another evacuee, Svitlana Yermakova, told Reuters they had to eat grass to survive.
“We chopped grass and squash… just to hold on,” she said, adding that she risked riding by bicycle through minefields to a nearby village to get food for herself and her dog.
To reach Ukrainian-held territory, Oleshky residents had to take a complicated route to leave the devastated town just a few kilometres from the front line.
They first crossed Crimea by bus to the Russian town of Anapa before flying to Belarus, from where they crossed into Ukraine.
Ambulances lined the street, and several large military tents were erected, where hot meals, tea and medical aid were provided.
Russian and Ukrainian officials say the ceasefire in Oleshky has held since Tuesday, allowing them to de-mine the roads and bring food, medicines and other supplies into the town again.
The truce is due to end on Sunday evening.
Some stay behind
Some residents have decided to remain in Oleshky, despite the ongoing lack of gas, electricity and running water.
Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said living conditions in the occupied Oleshky remained difficult, pledging she would continue to work with her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmytro Lubinets, to help those who stayed.
“The mission has come to an end,” she said on Telegram. “We have agreed to carry out regular humanitarian missions, which is a very important step.”
Oleshky had a pre-war population of about 24,000, which plunged to an estimated 1,700 before the evacuation.
Ukrainian officials have not said exactly how many residents were evacuated or how many remained.
Despite the ceasefire in Oleshky, fighting rages on in other parts of the front, with Russia and Ukraine keeping up drone attacks against each other.

Kiwis to be without Mulitalo after nasty high tackle
— reporting by AAP
New Zealand have been dealt a blow ahead of their do-or-die Rugby League World Cup semifinal, with Ronaldo Mulitalo handed a one-game ban.
The Kiwis' 78-0 thumping of Fiji on Saturday on the Gold Coast came at a cost, with the star winger sent off for a shoulder charge on Ronald Philitoga in the 52nd minute.
It led to a melee between Fiji and New Zealand players, which culminated in halfback Brandon Wakeham punching Mulitalo in the head. The action earned the Fijian his marching orders as well.
On Sunday, the judiciary deemed Mulitalo's tackle careless and charged him with a grade-two offence.
But much to his relief he was only given a one-game suspension if he takes an early plea, meaning the winger would be eligible to return for the grand final if New Zealand win their semi next Saturday in Newcastle.
Multialo's ban will hurt the Kiwis, because he has scored three tries and been typically busy under the high ball.
New Zealand face a challenge to qualify for the final, playing either Samoa or Tonga.
Wakeham also avoided a heavy ban, handed a one-game suspension, although that won't matter because Fiji have been eliminated from the global showpiece.

Key Event
REPORT: Jillaroos thrash Wales in record-breaking World Cup win
— reporting by AAP
Australia have broken the record for the biggest victory in women's rugby league by scoring 21 tries in a 124-6 thumping of Wales.
Both Jess Sergis and Jaime Chapman, who scored a double-hat-trick at Western Sydney Stadium on Sunday, recorded more running metres than the entire Welsh side.
Winger Chapman's six-try haul equalled the record for most tries in a game for the Jillaroos, who will face Fiji in a semifinal next Sunday at the Sydney Football Stadium.
The one-sided result surpassed France's 116-0 win over Serbia in 2023 as the heaviest victory in the history of the international women's game.
Australian five-eighth Jesse Southwell was almost perfect on the kicking tee, slotting 20 conversions from 21 attempts.
Coupled with a try, the five-eighth's 44 individual points are a new Jillaroos record.
A clunky opening for the Aussies was put to bed when Olivia Kernick crossed for the first points of the afternoon before Chapman burned Wales on the outside for the next two tries — all three scored without Wales touching the ball.
The Welsh did not have another possession for the entire first half as Australia cruised to a 60-0 half-time lead.
Whilst suffering a historic defeat, the Welsh also put on the first points scored against the Jillaroos all tournament.
Wales got themselves on the board in the 59th minute when Tayla Preston grubbered through to Paige Travis for a much-celebrated try.
Sergis had four tries, while Keilee Joseph, Abbi Church and Tamika Upton crossed for doubles.
Kernick, Southwell, Kezie Apps, Sariah Paki, and Keeley Nizza had a try each.
Ruthless Jillaroos dissect dismantling
Jillaroos coach Jess Skinner and captain Isabelle Kelly have spoken to the media after their thumping win over Wales.
Skinner said despite the lopsided nature of the Jillaroos' pool games, there are positive signs for the future of the game.
"I love women's international rugby league, and I think our Pasifika crew are really building nicely to that.
It would be really great to get some investment there in the Northern Hemisphere.
We know what it took Wales to get here and the work that they've done. Our jersey was there not too long ago as well.
So a way that we did that was our [Pacific Championships] concept. We built NRLW as well. That was probably the biggest one for us.
So it'd be really good to see even the Super League to get a little bit more investment and stronger support over there. And I think that'll help that region a lot.
And not taking anything away. This is a World Cup, and Wales has done the work to be here. They've qualified to be here unfortunate result for them today. But we're playing every game to to put our best foot forward to win this thing."
Kelly had similar sentiments.
"I've been really impressed with Samoa this year. I think what they're doing and girls going back and pledging their allegiance to their nations has been incredible.
I think they're leading that, and I think how well they're doing is only going to inspire other girls to do so.
We don't go out there and say that we want to put a certain amount of points on team.
We go out there to be competitive and play the best footy that we can. So I think it's going to take time, but it's definitely starting to happen now."
Key Event
The records which the Jillaroos set today
Highest score in an international match men or women: 124
- The previous high score was a men's Test in 2003, when France defeated Serbia 120-0.
Highest score in a Rugby League World Cup match men or women:124
Previous records were:
- Men's: Australia 110-4 Russia in 2000
- Women's: Australia 92-0 France in 2022, and New Zealand 92-0 France 2026
Largest margin in a women's international: 118
- The previous record was France's 116-0 win over Serbia in 2023
Most tries scored in a women's international: 21
- The previous record was 20 during France's 116-0 win over Serbia in 2023
Most goals kicked in a women's international: 20
- The previous record was 18 during France's 116-0 win over Serbia in 2023
Most individual goals kicked in rugby league international men or women: 20 (Jesse Southwell)
- The previous record was 18 by Ryan Girdler during Australia's 110-4 win over Russia in 2000
Most individual tries in a women's international: 6 (Jamie Chapman)
- Equals the record with Fuarosa Time (New Zealand, 2003), Honey Hireme (New Zealand, 2017), and Julia Robinson (Australia, 2024)

What is celebrated on November 1 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:32:29 EET
12:32:29 KST

What is celebrated on November 1 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On November 1, Ukraine celebrates Social Services Worker’s Day. Around the world, Vegan Day, Eco-Labeling Day, and Ballet Day are observed.
On November 1, Ukraine celebrates Social Worker’s Day, while around the world, under the auspices of international organizations, World Vegan Day, World Ecolabel Day, and World Ballet Day are observed. In the church calendar, according to the new style, Saints Cosmas and Damian of Asia, the Unmercenary Physicians and Wonderworkers, are commemorated, while according to the old style, Saint Joel the Prophet and Saint John of Rila are remembered, UNN reports.
World Vegan Day
A global environmental observance established in 1994 by Louise Wallis, head of The Vegan Society, to mark the 50th anniversary of the organization’s founding in the United Kingdom and the introduction of the term "vegan".
The event opens International Vegan Month and aims to promote a plant-based lifestyle, highlight issues of ethical treatment of animals, minimize the negative impact of livestock farming on climate change, and promote the health benefits of a complete plant-based diet.
World Ecolabel Day
An international environmental observance established by the Global Ecolabelling Network.
The day is intended to raise consumer and business awareness of the importance of ecolabelling, which confirms the environmental safety of products throughout their entire life cycle - from the extraction of raw materials to disposal. The event encourages responsible consumption and the production of goods that do not harm the environment.
World Ballet Day
A global arts celebration established at the initiative of leading opera and ballet theaters around the world, including the Royal Ballet in London.
On this day, leading ballet companies around the world hold hours-long live broadcasts, showing viewers the process of morning barre training, rehearsals for premiere performances, backstage life, and master classes by renowned choreographers, thereby popularizing classical and contemporary ballet.
Social Worker’s Day in Ukraine
An official professional holiday established by a Decree of the President of Ukraine in 1999, observed annually on the first Sunday of November.
The event honors the dedicated work of specialists in social protection authorities, pension services, employment centers, and social services, who provide daily support to low-income groups, people with disabilities, veterans, pensioners, and internally displaced persons.
All Saints' Day
A major holiday in the Western Christian calendar that is an official public holiday in many countries of Europe and Latin America.
Established in the eighth century by Pope Gregory III, the holiday is dedicated to commemorating all canonized saints, as well as martyrs and righteous people whose names have remained unknown to the general public.
Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate Saints Cosmas and Damian of Asia, the Unmercenary Physicians and Wonderworkers, and their mother, Saint Theodota. The physician brothers studied the art of medicine and received from God the gracious gift of healing spiritual and bodily ailments through prayer.
They accepted no payment from the sick for their work, following Christ’s command, which is why they were called the Unmercenary Physicians.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate Saint Joel the Prophet - one of the 12 Minor Prophets of the Old Testament, who foretold the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles.
They also remember Saint Martyr Huar and Saint John of Rila - a prominent Bulgarian ascetic and founder of the renowned Rila Monastery.

Hezbollah is not likely to join in if the United States and Iran renew military operations against each other unless Iran’s leadership faces an existential threat, according to a Saturday report from United Arab Emirates state-owned news outlet, The National.
Hezbollah would, according to a senior Lebanese official, join the fight despite its weakened military capacity if the Iranian regime's survival was found to be at stake.
The official said that an explicit red line was crossed in the previous bout, when the Khamenei was killed in a joint US-Israeli strike on February 28.
“We knew earlier this year, when the war in the region first broke out, that Hezbollah would join the fighting if [late Iranian supreme leader Ayatollah Ali] Khamenei were killed,” said the anonymous official. “We even informed the Americans about it.”
KAN news reported last month that Hezbollah terror operatives have maintained their presence in southern Lebanon's pilot zones, gathering intelligence and recuperating their fighting ability.
Hezbollah rearming with Iranian funds
Hezbollah has spent at least three months preparing for a resumption of hostilities with Israel, after receiving an infusion of cash from Iran, according to Lebanese security personnel briefed on its activities.
The terror organization remains committed to attacking Israel and has used a lull in hostilities since June to rearm, with a focus on procuring explosives and producing drones that can be flown into the security zone, two Lebanese security sources told Reuters.
One of the sources, and another close to Hezbollah, said the group had received tens of millions of dollars from Iran to help boost its military capabilities. That is in addition to around $200 million that the terror group previously received from Tehran, which Reuters reported earlier this month.
The group has been restoring command-and-control structures that broke down in key battles, according to one of those sources and three other security officials familiar with the group's operations.
In response to questions from Reuters, Hezbollah's media office rejected the suggestion that its command-and-control systems had broken down.
A US State Department spokesman said Washington would keep strangling Hezbollah's finances through sanctions and other measures. A US Treasury spokesperson said Iran was running out of money and ways to move money.
Trump pulling for Lebanese peace, Israeli withdrawal
US President Donald Trump pledged to secure a full Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon if Beirut agrees to join the Abraham Accords, a senior Gulf diplomatic source told the Lebanese newspaper Ad-Diyar.
The claim was published in an article by Lebanese journalist Nour Naameh amid ongoing diplomatic efforts and concerns in Lebanon over the potential consequences of another military confrontation between the US and Iran.
According to the report, the source described the American promises as official commitments. However, the newspaper provided no documents supporting the claims, did not identify the diplomat or the country he represents, and offered no confirmation from the White House.
The report also did not specify when the commitments were made, who they were communicated to, or whether a timetable had been set for their implementation.
Senior Israeli officials responded to the report by insisting that Israel would not withdraw its forces before Hezbollah was disarmed.
Anna Barsky and Reuters contributed to this report.

Binance’s US$6b crypto heist: Five things to know about North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
03:23:00 UTC
12:23:00 KST

Binance’s US$6b crypto heist: Five things to know about North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers
- North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers are blamed for a record US$6 billion Binance crypto theft. US authorities say the group is linked to Lazarus and Pyongyang’s cyber warfare programme.
- TraderTraitor uses fake job offers and malware to steal data and digital assets. The FBI says hackers have also hit DMM Bitcoin, Atomic Wallet, Alphapo, CoinsPaid and Bybit.
- Stolen crypto is laundered through mixing services and private exchanges, then used for weapons research and procurement. Analysts say cybercrime gives North Korea fast money despite sanctions.
AI generated
SEOUL – North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking group has been blamed by US authorities for stealing more than US$6 billion (S$7.7 billion) in virtual assets from Binance, in what is believed to be the largest crypto heist in history.
The Oct 29 attack is the latest in a string of high-profile cyberthefts linked to Pyongyang, which has built a formidable hacking operation, generating funds believed to help finance its weapons programme.
Here are five things to know about the group and its place in North Korea’s cyber warfare programme:
Who are they?
TraderTraitor is the name given to a North Korean hacking operation linked to the broader Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it hacked Sony Pictures in retaliation for The Interview, a satirical film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Pyongyang has invested heavily in developing its cyber capabilities since at least the mid-1990s, building a force that South Korean intelligence estimated in 2024 comprised around 8,400 personnel.
“North Korea has built a capable cyber force, funnelling many of the country’s top students into computer science and IT training,” the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on its website.
Much of the hacking activity is known to have been directed by Pyongyang’s Reconnaissance General Bureau, its primary foreign intelligence agency.
“The top two students in my class were recruited to the hacking unit,” South Korean MP Park Choong-kwon, who studied at the North’s elite National Defense University before his defection, told AFP in a 2024 interview.
How do they operate?
TraderTraitor actors have been known to pose as recruiters offering lucrative jobs to trick victims into downloading malicious software.
The malware can allow hackers to infiltrate victims’ computer systems and steal sensitive information and digital assets.
In a 2024 heist involving the theft of US$308 million from Japanese cryptocurrency exchange DMM Bitcoin, a North Korean hacker posing as a recruiter on LinkedIn contacted an employee of a separate virtual currency wallet software company.
They sent the employee what appeared to be a pre-employment test, which actually contained a malicious line of code.
That allowed the hacker to compromise their system and impersonate the employee, the FBI said.
What have North Korean hackers done?
High-profile cyberattacks attributed to North Korean hackers include the theft of US$81 million from Bangladesh’s central bank in 2016 and the WannaCry ransomware attack that disrupted computers worldwide in 2017.
In 2022, US authorities blamed Lazarus-linked hackers for stealing around US$620 million from the Ronin blockchain network.
The FBI subsequently attributed three more cryptocurrency heists in 2023 to TraderTraitor actors, involving the theft of nearly US$200 million from Atomic Wallet, AlphaPo and Coinspaid.
The scale of the thefts increased dramatically in February 2025, when the FBI blamed TraderTraitor for stealing around US$1.5 billion in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit.
“TraderTraitor actors are proceeding rapidly and have converted some of the stolen assets,” the FBI said at the time.
How does North Korea use stolen funds?
The North Korean regime launders stolen cryptocurrency and converts it into cash “through mixing services or private exchanges”, Lim Eul-chul, a professor at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University, told AFP.
“The proceeds are then channelled directly into military research, the illicit procurement of weapons components and the defence industry,” he added.
A 2024 United Nations report said proceeds from North Korean cyberattacks “reportedly helped to fund the country’s development of weapons of mass destruction”.
Why cybercrime?
Analysts say Pyongyang’s illicit cyber activity is driven by its ability to obtain vast sums of money quickly and at “minimal cost”.
“While international sanctions severely restrict North Korea’s ability to earn foreign currency through conventional trade, cyber theft allows it to acquire billions of dollars with minimal personnel and resources,” said Lim.
“Hacking offers Pyongyang a way to obtain funds outside conventional banking channels, taking advantage of the pseudonymous and borderless nature of digital assets to bypass financial restrictions,” he added. AFP

AI generated
LA PAZ – Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz declared a state of emergency on Oct 31 to free up resources for dealing with the impact of the El Nino weather phenomenon, wreaking havoc around the world.
The decree calls for deploying more rescue teams in hard-hit areas as Bolivia grapples with both flooding and drought because of El Nino, Paz said in an address to the nation.
“This phenomenon will have very severe impacts in terms of drought and floods, and we need the cooperation of all institutions,” he said.
Drought is affecting 78,000 families in six of the country’s nine departments and has led to the loss of more than 75,000 head of cattle, according to a government report this week.
El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
The United Nations warned this week that the El Nino could have “unprecedented” strength that would bring havoc to Latin America, eastern and southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific.
Among Bolivia’s neighbours, Peru has seen increased temperatures and wildfires, which have already claimed the lives of at least 12 people.
Chile has experienced the rainiest October ever recorded in Santiago, the capital. AFP

Nauru became the 194th country with which Kazakhstan has established diplomatic ties.
Thus, Kazakhstan has completed the process of establishing diplomatic relations with all United Nations member states, including Nauru, as well as the two Observer States at the Organization. This marks an important milestone in the history of Kazakhstan’s diplomacy.
The signing of the document laid the foundation for the development of bilateral cooperation based on the principles of the UN Charter and international law, including mutual respect for national sovereignty and territorial integrity, equality of States, and non-interference in each other’s internal affairs.

Particular attention was paid to strengthening cooperation within the United Nations and other multilateral forums. The two sides emphasized the importance of maintaining regular dialogue on current issues on the international agenda and developing partnerships between Kazakhstan and countries of the Pacific region.
